title: 7  Sector Overview
text:
7.1 How a sector is modelled: the flow model
This part of the documentation sets out how CIMS represents each part of the economy. Every sector is a self-contained sub-model — a flow model of the energy services and products that drive its energy use and emissions — but all of them are built from the same handful of ideas: hierarchical nodes linked by engineering ratios, technologies competing on lifecycle cost at the lowest nodes, and a split between the things a sector produces and the auxiliary services it consumes. The chapters that follow take each sector in turn; this overview sets out the shared structure they rest on, the conventions they have in common, and a map of which sectors are covered and how they relate.
In CIMS, the product and energy-service demands of a sub-sector are linked in a flow model that traces the sequence of activities needed to generate the sector’s output. A CIMS flow model is geared toward representing technology evolution and energy consumption, rather than the monetary flows of an econometric model (where units are typically in dollars) or the literal mechanical detail of the blueprints and process-flow diagrams an engineer would use. Because the emphasis is on energy rather than material flow, each node represents a process stage at which energy consumption can be distinctly estimated. Nodes are arranged hierarchically and linked by engineering ratios — the physical quantity of input each stage requires per unit of its output — and technology competitions take place at the lowest-level nodes in the hierarchy.

title: 7  Sector Overview
text:
7.2 Nodes and competition rules
Each sector sub-model is a hierarchical tree, implemented in the model code as a NetworkX directed tree. Every node carries a competition rule that determines how the demand passed down to it is allocated among its children:

Fixed-ratio nodes split demand among their children in fixed, exogenously specified proportions — the engineering ratios that capture the unavoidable sequence of process steps required to produce the sector’s output.
Tech-compete nodes host a competition among alternative technologies that can provide the same service. Each technology carries a capital cost, a fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, service requests for the energy and upstream services it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised and combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost. Market shares are then assigned by the standard CIMS technology-choice rule of Chapter 4, on the basis of those lifecycle costs and a heterogeneity (variance) parameter that governs how sharply the competition responds to cost differences.

The interplay of these two rules is what gives each sector its shape: a fixed-ratio backbone fixes the process chain, while tech-compete leaves decide which equipment and fuels actually serve each step — and it is at those leaves that policy, whether a carbon price, a regulation, or a subsidy, changes the outcome.

title: 7  Sector Overview
text:
7.3 Product and Service sub-trees
At the top of each sector tree, the nodes are organised into two sub-trees, a Product sub-tree and a Service sub-tree:

The Product sub-tree is the physical production chain: the sequence of process stages that converts raw inputs into the sector’s saleable output — tonnes of steel, square metres of floor space, vehicle-kilometres, and so on. It is driven by the sector’s exogenous output or activity forecast, and its shape is specific to each sector’s process flow.
The Service sub-tree holds the auxiliary energy and utility services that production technologies request rather than producing themselves — for example space heating and cooling, lighting, machine drive, steam and cogeneration, fuel blending, and carbon capture where applicable. Factoring these shared loads into their own sub-tree avoids re-specifying the same equipment inside every process stage, and lets efficiency and fuel-switching measures compete once and serve the whole sector.


7.3.1 Auxiliary services and the MECS structure
For the industrial sectors, the auxiliary services follow the end-use structure of the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey (MECS) — in particular, Machine Drive is disaggregated into compressed air, fans, materials handling, materials processing, and pumps. Each service is represented at a general level, as a competition between existing and more efficient equipment with fuel-switching options where relevant, rather than as a detailed equipment catalogue. The specific set of services varies by sector; the buildings and transportation sectors, for instance, carry their own service definitions, which are described in their respective chapters. The cross-cutting services that many sectors share — machine drive, low-temperature heat and steam, cogeneration, carbon capture, and energy storage — are documented once in the General Services part rather than repeated in every chapter.

title: 7  Sector Overview
text:
7.4 The sectors represented
The sub-models fall into a few natural groups, reflecting how energy and materials move through the economy.
Energy supply and transformation covers the industries that produce and convert the fuels everything else burns: Coal Mining, Natural Gas, Petroleum Crude, and Petroleum Refining on the fossil side; Electricity as the central energy carrier; and the low-carbon fuels Ethanol, Biodiesel, and Hydrogen. Because these sectors supply the fuel blends and electricity that every demand sector draws on, their emissions intensity propagates throughout the model.
Extraction and heavy industry covers the material-producing sectors: Mining, Industrial Minerals (including cement and lime), Chemical Products, Pulp and Paper, Metal Smelting, Iron and Steel, and the catch-all Light Industrial. These carry the richest Product sub-trees and the largest process-heat and process-emission loads, and they are where carbon capture and deep fuel-switching matter most.
Buildings and construction covers the built environment: Construction, the activity of building itself, and the Residential and Commercial sectors, which represent the heating, cooling, lighting, and plug loads of the building stock once it is in use.
Transportation covers the movement of people and goods, split into Transportation (Passenger) and Transportation (Freight), each resolving its vehicle fleet by mode and powertrain.
Emissions-driven and land-based sectors are those whose footprint is dominated by something other than energy use, and whose activity is therefore often measured directly in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent: Waste (landfill methane), Agriculture, and Forestry, together with the negative-emissions and land-accounting sectors Carbon Dioxide Removal and LULUCF. Several of these are deliberately simplified placeholders today, and their chapters flag what a fuller representation would add.

title: 7  Sector Overview
text:
7.5 What each sector chapter contains
The sector chapters follow a common template, so that the same questions can be asked of every part of the economy. Each opens with the sector’s scope — what it does and does not include, and where adjacent activities are handled to avoid double-counting — and a real-world context section that grounds the model in the actual industry: its scale in Canada, its emission sources, and the levers available to reduce them. A model structure section then walks through the sector’s tree, anchored by a hand-drawn flow figure, distinguishing the fixed-ratio production chain from the tech-compete leaves and naming the services it draws on.
A decarbonisation technologies section surveys the low- and zero-carbon options for the sector, usually with two tables: a maturity table that places each option on the spectrum from commercial to emerging, and an indicative techno-economic cost table in 2025 Canadian dollars. These cost figures are order-of-magnitude values drawn from public literature, included for relative comparison rather than budgeting, and kept deliberately separate from the calibrated values the model carries internally. An economics section explains how the competition resolves for that sector and records its emissions accounting; a regional coverage section notes which regions carry the sector and how they differ; and a limitations and planned extensions section, with embedded TODOs, records the known gaps and the priorities for future work.

title: 7  Sector Overview
text:
7.6 Cross-cutting conventions
A few conventions hold across all the sector chapters and are worth stating once.
The trees are written as a region-agnostic master tree and then instantiated for each of the seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — which share a structure but differ in their activity forecasts, fuel prices, and grid emissions intensity. Not every sector appears in every region; coal mining, for instance, is carried only where coal is actually mined.
Technology choice everywhere uses behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital. These higher rates capture the short payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real investment decisions, and they are applied throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4.
Emissions accounting combines combustion CO₂ from the fuels each technology requests with process emissions released by chemical reactions independent of energy use — calcination in cement, for example — and, in a few sectors, fugitive methane, all expressed on a CO₂-equivalent basis so that high-warming gases enter at their full weight. Fuels reach the demand sectors as blends, so a rising renewable content in a blend lowers the lifecycle carbon of every technology that draws on it, and carbon capture is represented as a shared service that sectors can call on where it applies.
Taken together, these shared structures are what let CIMS treat a landfill, a steel mill, and a passenger-vehicle fleet within one consistent framework: each is a flow model of competing technologies, driven by an activity forecast, discounted behaviourally, and accounted on a common emissions basis. The chapters that follow apply that framework, one sector at a time.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.1 Scope
Coal mining is one of CIMS’s energy-supply and extractive sub-models: it produces coal for metallurgical use (coking coal for steelmaking) and for thermal use (power and industrial heat). The emphasis, as in the other extractive sectors, is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — the production chain, the technologies that compete at each stage, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. Coal mining has a distinctive emissions signature: alongside the diesel its mobile equipment burns, it releases fugitive methane liberated from the coal seam during extraction, and this coal-mine methane is the sector’s largest greenhouse-gas source — yet, as discussed below, the current model carries no technology to abate it.
CIMS represents the extraction, size reduction, and finishing of coal — from the mine face through crushing, milling, washing, and drying to a saleable product. The driving variable is coal output in tonnes. Both metallurgical (coking) coal and thermal coal are within scope; the chain includes a Metallurgical Finishing stage (washing, cleaning/drying, tailings) that prepares coking coal to the specification the steel industry needs.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere to avoid double-counting: the combustion of thermal coal for power is in Electricity and for industrial heat in the relevant industrial chapters; the conversion of coking coal to coke and its use in ironmaking are in Iron and Steel; and other (non-coal) mining is in the Mining sector. This chapter covers the mining of the coal itself.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.2 Real-world context
Canada produced about 42.6 Mt of coal in 2024, roughly two-thirds of it metallurgical (Natural Resources Canada 2025). The geography is concentrated in the West: British Columbia accounts for around 69% of tonnage (the Elk Valley coking-coal mines), Alberta about 19% (metallurgical and thermal), and Saskatchewan about 11% (lignite/thermal). The two coal types are on opposite trajectories. Thermal coal is in steep decline as Canada phases out unabated coal-fired electricity by 2030 and moves to end thermal-coal exports, while metallurgical coal — for which there is no current large-scale substitute in conventional steelmaking — has held up and is increasingly framed as an export commodity (Natural Resources Canada 2025). Canadian coal production has fallen about 31% over the past decade, almost all of it thermal.
The sector’s emissions come from two places. Diesel powers the trucks, shovels, and other mobile equipment, as at any large mine. More distinctively, methane trapped in the coal seam is released during extraction — fugitive coal-mine methane (CMM), much of it carried out in the ventilation air (VAM). Coal-mine methane is the dominant greenhouse-gas source from coal mining, on the order of 60% of the total, and mature technologies exist to drain and destroy it — gas drainage, and ventilation-air-methane oxidation that can destroy more than 98% of the methane in mine ventilation air (International Energy Agency 2023; CSIRO 2026). The CIMS structure carries the fugitive-methane factor on the extraction node and the diesel emissions on the mobile equipment, but — as noted below — it does not yet offer a methane-capture option.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the coal production chain — and a Service sub-tree of auxiliary energy services. Figure 8.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the production chain is a fixed-ratio sequence and the technology choices occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 8.1: Energy-service flow model of the coal mining sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree runs from Raw Product (extraction, mine ventilation, transportation) through Size Reduced Product (crushing and milling) to Metallurgical Finishing (washing, cleaning/drying, tailings); the Service sub-tree holds the MECS-aligned machine drive and building services. Fugitive coal-mine methane is released at extraction.




8.3.1 Products: the coal production chain

Raw Product — the mine itself: Extraction (competing diesel, biodiesel, and electric equipment), Mine Ventilation, and Transportation (diesel and biodiesel trucks, or conveyance). The Extraction node carries the fugitive-methane emission factor.
Size Reduced Product — Primary Crushing, Primary Milling, and Secondary Milling of the run-of-mine coal.
Metallurgical Finishing — preparing coking coal: Washing (wash mill), Cleaning (rotary, spray, or fluidized-bed drying, on coal, natural gas, or electricity), and Tailings Disposal (reclamation, with diesel, biodiesel, or electric options).

The master tree also defines Simplified Extraction and Simplified Production nodes — lower-resolution alternatives to the full chain for regions or runs where the detailed structure is not warranted.


8.3.2 Services
The services follow the standard pattern and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part: Machine Drive (see Industrial Machine Drive Systems) carries the large motor loads (the model’s current files still use the older per-horsepower and separate compression/conveyance/pumping/ventilation structure), together with HVAC, Lighting, and the Methane Blend gaseous-fuel node.

Migrate them to the region-agnostic master tree and the shared General Services chapters.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Coal mining’s emissions split into fugitive methane (the larger share) and diesel combustion in mobile equipment, with smaller process-heat (drying) and electricity loads. The decarbonisation levers therefore are methane capture, equipment electrification or fuel-switching, and efficiency. Table 8.1 summarises maturity and Table 8.2 gives indicative costs. A crucial caveat: the single largest lever — methane capture — is not yet represented in the model.

8.4.1 Capturing coal-mine methane
The most important lever is the one the model is missing. Because methane has a high global-warming potential and is released in large quantities during mining, draining and using it (where concentrations allow) and oxidising the dilute methane in ventilation air (VAM) together address the majority of the sector’s emissions, with mature technology that can destroy more than 98% of vent methane (CSIRO 2026; International Energy Agency 2023). The model currently applies the same fugitive-methane factor to every extraction option, with no capture alternative.

Fugitive methane is the largest single source of coal-mining emissions and has commercially available abatement, but the current tree offers no option to reduce it — every extraction technology carries the same methane factor.


8.4.2 Electrifying and fuel-switching mobile equipment
As in metal mining, the diesel load is addressed by battery-electric and biodiesel extraction and haulage (already options at the Extraction and Transportation nodes), electric coal drying, ventilation-on-demand, and efficient motors, fans, and conveyors in the machine-drive service. These are the same levers detailed in the Mining chapter.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output basis, service requests for the energy it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Coal mining technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes in the current data, with some auxiliary nodes at 50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the short payback horizons and adoption barriers typical of resource industries; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 10.
The emissions accounting combines combustion CO₂ from diesel and drying fuel with the distinctive fugitive CH₄ factor on extraction (entering on a CO₂-equivalent basis at methane’s high warming potential). Because there is no methane-capture option and no CCS service, the model’s only channels for emissions reduction are equipment electrification, fuel-switching to biodiesel, and efficiency — which reach the combustion emissions but leave the dominant fugitive methane untouched. This is the most consequential representational gap in the sub-model, and it means the model understates the abatement available to the sector.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.6 Regional coverage and differences
Four regions carry coal mining — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, and Saskatchewan — reflecting where Canadian coal is actually mined:

British Columbia dominates, with metallurgical (coking) coal from the Elk Valley; this production is export-oriented and durable.
Alberta has both metallurgical and thermal coal, with thermal declining as coal power is phased out.
Saskatchewan mines lignite/thermal coal, the most exposed to the power phase-out.
The Atlantic region has a small coal presence.

Ontario, Québec, and Manitoba are absent, consistent with the absence of coal mining there.
TODO: Represent the diverging trajectories of metallurgical versus thermal coal explicitly — durable, export-driven coking-coal demand versus a sharp thermal-coal decline under the coal-power phase-out and export restrictions — since lumping them understates the structural change underway in the sector.

title: 8  Coal Mining
text:
8.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The coal mining sub-model captures the production chain and its diesel and electricity loads in good detail, but it has one large gap and several smaller ones. The large gap is the absence of any coal-mine-methane abatement technology, which omits the sector’s single most important emissions lever. The smaller debts are the older auxiliary structure (to be migrated to MECS machine drive), the lack of an explicit metallurgical-versus-thermal split, and reliance on inherited cost data. The TODOs above record these priorities.

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.1 Scope
The natural gas supply sector is one of CIMS’s energy-supply sub-models, covering the upstream and midstream chain — extracting raw gas, processing it, and moving it through transmission and distribution to the point of use. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the production chain, the technologies that compete at each stage, and — distinctively for this sector — the emission-source nodes where methane and CO₂ escape. The tree is region-agnostic. Natural gas is defined, for climate purposes, by methane: the gas is itself almost pure methane, and the leaks, vents, and flares along the supply chain make fugitive and vented methane the sector’s largest controllable emission — and, fortunately, one of the cheapest to abate anywhere in the economy.
CIMS represents the supply of natural gas: extraction (conventional, shale, tight, and coalbed methane), field and plant processing, transmission, and distribution, together with the venting, fugitive, flaring, and formation-CO₂ emission sources that occur along the way and the energy the sector consumes for compression, drilling, and heat. The driving variable is gas throughput. The model also carries the oil-and-gas fuel blends (diesel, gasoline, methane) the sector burns for its own operations.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: the combustion of the delivered gas by end users is accounted in the demand sectors (residential, commercial, industry, electricity); crude oil production is in Petroleum Crude; and downstream gas use as a chemical feedstock is in Chemical Products and as a hydrogen feedstock in Hydrogen. This chapter covers getting the gas out of the ground and to market.

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.2 Real-world context
Canada is one of the world’s largest natural gas producers, with output concentrated in the Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin — above all the Montney play straddling Alberta and British Columbia. The sector’s defining climate issue is methane. Because methane has a high global-warming potential and the product is itself methane, leaks and intentional releases along the chain — fugitive equipment leaks, vented gas from pneumatic devices and tanks, flaring, well blowdowns, and liquid unloading — together make up the sector’s largest greenhouse-gas source, and one of the largest controllable methane sources in the economy.
The decisive fact is that this methane is cheap to abate. Canada has set a target to cut oil-and-gas methane by 75% below 2012 levels by 2030, and the measures to do it — leak detection and repair, vapour-recovery units, zero-bleed (electric) pneumatic controllers, vent and blowdown capture, plunger lifts, and flare reduction — are among the lowest-cost greenhouse-gas abatement options available, on the order of $11–48 per tonne of CO₂-equivalent, with much of the captured gas recoverable for sale (Environmental Defense Fund 2023; Environment and Climate Change Canada 2024). Alberta accounts for roughly 68% of the sector’s methane, while British Columbia has already cut its oil-and-gas methane about 51% from 2014 levels while increasing production (Environmental Defense Fund 2023). The CIMS structure is built precisely around this: it represents each emission source as its own node with a competition among abatement levels, so the model can buy down methane the way the real policy does.

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the gas supply chain, including its emission sources — and a Service sub-tree of the oil-and-gas fuel blends. Figure 9.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the emission-source nodes host competitions among abatement options.






Figure 9.1: Energy-service flow model of the natural gas supply sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree runs Supply (extraction, processing, and the venting/fugitive/flaring/formation-CO₂/testing emission sources, each with an abatement competition, plus a CCS service) → Transmission → Distribution; the Service sub-tree holds the oil-and-gas fuel blends the sector burns. Methane is the dominant emission, and most nodes carry an explicit abatement choice.




9.3.1 Products: the supply chain and its emission sources
The Supply node is the heart of the model. It combines the productive steps with the emission sources:

Extraction — conventional, shale, tight, and coalbed methane, with drilling, compression, off-road transport, and efficient variants; the energy of getting gas out of the ground.
Processing — separating and cleaning the raw gas (with compression).
Emission sources, each with an abatement competition:

Fugitive — equipment leaks, competing leak-detection-and-repair (LDAR) intensities (No / Low / Med / High LDAR, cutting the methane factor from 1.0 to 0.75, 0.25, and 0.1).
Venting — Point Venting (no vapour-recovery unit, VRU, or flare install) and Diffuse Venting.
Controls — pneumatic devices, competing high-, medium-, and low-bleed and electric (zero-bleed, instrument-air or electric controllers).
Flaring — with or without CCS.
Formation CO₂ — the CO₂ separated from the raw gas (acid gas), with or without CCS.
Testing and Maintenance — blowdowns (capture high/low), liquid unloading (plunger install), and well tests.

CCS — a shared capture service (95% capture) for the flaring and formation-CO₂ streams.

Downstream, Transmission (with compression) and Distribution move the gas to market, each carrying its own (smaller) emission factors.


9.3.2 Services: the sector’s own fuel use
The Service sub-tree holds the oil-and-gas fuel blends — diesel, gasoline, and methane — that the sector’s own engines, compressors, and heaters consume, allowing the model to track (and decarbonise) the energy the gas industry uses on itself, including electrification of compression and drives.

Document and, where appropriate, consolidate the market/trade representation, and add an explicit LNG export pathway (the LNG Compression node exists but the export chain is not fully built out).

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Natural gas decarbonisation is, overwhelmingly, methane abatement — stopping the leaks, vents, and flares — supplemented by electrifying the sector’s compression and heat and capturing concentrated CO₂ streams. Table 9.1 summarises maturity and Table 9.2 gives indicative costs. The striking feature is how cheap, even profitable, much of this is.

Costs are given as cost of abatement per tonne of CO₂-equivalent, since most measures are equipment changes whose benefit is avoided methane (often partly offset by the value of the recovered gas). They are indicative, for relative comparison rather than budgeting, and are separate from the values the model carries internally.

9.4.1 Methane abatement: the dominant, low-cost lever
The overwhelming priority is methane. Leak detection and repair finds and fixes fugitive leaks; zero-bleed electric pneumatics replace the gas-driven controllers that vent by design; vapour-recovery units capture vented gas; blowdown and vent capture and plunger lifts address maintenance and liquid-unloading releases; and flare reduction converts otherwise-vented methane to CO₂ or captures it. The model represents each of these as an abatement competition at the relevant emission node. Because the captured methane is saleable gas, many of these measures are net cost-saving — which is why the sector-wide 75% reduction is achievable at an average cost of only around $11–48/tCO₂e (Environmental Defense Fund 2023).


9.4.2 Electrifying operations and capturing CO₂
Beyond methane, the sector burns gas for compression, drilling, and heat; switching these to electric drives and compression (the Controls “electric” and the fuel-blend electrification options) removes that combustion CO₂. Where the raw gas contains formation CO₂ (acid gas) or where gas is flared, the concentrated CO₂ streams can be routed to CCS at 95% capture — among the lower-cost capture opportunities because the CO₂ is already concentrated.

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.5 Economics
Technology choice at every node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, operating cost, an output basis, service requests for the energy it consumes, any recovered-gas credit, and availability and lifetime years; these are combined into a lifecycle cost and converted to market shares.
Natural gas technologies are discounted at a high rate — about 35% at most nodes, with some at 20% in the current data. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers typical of the industry; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters govern how sharply the abatement competitions respond to cost.
The emissions accounting is unusually detailed on the source side: the model carries explicit CH₄ factors on the fugitive, venting, control, blowdown, liquid-unloading, and distribution nodes (entering on a CO₂-equivalent basis at methane’s high warming potential), CO₂ factors on flaring and formation gas, and a CCS removal factor on the equipped routes. Combustion CO₂ from the sector’s own fuel use enters through the oil-and-gas fuel blends. A distinctive economic feature is that abatement often carries a recovered-gas value that partly or fully offsets its cost, so a carbon price (or a methane regulation) can drive large reductions at very low or negative net cost — which the model reproduces through the abatement competitions.

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.6 Regional coverage and differences
The sector is represented for the producing regions and for trade. Alberta and British Columbia dominate production (the Montney and related plays) and therefore the sector’s emissions and abatement opportunity; Saskatchewan adds production; Ontario, Québec, Manitoba, and the Atlantic carry mainly transmission and distribution. The model also includes a national (CAN) aggregate and a Rest-of-World region to handle trade and, prospectively, LNG export. Regional differences are large: Alberta holds most of the methane-abatement opportunity, while British Columbia has already moved further on methane controls.
TODO: Calibrate the regional production mix (conventional / shale / tight / coalbed methane) and the baseline methane-source intensities against Canada’s National Inventory Report and provincial methane data, since both the emissions and the abatement potential depend heavily on them.

title: 9  Natural Gas
text:
9.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The natural gas sub-model is unusually well suited to its central question — methane abatement — because it resolves the individual emission sources and gives each an abatement competition. Its main limitations are the incomplete build-out of the LNG export chain, the somewhat separate market/trade representation, and reliance on inherited methane-source intensities that should track the rapidly evolving federal and provincial methane regulations. The TODOs above record these priorities.

title: 10  Petroleum Crude
text:
10.1 Scope
Crude oil and bitumen production is one of CIMS’s energy-supply sub-models, covering the upstream oil industry — conventional crude oil and, dominating both output and emissions in Canada, the oil sands (surface mining, in-situ recovery, and upgrading to synthetic crude). The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the production routes, the technologies that compete at each, and the energy services — above all steam — that drive them. The tree is region-agnostic. The defining feature of the sector is that the energy used to produce the oil — particularly the natural gas burned to raise steam for in-situ bitumen recovery — is itself a very large emissions source, so the sector’s decarbonisation is mostly about how that production energy is supplied and whether its CO₂ is captured.
CIMS represents the production of crude oil and bitumen: conventional light, medium, and heavy crude (onshore and offshore), and the oil sands in their three forms — surface mining, in-situ recovery, and upgrading of bitumen to synthetic crude oil. The driving variable is oil/bitumen output. The model carries the supporting energy services — steam, process hydrogen (for upgrading), industrial engines, and a CCS service.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: refining crude into fuels and products is in Petroleum Refining; natural gas production is in Natural Gas; the combustion of the refined fuels is in the demand sectors; and the hydrogen the sector uses can be drawn from the Hydrogen sub-model. This chapter covers getting the oil and bitumen out of the ground and to a refinery-ready state.

title: 10  Petroleum Crude
text:
10.2 Real-world context
Canadian crude production is dominated by the Alberta oil sands, the largest source of both output and emissions in the sector, supplemented by conventional crude (Saskatchewan, Alberta) and offshore production in the Atlantic (Newfoundland). The oil sands come in two forms: surface mining and upgrading, which digs out near-surface bitumen and upgrades it to synthetic crude; and in-situ recovery, which uses steam to mobilise deeper bitumen and now rivals mining as the main production route.
The sector’s emissions profile is distinctive. For in-situ production, the single largest source is steam generation — natural gas burned to make the steam that lowers bitumen viscosity in steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) and cyclic steam — so the carbon intensity of a barrel depends heavily on how much steam it needs and how that steam is produced ( 2025). Upgrading adds the emissions of coking, hydrotreating, and the hydrogen it consumes. The decarbonisation levers follow directly: solvent-assisted in-situ processes that cut steam use (with potential to lower intensity by up to ~50%), low-carbon steam (electric, hydrogen, nuclear, cogeneration), and carbon capture — the focus of the Pathways Alliance, whose proposed oil sands CCS network would be among the world’s largest (Pathways Alliance 2024; 2025). The CIMS structure captures all of these as competing technologies at the production and steam nodes.

title: 10  Petroleum Crude
text:
10.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the production routes — and a Service sub-tree of the energy services that supply them. Figure 10.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4).






Figure 10.1: Energy-service flow model of the petroleum crude sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree holds conventional crude (light/medium onshore and offshore, heavy) and the oil sands (in-situ recovery, surface mining, and upgrading to synthetic crude); the Service sub-tree supplies the steam, hydrogen, industrial engines and CCS the production routes draw on. Steam generation is the dominant emission source for in-situ bitumen.




10.3.1 Products: conventional crude and the oil sands

Light/Medium crude — Onshore and Offshore conventional production.
Heavy crude — conventional heavy oil.
Exploration — the upstream drilling and appraisal activity.
Bitumen — the oil sands, in three linked nodes:

In-Situ — competing SAGD, SAGD with enhanced leak detection (ELDAR), Cyclic Steam, Solvent, and Hybrid Thermal-Solvent recovery. These differ in steam intensity (and therefore CO₂) and in methane (the solvent and hybrid routes cut both).
Mining — surface mining (Existing and Improved).
Upgrading — converting bitumen to synthetic crude, competing conventional Upgrading, Efficient, ELDAR, and ELDAR + CCS routes.




10.3.2 Services: steam, hydrogen, engines, and capture

Steam — the most important service, because in-situ recovery is steam-intensive. It competes natural-gas, heavy-fuel-oil, and petcoke boilers (with CCS variants), natural-gas cogeneration (with and without CCS), and electric, hydrogen, and nuclear steam. The choice here largely determines an in-situ barrel’s carbon intensity.
Still Gas — steam raised from refinery/upgrader still gas, with boiler and cogeneration options (with and without CCS).
Hydrogen — for upgrading (can be sourced from the Hydrogen sub-model’s grey, blue, and green routes).
Industrial Engines — diesel, gasoline, and propane mobile equipment (mine trucks, and the like).
CCS — the shared capture service (90% capture), central to deep decarbonisation of the sector.

TODO: Link the sector’s hydrogen demand explicitly to the Hydrogen sub-model’s production competition, so that upgrading hydrogen carries the cost and carbon intensity of the chosen (grey, blue, or green) route rather than an assumed value.

text:
10.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Oil-sands and crude decarbonisation works through reducing steam demand (solvent processes), decarbonising the steam and process energy (electric, hydrogen, nuclear, cogeneration), capturing CO₂ (the Pathways CCS network), and controlling methane. 10.4.1 Reducing and decarbonising steam
For in-situ bitumen, the game is steam. Solvent and hybrid thermal-solvent processes inject light hydrocarbons (often propane) in place of, or alongside, steam, cutting the steam needed per barrel and lowering carbon intensity by up to about 50% ( 2025). Where steam is still needed, the Steam service can switch from gas boilers to cogeneration, electric, hydrogen, or even nuclear steam — the choice that most determines an in-situ barrel’s footprint.


10.4.2 Carbon capture and methane control
Because the oil sands produce large, relatively concentrated CO₂ streams (from steam generation, upgrading, and hydrogen production), CCS is the central deep-decarbonisation lever, and the proposed Pathways Alliance network would capture CO₂ from a cluster of oil-sands facilities at large scale (Pathways Alliance 2024). The model represents this through the CCS-equipped steam, upgrading, and still-gas routes and the shared CCS service. Enhanced leak detection (ELDAR) cuts the sector’s fugitive and vented methane, often at net-negative cost.

title: 10  Petroleum Crude
text:
10.5 Economics
Technology choice at every node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, operating cost, an output (per-barrel) basis, service requests for the steam, hydrogen, and engine energy it consumes, any recovered-gas credit, and availability and lifetime years; these are combined into a lifecycle cost and converted to market shares.
Petroleum-crude technologies are discounted at a high rate — about 35% at most nodes, with some at 20–40% in the current data. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the payback horizons and risk typical of the industry; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4.
Emissions are tracked as CO₂ (chiefly from steam, upgrading, and engine combustion) and CH₄ (fugitive and vented, with the ELDAR and solvent routes carrying lower factors), and the CCS service applies a 90% removal factor to the equipped routes. Because in-situ carbon intensity is dominated by steam, the carbon price acts most powerfully through the Steam competition — making solvent processes, electric/hydrogen/nuclear steam, cogeneration, and CCS progressively more attractive as it rises — while methane controls add cheap, often profitable, abatement.

title: 10  Petroleum Crude
text:
10.6 Regional coverage and differences
Six regions carry crude production, but it is highly concentrated:

Alberta dominates, with essentially all of the oil sands (mining, in-situ, and upgrading) plus conventional crude — and therefore most of the sector’s energy use and abatement opportunity.
Saskatchewan carries conventional heavy and light/medium crude.
The Atlantic region carries offshore light/medium production (Newfoundland).
British Columbia, Manitoba, and Ontario carry smaller conventional volumes.

Because the oil sands are so steam- and energy-intensive, Alberta holds the overwhelming majority of the sector’s decarbonisation challenge and opportunity.

title: 10  Petroleum Crude
text:
10.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The petroleum-crude sub-model captures the essential structure — conventional and oil-sands routes, the dominant steam service with its full range of low-carbon options, and CCS — which makes it well suited to analysing oil-sands decarbonisation. Its main limitations are the loose coupling of upgrading hydrogen to the hydrogen sub-model, reliance on inherited steam-to-oil and cost assumptions, and the need to keep the solvent-SAGD and CCS options aligned with fast-moving industry projects. The TODOs above record these priorities.

title: 11  Petroleum Refining
text:
11.1 Scope
Petroleum refining is one of CIMS’s energy-supply and processing sub-models: it converts crude oil and bitumen into refined products — gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, fuel oils, petrochemical feedstocks, asphalt, lubricants, and coke. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the process units that turn crude into products, the technologies that compete at each, and the energy services — above all process heat, steam, and hydrogen — that drive them. The tree is region-agnostic. The defining feature of refining is that almost all of its emissions come from burning fuel for process heat and steam (much of it the refinery’s own still gas) and from on-site hydrogen production, so its decarbonisation is about electrifying and decarbonising that energy and capturing the concentrated CO₂ streams — against a backdrop of long-run demand decline as transport electrifies.
CIMS represents the refining of crude oil and synthetic crude into finished products, through the standard process units: distillation (atmospheric and vacuum), cracking (coking and hydrocracking), hydrotreating (desulphurisation and sulphur recovery), reforming, alkylation, and isomerisation, plus by-products such as asphalt and lubes. The driving variable is refinery throughput/product output. Lubricating-oil, grease, and asphalt manufacture are included where carried out within refineries. The model carries the supporting energy services — direct process heat, steam, still gas, hydrogen, machine drive, and a CCS service.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: crude oil and bitumen production (including oil-sands upgrading) is in Petroleum Crude; natural gas processing is in Natural Gas; petrochemicals made from refinery streams are in Chemical Products; and the combustion of the finished fuels is in the demand sectors. This chapter covers the refinery itself.

title: 11  Petroleum Refining
text:
11.2 Real-world context
Canada has a modest fleet of refineries spread across the country, supplying gasoline, diesel, and other products to domestic and export markets. A refinery’s energy use and emissions depend on its complexity — the type of crude it runs and how much cracking, hydrotreating, and reforming it does to make high-value products. The bulk of refinery emissions come from burning fossil fuels for process heating and steam generation, with a further significant share from hydrogen manufacturing (steam methane reforming for hydrotreating and hydrocracking) (World Resources Institute 2023). Much of the process fuel is the refinery’s own still gas (off-gas from the process units).
The decarbonisation levers follow from that emissions structure, and Canada’s Roadmap for the Decarbonization of the Oil and Gas Sector names them directly: electrifying low- and medium-grade process heat, fuel-switching to low- and zero-carbon hydrogen for high-temperature heat, energy efficiency, and CCUS — and refining is regarded as one of the lower-cost CCS opportunities, with concentrated CO₂ available from the hydrogen plant and other units (Natural Resources Canada 2024; World Resources Institute 2023). Over the longer term, refinery throughput is expected to decline as road transport electrifies, shifting the product slate toward aviation, petrochemicals, and exports. The CIMS structure captures the decarbonisation levers as competing technologies at the heat, steam, still-gas, and hydrogen services, with a shared CCS service.

title: 11  Petroleum Refining
text:
11.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the refinery process chain — and a Service sub-tree of the energy services. Figure 11.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the process chain is largely fixed-ratio, and the technology choices occur in the energy services.






Figure 11.1: Energy-service flow model of the petroleum refining sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree is the refinery process chain — distillation, cracking (coking, hydrocracking), hydrotreating (desulphurisation, sulphur recovery), reforming, alkylation/isomerisation, and by-products (asphalt, lubes); the Service sub-tree supplies the direct process heat, steam, still gas, hydrogen, machine drive, and CCS the process units draw on.




11.3.1 Products: the refinery process chain
The Refined Petroleum Products node holds the process units:

Petroleum Fractions — the main chain: distillation (atmospheric and vacuum) separates crude into fractions; cracked gas oil upgrades heavy fractions via coking and hydrocracking (at low, medium, and high conversion); hydrotreating (desulphurisation and sulphur recovery) cleans the products; and asphalt and lubes are by-product streams.
Alkylates — alkylation and isoparaffins (isomerisation), which make high-octane gasoline blendstocks.
Reforming — catalytic reforming for octane and aromatics (and a hydrogen by-product).

These units are the demand for the energy services; their relative throughput sets how much heat, steam, and hydrogen the refinery needs.


11.3.2 Services: heat, steam, still gas, hydrogen, and capture

Direct Heat — the process furnaces, competing natural-gas, heavy- and light-fuel-oil, LPG, and petcoke firing (with efficiency variants) and electric heaters (high and low efficiency). This is the central electrification lever for low- and medium-grade heat.
Steam — boiler- and cogeneration-raised steam, competing the full range of fuels (NG, oil, LPG, petcoke, with efficiency and CCS variants), electric and hydrogen steam, and gas cogeneration (CCGT/SCGT/back-pressure turbines, with and without CCS).
Still Gas — the refinery’s own off-gas, used in heaters (with efficiency and CCS variants) and boilers; the dominant self-generated fuel.
Hydrogen — on-site steam methane reforming (standard, efficient, and efficient + CCS for blue hydrogen), for hydrotreating and hydrocracking.
CCS — the shared capture service (90% capture), well suited to the concentrated CO₂ from the hydrogen plant and other units.
Machine Drive, HVAC, Lighting, Methane Blend — the shared utilities.

11.4.1 Decarbonising process heat and steam
Process furnaces and boilers are the largest emission source, so the central lever is how their heat is supplied. The model competes electric heaters (viable for low- and medium-grade heat), hydrogen firing (for high-temperature duty that is hard to electrify), and efficiency-improved fossil firing, at the Direct Heat, Steam, and Still Gas services, alongside cogeneration. Electrifying the electrifiable heat and switching the rest to hydrogen is the backbone of a low-carbon refinery (World Resources Institute 2023).


11.4.2 Low-carbon hydrogen and CCS
Hydrogen manufacturing is the second-largest emission source. The model already competes blue hydrogen (SMR with CCS) at the Hydrogen service; linking it to the Hydrogen sub-model would also allow green (electrolytic) hydrogen. Because the hydrogen plant and several process units produce concentrated CO₂ streams, CCS is comparatively low-cost in refining, and the model routes the CCS-equipped heat, steam, still-gas, and hydrogen options to the shared capture service.

title: 11  Petroleum Refining
text:
11.5 Economics
Technology choice at every node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, operating cost, an output basis, service requests for the fuel, steam, hydrogen, and electricity it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are combined into a lifecycle cost and converted to market shares.
Petroleum-refining technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes, with auxiliary and capital-intensive nodes at 40–50% in the current data. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the short payback horizons and risk aversion typical of the industry; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters govern how sharply the energy-service competitions respond to cost.
Emissions are overwhelmingly combustion CO₂ from process heat, steam, still gas, and the hydrogen plant, entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price; the CCS service applies a 90% removal factor to the equipped routes. Because so much of the fuel is self-generated still gas, the carbon price acts on the choice of how to supply heat and hydrogen — electrify, switch to hydrogen, or capture — rather than on a single dominant process emission. A structural consideration the model can represent is that refinery throughput is expected to decline over the long run as transport electrifies, which reduces absolute emissions independently of the per-barrel decarbonisation choices.

title: 11  Petroleum Refining
text:
11.6 Regional coverage and differences
Six regions carry refining — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — corresponding to where Canada’s refineries are located. Regional differences show up in refinery complexity and product slate, in the fuel mix available for process heat (cheaper gas in the West), and in grid carbon intensity, which determines how much electrifying process heat actually reduces emissions (large in hydro-rich Québec and British Columbia, smaller in Alberta and Saskatchewan until their grids decarbonise).

title: 11  Petroleum Refining
text:
11.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The petroleum refining sub-model captures the process chain and, in detail, the energy services that dominate its emissions — direct heat, steam, still gas, and hydrogen — with a full set of electrification, hydrogen, cogeneration, and CCS options. Its main limitations are the older auxiliary structure (to be migrated to MECS machine drive), the on-site-only hydrogen representation (to be linked to the hydrogen sub-model), and reliance on inherited refinery-configuration and cost data. A broader consideration is the sector’s long-run decline: as transport electrifies, the most consequential question for refining emissions may be how fast throughput falls, which is driven by the demand sectors rather than within this sub-model. The TODOs above record the priorities.

title: 12  Electricity
text:
12.1 Scope
Electricity generation is the central energy-supply sub-model in CIMS: it converts fuels and renewable resources into the power that every other sector draws on, and as the rest of the economy electrifies, what happens here increasingly determines system-wide emissions. The emphasis, as elsewhere, is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — how demand is split across the load curve, the generation technologies that compete to meet each part of it, and the services (storage, transmission, capture) that support them. The model tree is region-agnostic, but electricity is the sector where regional differences are largest, because each province’s grid is built on a different resource base.
CIMS represents utility-scale electricity generation and the supporting storage, transmission, and carbon-capture services. Electricity co-generated within industry is accounted for in the industrial sub-models (see, for example, the cogeneration options in Pulp and Paper and Low-Temperature Industrial Heat) and is not double-counted here — with the deliberate exception that all renewable generation is accounted in the electricity model regardless of whether a utility or an industrial site operates it. Final electricity demand across the economy drives the sub-model; imports and exports are handled through the macroeconomic module, with an own-price elasticity for export demand of about −1.07.
The combustion of the electricity once delivered, and the end-use equipment that consumes it, belong to the demand sectors. This chapter covers only how the power is generated and delivered.

title: 12  Electricity
text:
12.2 Real-world context
Canada has one of the cleanest electricity systems in the world. In 2024 renewables supplied about 65.5% of generation — hydropower 55.3% (with Québec alone producing about half of national hydro), wind 7.2%, and solar 1.3% — nuclear 13.7% (almost entirely Ontario’s CANDU reactors), and fossil fuels 20.8% (natural gas 15.8%, coal 4.1%) (Natural Resources Canada 2024). More than four-fifths of recent generation investment has gone to non-emitting sources (Natural Resources Canada 2024).
The system is, however, deeply regional. British Columbia, Québec, and Manitoba run on hydro and are almost emissions-free; Ontario combines nuclear, hydro, and a growing renewable share; the Atlantic provinces are mixed (Prince Edward Island is essentially all wind); and Alberta and Saskatchewan are the fossil-heavy outliers, historically coal and now increasingly natural gas. Federal regulation is phasing out conventional coal generation and pushing toward a net-zero grid, so the model’s central question is how each province’s mix evolves from its very different starting point. The CIMS structure is built to answer exactly that: it competes a full set of generation technologies — variable renewables, firm low-carbon resources, and flexible balancing resources — within a load-duration framework, and adds the storage, transmission, and capture services that a high-renewables grid needs.

title: 12  Electricity
text:
12.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into a Product sub-tree — generation, organised by position on the load curve — and a Service sub-tree holding CCS, Storage, and Transmission. Figure 12.1 shows the structure.
Total generation is split across Base Load, Shoulder Load, and Peak Load nodes using ratios derived from historical load-duration curves (the user-specified fixed_matrix_ratio decision rule). A load-duration curve re-orders the year’s hourly demand from highest to lowest; its height gives the capacity required and its width the utilisation, so the three nodes correspond to power that is needed almost all the time (base), part of the time (shoulder), and only at peak. Within each node, technologies compete on the basis of their annual levelized cost (see Chapter 4).






Figure 12.1: Energy-service flow model of the electricity sector (region-agnostic master tree). Total demand is split by load-duration-curve ratios into Base, Shoulder, and Peak Load nodes, each hosting a competition among generation technologies; a Service sub-tree provides CCS (coal, gas, biomass), Storage (battery and seasonal), and Transmission.




12.3.1 Products: base, shoulder, and peak generation
The traditional baseload/load-following/peaking classification is, as the model’s own framing notes, less meaningful in a system with large wind and solar shares, where dispatch is driven by renewable variability and most low-carbon options are capital-intensive with near-zero variable cost. CIMS therefore keeps the base/shoulder/peak split as the demand-side framework but populates it with three functional classes of technology:

Variable renewables (VRE) — wind (onshore, offshore), solar PV, run-of-river hydro: zero fuel cost, output set by the resource, valuable when available.
Firm low-carbon resources — reservoir hydro, nuclear (including small modular reactors, SMRs), geothermal, biomass and biogas, and fossil plants with CCS: dispatchable over long durations.
Fast-burst balancing resources — short-duration battery storage and flexible demand: energy-limited, used to balance supply and demand over short, high-value periods.

In the model the Base Load node hosts the widest set — wind (with battery or seasonal storage), solar PV (with battery), hydro reservoir and river, nuclear and nuclear SMR, natural gas combined-cycle (CC) and simple-cycle (SC), gas CC with CCS, coal and coal with CCS, biomass and biomass with CCS, geothermal/geoexchange, and waste-to-energy. Shoulder Load hosts a similar but slightly narrower set, and Peak Load is limited to fast-responding plant (gas simple-cycle, reservoir hydro, oil, and wind-plus-seasonal-storage) — long-start plant such as nuclear cannot serve peak. The split between conventional and renewable generation within a node can be user-specified over time or determined endogenously by relative levelized cost.


12.3.2 Services: storage, transmission, and capture

Storage — Battery (short-duration, the fast-burst balancing resource) and Seasonal (long-duration storage that lets variable renewables serve firm demand). Storage is what allows high-VRE grids to remain reliable.
Transmission — the delivery network that all generation requests.
CCS — the shared carbon-capture service, with coal, natural gas, and biomass variants; biomass-with-CCS generation is net-negative.

12.4.1 Variable renewables plus storage
The cheapest new energy in most of Canada is now onshore wind and solar PV, but their variability means that beyond modest shares they need balancing. The model represents this directly: wind and solar appear both alone and paired with battery (short-duration) or seasonal (long-duration) storage, and the Storage service is what lets a high-renewables node meet firm demand. As battery costs fall — utility four-hour storage is approaching US$100/MWh — the VRE-plus-storage combination displaces more gas.


12.4.2 Firm low-carbon resources
Where firm capacity is needed over long durations, the model competes reservoir hydro (Canada’s traditional firm clean resource, though site-limited), nuclear including small modular reactors (Ontario is building Canada’s first SMR), geothermal, biomass, and gas or coal with CCS. These are the technologies that can replace unabated fossil baseload while keeping the grid reliable in low-wind, low-sun periods.


12.4.3 Carbon capture and net-negative power
In the gas- and coal-heavy provinces, CCS on combined-cycle gas, on the existing coal fleet (Saskatchewan’s Boundary Dam is a pioneer), or on biomass plants captures most of the combustion CO₂; biomass with CCS goes further and delivers net-negative generation. The shared CCS service and its costs are detailed in the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage chapter.

title: 12  Electricity
text:
12.5 Economics
Technology choice within each load node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4, here on an annual levelized-cost basis: each technology carries an overnight capital cost, fixed and variable operating costs, a capacity factor, fuel service requests where applicable, and availability and lifetime years, which are annualised and combined into a levelized cost per MWh and converted to market shares.
Electricity technologies are discounted at lower rates than most demand sectors — around 12.5–25% in the current data — reflecting the regulated, capital-intensive, long-horizon nature of generation investment. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than pure financial costs of capital, but for a regulated utility they sit closer to the financial end of the range than the 35%+ used in the demand sectors; CIMS applies them throughout the levelized-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 10–25.
Emissions are tracked as CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O and arise from fuel combustion in the fossil and biomass plants, entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price; the CCS service applies a removal factor to the captured routes, which can drive biomass-CCS generation net-negative. Because electricity is an input to every other sector, the carbon price acts here with unusual leverage: it raises the cost of unabated coal and gas relative to renewables, nuclear, and CCS, shifting the generation mix and, through the price of delivered electricity, the economics of electrification everywhere else in the model. Electricity imports and exports respond to relative prices through the macroeconomic module’s trade elasticities.

title: 12  Electricity
text:
12.6 Regional coverage and differences
Electricity is the sector where the region-agnostic tree resolves to the most different outcomes, because each of the seven modelled regions starts from a distinct resource base:

Québec, British Columbia, and Manitoba are dominated by hydro and are already almost emissions-free; their decarbonisation question is mainly how to add capacity (hydro, wind) for growing electrified demand.
Ontario runs on nuclear and hydro with growing renewables, and faces choices about nuclear refurbishment, SMRs, and wind/solar/storage.
Alberta and Saskatchewan are the fossil-heavy provinces, where the coal phase-out and the competition among gas, gas-plus-CCS, wind, solar, and storage is most consequential.
The Atlantic region is mixed, with significant wind potential.

title: 12  Electricity
text:
12.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The electricity sub-model captures the essential structure of a modern power system — a load-duration split, three functional technology classes, and the storage and transmission services a high-renewables grid needs — but it remains a simplified representation of a system whose real behaviour is hourly and spatial. Its main limitations are the coarse (base/shoulder/peak) time resolution relative to the sub-hourly dynamics that actually drive VRE integration, the simplified storage and transmission representation, and reliance on inherited cost and load-curve assumptions. The TODOs above record the priorities, of which keeping the cost and capacity-factor data current and reconciling storage with the dedicated Energy Storage chapter are the most important.

title: 13  Ethanol
text:
13.1 Scope
Ethanol production is one of CIMS’s energy-supply sub-models: it produces a low-carbon liquid fuel that the transport sector blends with gasoline. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — the production routes, the technologies that compete at each service, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. Two features define the ethanol sub-model: it carries two distinct production routes — first-generation corn (grain) fermentation and second-generation cellulosic conversion — that differ markedly in carbon intensity; and, because fermentation releases a stream of nearly pure, biogenic CO₂, it is one of the cheapest places in the whole energy system to apply carbon capture, which the sub-model represents through a CCS service.
CIMS represents the production of fuel ethanol by two routes: corn (and, in Western Canada, wheat) starch fermentation, and cellulosic conversion of crop residues and other lignocellulosic material. The sub-model covers the conversion plant and its inputs — agricultural feedstock, process steam, electricity, and a gaseous process fuel — and produces ethanol as an output that flows into the gasoline blend. Demand is set by the blending and fuel-switching choices in the consuming sectors and by renewable-fuel policy, rather than by an exogenous production target.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: biodiesel has its own Biodiesel chapter; gasoline is produced in Petroleum Refining; the combustion of the ethanol blend happens in the transport sectors; and feedstock cultivation is represented here only through an Agricultural Input service rather than the full Agriculture sub-model.

title: 13  Ethanol
text:
13.2 Real-world context
Canadian ethanol is predominantly first-generation: corn in Eastern Canada (Ontario in particular) and wheat in the West, fermented to ethanol and blended into gasoline under the federal Clean Fuel Regulations and provincial renewable-content mandates (Natural Resources Canada 2024). Cellulosic ethanol — made from crop residues, wood, and other lignocellulosic feedstock — is a second-generation technology that is much less developed but carries a substantially lower carbon intensity, because it is not burdened by the cultivation emissions (fertiliser N₂O, farm diesel, land use) of a dedicated grain crop and uses material that would otherwise decay or be burned (Tullo 2023).
The sector has one striking decarbonisation feature. The fermentation step that turns sugars into ethanol releases roughly an equal mass of CO₂, and that CO₂ is biogenic and almost pure — it needs little separation before it can be compressed and stored. This makes ethanol plants among the lowest-cost carbon-capture opportunities anywhere, and capturing biogenic fermentation CO₂ delivers net-negative emissions (BECCS). The CIMS structure reflects both points: it separates the corn and cellulosic routes, carries life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O accounting through the feedstock and process services, and provides a CCS service the routes can draw on.

title: 13  Ethanol
text:
13.3 Model structure
The sub-model divides into a Product sub-tree — the two production routes — and a Service sub-tree of the inputs they draw on. Figure 13.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the production chains are fixed-ratio sequences and the technology choices occur at the service leaves.






Figure 13.1: Energy-service flow model of the ethanol sub-model. Two production routes — Corn (grain fermentation) and Cellulosic — convert feedstock into ethanol, drawing on an Agricultural Input service, process Steam, a gaseous Methane Fuel supply, electricity, and a shared CCS service well suited to the pure biogenic CO₂ from fermentation; life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O are tracked.




13.3.1 Products: corn and cellulosic routes

Corn — first-generation starch fermentation. It draws on the Agricultural Input service (the grain feedstock and its cultivation energy) and on Steam for cooking, distillation, and drying, and is the more steam-intensive of the two routes.
Cellulosic — second-generation conversion of lignocellulosic feedstock (crop residues, wood). In the model it draws less on the agricultural-cultivation input and instead consumes some industrial diesel for feedstock handling, plus Steam; its lower cultivation burden gives it a lower life-cycle carbon intensity.



13.3.2 Services: feedstock, heat, fuel, and capture

Agricultural Input — feedstock cultivation, competing diesel-powered, efficient-diesel, and biodiesel-powered farming, so the energy and emissions of growing the grain are represented (including the option to displace farm diesel with biodiesel).
Steam — process heat, competing natural-gas, coal, and electric boilers, cogeneration, and CCS-equipped variants.
Methane Fuel — the gaseous-fuel supply, competing natural gas against biogas, biomass gasification, and hydrogen.
CCS — the shared carbon-capture service, especially valuable here because of the pure fermentation CO₂.

13.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Ethanol decarbonisation means lowering life-cycle carbon intensity — shifting toward cellulosic feedstock, cleaning up process energy, and, distinctively, capturing the pure fermentation CO₂ for net-negative emissions. Table 13.1 summarises maturity and Table 13.2 gives indicative costs.

13.4.1 Capturing fermentation CO₂ (the cheapest BECCS)
The standout option is capturing the fermentation CO₂. Unlike a flue gas, it emerges nearly pure, so only compression and dehydration are needed before storage — capture costs are a small fraction of those for dilute industrial streams. Because the carbon is biogenic, storing it yields net-negative emissions. The model represents this through the CCS service; given the cost advantage, it is the single most valuable lever in the sub-model.

13.4.2 Feedstock and process energy
Shifting from corn to cellulosic feedstock lowers the cultivation burden, and within the corn route the Agricultural Input options (efficient or biodiesel-powered farming) reduce field emissions. On the plant side, switching Steam to electric, biomass, or biogas, or adding CCS to gas-fired steam, cuts the conversion footprint — the same low-carbon heat options described in the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter.

title: 13  Ethanol
text:
13.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output basis, service requests for the inputs it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Ethanol technologies are discounted at rates of roughly 10–40% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real investment decisions; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 10–25 across the competitions.
As with biodiesel, the emissions accounting is life-cycle: the sub-model carries CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O factors so that agricultural N₂O, process CH₄, and CO₂ are all represented, and the net benefit of ethanol emerges from the difference between these emissions and the gasoline it displaces. The CCS service applies an emissions-removal factor to the routes that request it — and because the captured fermentation CO₂ is biogenic, that removal can drive the route’s net emissions below zero. The carbon price therefore rewards the cellulosic route, clean process energy, and above all fermentation-CO₂ capture.

title: 13  Ethanol
text:
13.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry both the corn and cellulosic routes. In practice corn ethanol is concentrated in Ontario and the East, wheat-based grain ethanol in the Prairies, and cellulosic feedstock potential follows crop-residue and forestry availability. Regional differences show up in feedstock mix and in the carbon intensity of the grid supplying process electricity.

title: 13  Ethanol
text:
13.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The ethanol sub-model is compact and supply-side. Its main limitations: it treats feedstock through a single Agricultural Input service rather than linking to the agriculture sub-model; it applies a single CCS cost rather than recognising the unusually cheap fermentation-CO₂ capture; and its corn/cellulosic split and intensities are inherited from older calibrations. The TODOs above record these priorities, of which making the cheap fermentation-CO₂ BECCS pathway explicit is the most consequential for emissions outcomes.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.1 Scope
Biodiesel production is one of CIMS’s energy-supply sub-models rather than an end-use sector: it produces a low-carbon liquid fuel that other sectors — chiefly freight and passenger transport, and industrial and agricultural diesel use — consume in place of, or blended with, fossil diesel. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the production node, the technologies that compete at each service, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. The defining feature of biodiesel is that most of its life-cycle greenhouse-gas footprint sits upstream of the plant, in the feedstock, so the sub-model carries explicit agricultural inputs and life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O accounting rather than treating the fuel as automatically carbon-neutral.
CIMS represents the production of biodiesel (fatty-acid methyl ester, FAME) by transesterification of vegetable oils and animal fats. The sub-model covers the conversion plant and its main inputs — the agricultural feedstock, process steam, electricity, and a gaseous process fuel — and produces biodiesel as an output that flows into the fuel supply. Demand is set by the blending and fuel-switching choices made in the consuming sectors and by policy (renewable-fuel mandates), rather than by an exogenous production target.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: ethanol is a separate fuel with its own Ethanol chapter; fossil diesel is produced in Petroleum Refining; and the combustion of biodiesel happens in the transport and other end-use sectors, where the blended fuel is burned. The cultivation of the feedstock crop is represented here only through an Agricultural Input service that carries its energy and emissions, not through the full Agriculture sub-model.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.2 Real-world context
Biodiesel is a mature, drop-in-capable diesel substitute, and in Canada its production is tied to agriculture and to fuel policy. The country has a handful of biodiesel plants (and a growing number of renewable diesel plants, a different, hydrotreating route), and the dominant feedstock is canola — around 90% of domestic biomass-based diesel is made from Canadian canola — supplemented by tallow and used cooking oil (Natural Resources Canada 2024; Canada Energy Regulator 2023). Demand is driven by the federal Clean Fuel Regulations and provincial renewable-content mandates, which reward fuels by their measured carbon intensity.
That last point is central. Biodiesel is not automatically low-carbon: its life-cycle intensity depends heavily on the feedstock and on the energy used to grow and process it. Crop feedstocks carry the emissions of cultivation — diesel for farm equipment, and N₂O from nitrogen fertiliser, a potent greenhouse gas — whereas waste and residue feedstocks such as tallow and used cooking oil avoid most of that burden and can achieve 79–86% lower life-cycle emissions than fossil diesel (Canada Energy Regulator 2023). The CIMS structure mirrors this by separating the conversion step from an explicit Agricultural Input service and by carrying life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O factors, so the modelled benefit of biodiesel reflects how it is made rather than assuming neutrality.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.3 Model structure
The sub-model divides into a Product sub-tree — the conversion process — and a Service sub-tree of the inputs it draws on. Figure 14.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the production chain is a fixed-ratio sequence and the technology choices occur at the tech-compete leaves of the services.






Figure 14.1: Energy-service flow model of the biodiesel sub-model. A transesterification Production node converts agricultural feedstock into biodiesel, drawing on an Agricultural Input service (feedstock cultivation, diesel- or biodiesel-powered), process Steam, a gaseous Methane Fuel supply, electricity, and a shared CCS service; life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O are tracked.




14.3.1 Product: transesterification
The Production node is biodiesel production by transesterification — reacting the feedstock oil with methanol to yield FAME and glycerol. In the model it consumes three things per unit of biodiesel: electricity, an Agricultural Input (the feedstock), and Steam (process heat). The master tree names this product node Transesterification.


14.3.2 Services: feedstock, heat, fuel, and capture

Agricultural Input — the feedstock-cultivation service, competing diesel-powered, high-efficiency diesel, and biodiesel-powered farming. This is how the model captures the energy (and the diesel-versus-biodiesel choice) of growing the crop; the associated N₂O and other field emissions enter the life-cycle accounting here.
Steam — process heat for the reaction and separation, competing natural-gas, coal, and electric boilers, cogeneration units, and CCS-equipped boiler variants.
Methane Fuel — the gaseous-fuel supply, competing natural gas against biogas, biomass gasification, and hydrogen.
CCS — the shared carbon-capture service that the CCS-equipped steam routes request.



14.3.3 Renewable diesel — a gap
The model represents only the transesterification (FAME) route. The fast-growing renewable diesel (hydrotreated vegetable oil, HVO/HDRD) route — chemically a true drop-in diesel made by hydrogenation rather than transesterification — is not represented, even though new Canadian capacity is overwhelmingly of this type.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Because biodiesel is already a low-carbon fuel relative to fossil diesel, “decarbonising biodiesel” means lowering its life-cycle carbon intensity — choosing better feedstocks and cleaning up the energy used to grow and process it — so that it earns more credit under carbon-intensity-based policy.
