14.4.1 Feedstock is the main lever
The largest determinant of biodiesel’s carbon intensity is the feedstock. Switching from crop oils (canola) to waste and residue oils (tallow, used cooking oil) removes most of the cultivation emissions — including the fertiliser-driven N₂O — and can cut life-cycle emissions to 79–86% below fossil diesel (Canada Energy Regulator 2023). The model captures the cultivation side through the Agricultural Input service, including the option to run farm equipment on biodiesel rather than fossil diesel, which closes part of the loop. Feedstock supply is, however, constrained: waste oils are limited, so feedstock competition with renewable diesel and other uses is a real-world limit the model should eventually reflect.


14.4.2 Cleaning up process energy
The plant’s own emissions come from process heat and electricity. Switching steam to electric boilers (clean where the grid is clean), to biomass or biogas, or adding CCS to gas-fired steam reduces the conversion step’s footprint; the Methane Fuel node lets natural gas be displaced by biogas, biomass gas, or hydrogen. These are the same low-carbon heat options described in the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output basis, service requests for the inputs it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Biodiesel technologies are discounted at rates of roughly 10–40% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real investment decisions; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 10–25 across the competitions.
The emissions accounting is life-cycle in spirit, which distinguishes biodiesel from the end-use sectors. The sub-model carries CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O factors, so the agricultural N₂O from fertiliser and the CH₄ and CO₂ from process energy are all represented, and the net benefit of biodiesel emerges from the difference between these life-cycle emissions and the fossil diesel it displaces — rather than from an assumption that biofuel combustion is automatically zero-carbon. The CCS service applies an emissions-removal factor to the process-heat routes that request it. The carbon price therefore rewards low-intensity feedstocks and clean process energy, which is the mechanism by which carbon-intensity policy is represented.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the biodiesel structure. In practice the Western provinces (Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba) are the natural home of canola-based production, while waste-oil and tallow feedstocks are more widely distributed; the regional differences show up in feedstock availability and in the carbon intensity of the grid that supplies process electricity.

title: 14  Biodiesel
text:
14.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The biodiesel sub-model is compact and supply-side, and its main limitations follow from that: it represents only the transesterification route (omitting renewable diesel), it treats feedstock through a single Agricultural Input service rather than linking to the full agriculture sub-model, and it lacks an explicit feedstock-supply constraint. The TODOs above record these priorities, of which adding the renewable diesel (HVO) pathway is the most important, since it now dominates new Canadian capacity.

title: 15  Hydrogen
text:
15.1 Scope
Hydrogen production is one of CIMS’s energy-supply sub-models: it produces a versatile energy carrier and chemical feedstock that other sectors consume — in oil refining, ammonia and methanol synthesis, potentially in low-carbon steelmaking (direct reduction), and in transport. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the production routes that compete, the services they draw on, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. The defining feature of hydrogen is that the molecule is identical however it is made, but its emissions are entirely a function of the production route — the familiar “colours” of hydrogen — so the whole sub-model is essentially one competition among production technologies that differ enormously in carbon intensity.
CIMS represents the production of hydrogen by all the major routes — natural-gas reforming, coal and biomass gasification, water electrolysis, and ethanol reforming — at both centralised and distributed scale, together with the delivery infrastructure and a shared CCS service. The sub-model produces hydrogen as an output that flows to the consuming sectors; its demand is set by those sectors’ fuel-switching and feedstock choices and by policy, rather than by an exogenous production target.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: the end uses of hydrogen — as a refinery input (Petroleum Refining, Petroleum Crude), an ammonia/methanol feedstock (Chemical Products), a reductant in steel (Iron and Steel), or a transport fuel — are represented in those sectors. This chapter covers only how the hydrogen is made.

title: 15  Hydrogen
text:
15.2 Real-world context
Almost all hydrogen made in Canada today is “grey” — produced by steam methane reforming (SMR) of natural gas without capture, mostly in Alberta to serve oil-sands upgrading, refining, and ammonia production. Grey hydrogen is the cheapest, at roughly CAD 1.5–2.5/kg, but emits on the order of 9–10 kg of CO₂ per kg of hydrogen (Natural Resources Canada 2024). Canada’s Hydrogen Strategy and a new investment tax credit (15–40% of capital, the top rate for the cleanest hydrogen) aim to shift production toward low-carbon routes (Natural Resources Canada 2024).
Two such routes are advancing. “Blue” hydrogen — SMR or gasification with carbon capture (CCS) — is the basis of large Alberta projects such as the Air Products net-zero hydrogen complex (1,500 t/day with ~3 Mt CO₂/yr captured) and Linde’s clean-hydrogen facility; it costs roughly CAD 2–3.5/kg (Air Products 2024; Natural Resources Canada 2024). “Green” hydrogen — electrolysis powered by low-carbon electricity — is the lowest-emission route and is attractive where power is clean and cheap (Québec and BC hydro, Atlantic wind), but at roughly CAD 4.8–6.3/kg today it remains the most expensive (Natural Resources Canada 2024). The CIMS structure represents this whole ladder as a single production competition, with explicit life-cycle emissions and a CCS service, so the model can shift the production mix from grey toward blue and green as costs and the carbon price evolve.

title: 15  Hydrogen
text:
15.3 Model structure
The sub-model divides into a Product sub-tree — the hydrogen-production competition — and a Service sub-tree holding the delivery Infrastructure and the CCS service. Figure 15.1 shows the structure. The production node is a single tech-compete node (see Chapter 4); the incumbent in the current data is distributed SMR.






Figure 15.1: Energy-service flow model of the hydrogen sub-model. A single Production competition spans the “colours” of hydrogen — grey (SMR, coal/biomass gasification), blue (the same routes with CCS), and green (electrolysis; biomass-with-CCS is net-negative) — at centralised and distributed scale, drawing on a delivery Infrastructure service and a shared 90%-capture CCS service; life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O are tracked.




15.3.1 Product: the production competition
The Production node competes the full set of routes, each consuming a characteristic mix of fuel, feedstock, and electricity and (for the capture routes) requesting the CCS service:

Steam methane reforming (SMR) — centralised and distributed, and a centralised + CCS variant. NG-based; the distributed route is today’s incumbent. (Grey, and blue with CCS.)
Coal gasification + CCS — centralised; coal-based blue hydrogen.
Biomass gasification — centralised, and a + CCS variant. Renewable feedstock; with CCS it is net-negative (the captured CO₂ is biogenic).
Electrolysis — centralised and distributed; splits water using electricity, so its emissions track the grid (green where the grid is clean). Electricity-dominated, at roughly 0.2 GJ electricity per unit of hydrogen energy.
Ethanol reforming — distributed; reforms ethanol from the Ethanol sub-model.

The centralised versus distributed distinction matters because it trades production economies of scale against the Infrastructure (delivery, compression) cost: distributed production is made near the point of use and needs less delivery infrastructure, while centralised production is cheaper per unit but draws more heavily on the Infrastructure service.


15.3.2 Services: infrastructure and capture

Infrastructure — the delivery, compression, and storage needed to get hydrogen to users; every production route requests it (distributed routes less so).
CCS — the shared carbon-capture service, removing 90% of the CO₂ presented to it, requested by the SMR-, coal-, and biomass-with-CCS routes.

TODO: The hydrogen consumed elsewhere in CIMS is in several places drawn through generic fuel nodes (for example the Methane Blend service in industry, and the green-ammonia and HDRI-steel routes) rather than explicitly sourced from this sub-model. Link those hydrogen demands to the hydrogen Production competition so that the cost and carbon intensity of the hydrogen actually used is consistent across the model.

15.4.1 Blue hydrogen: SMR and gasification with CCS
The nearest-term low-carbon route keeps the established reforming or gasification process but adds carbon capture, cutting CO₂ by around 90%. It is the basis of Canada’s largest announced clean-hydrogen capacity, in Alberta, where low-cost natural gas and viable CO₂ storage favour it (Air Products 2024). In the model this is the SMR centralised + CCS, coal gasification + CCS, and biomass gasification + CCS routes, each requesting the shared CCS service.


15.4.2 Green and net-negative hydrogen
Electrolysis produces hydrogen with no direct CO₂; its footprint is the carbon intensity of the electricity, so it is genuinely “green” on Canada’s hydro and wind power but only as clean as the grid elsewhere. It is the most expensive route today, dominated by electricity cost and electrolyser capital, both of which are falling. Biomass gasification with CCS is distinctive: because the carbon is biogenic, capturing it yields net-negative hydrogen, one of the few production routes anywhere that removes CO₂ from the atmosphere.

title: 15  Hydrogen
text:
15.5 Economics
Technology choice at the production node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each route carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output basis, service requests for the fuel, feedstock, electricity, infrastructure, and capture it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Hydrogen technologies are discounted at roughly 25% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS this is a behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rate rather than a true financial cost of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real investment; CIMS applies it throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 25.
The emissions accounting is life-cycle, carrying CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O factors, so the upstream methane and the combustion and process CO₂ of each route are represented; the CCS service applies a 90% removal factor to the routes that request it, which can drive biomass-gasification hydrogen net-negative. Because the routes share an identical product, the carbon price acts directly on the production mix: as it rises, it raises the effective cost of grey SMR (through its large CO₂ factor) relative to the blue and green routes, shifting market share toward them. This makes hydrogen one of the clearest illustrations in CIMS of a carbon-price-driven technology transition.

title: 15  Hydrogen
text:
15.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the hydrogen structure, but the economic route differs sharply by region. Alberta and Saskatchewan, with cheap natural gas and CO₂ storage, favour blue hydrogen; Québec, British Columbia, and Manitoba, with abundant low-carbon hydro electricity, favour green electrolytic hydrogen; and the Atlantic region’s wind resource supports green production. The same competition therefore resolves to different winners in different regions, driven by local fuel and electricity prices.
TODO: Confirm the regional electricity and natural-gas prices and CO₂-storage availability that drive the blue-versus-green split, since the regional production mix is highly sensitive to them.

title: 15  Hydrogen
text:
15.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The hydrogen sub-model is compact but captures the essential structure of the production-route competition. Its main limitations are the loose coupling to the sectors that consume hydrogen, the absence of a turquoise (pyrolysis) route and of the investment tax credit, and reliance on inherited cost assumptions. The most important is the first: until the hydrogen demands in refining, ammonia, steel, and transport are explicitly sourced from this competition, the model can understate the system value of building clean-hydrogen supply. The TODOs above record these priorities.

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.1 Scope
The mining sector is represented in CIMS by an energy-service flow model. The emphasis is on the structure of that model — the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them — rather than on the geology or economics of individual mines. The model tree is region-agnostic: a single master structure is instantiated for every province and territory, and regional differences are expressed through which branches carry production and through the data attached to each node, not through separate per-region structures.
CIMS represents both metal mining and non-metal mining. Metal mining is split into open-pit and underground operations, and within open-pit into iron and non-iron ores. Non-metal mining is dominated, in energy terms, by potash, which is modelled in full; other non-metal commodities are lower-energy but are within the scope of the sector and are noted below where they are not yet built out. The driving variable for the sub-model is the physical throughput of ore, expressed in tonnes; a forecast of ore throughput drives the demand for every downstream process and energy service, and is set exogenously in the same way as the output of the other industrial branches.
Several activities that are colloquially called “mining” are deliberately handled elsewhere in CIMS to avoid double-counting energy and emissions:
The smelting and refining of mined concentrates is likewise excluded and handled in the Metal Smelting and Refining chapter; the mining sub-model stops at the mine gate, with a saleable concentrate or product as its final output.

title: 16  Mining
text:
Coal mining is covered in the Coal Mining chapter and the energy-supply component.
Oil and gas extraction and oil sands mining are covered under Petroleum Crude.
Cement, lime, glass, brick, and other non-metallic mineral products are covered under Industrial Minerals — these are downstream manufacturing branches, distinct from the extraction of the non-metal ores treated here.

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.2 Real-world context
Canada is one of the world’s leading mining nations, and the industry is highly regionalised. Metal mines produce base and precious metals — copper, nickel, zinc, gold, iron ore, and others — from both open-pit and underground operations. Saskatchewan is the world’s largest potash-producing region, accounting on the order of 30% of global potash production (Natural Resources Canada 2025), and also supplies roughly a quarter of the world’s uranium from the high-grade deposits of the Athabasca Basin (World Nuclear Association 2025). The Northwest Territories host Canada’s diamond industry, and Nunavut has growing gold and iron-ore production. Mining is capital-intensive and strongly export-oriented, so activity levels are driven by world commodity prices and ore grades rather than by domestic demand — which is why CIMS drives the sector with an exogenous throughput forecast rather than an endogenous demand response.
Mining is energy-intensive, and the energy is concentrated in a few activities. Comminution — the crushing, grinding, and milling that reduce run-of-mine rock to particles fine enough for mineral separation — is typically the single largest energy consumer at a metal mine; published estimates put it at roughly a quarter of final energy at an average mine site and a majority of mine electricity use (Coalition for Eco-Efficient Comminution 2021). Diesel dominates mobile equipment, particularly haulage, and is the largest single fuel at many sites; many remote northern mines are off-grid and rely heavily on diesel generation for all loads. Ventilation is a large and distinctively underground electricity load, since deep mines must move enormous volumes of air for air quality and temperature control. The CIMS structure is built around exactly these distinctions: it separates open-pit from underground mining, breaks the ore-processing chain into its comminution stages, and represents ventilation, fans, pumping, and the other utility loads through the shared machine-drive service (see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter).

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into two sub-trees: a Product sub-tree, which is the physical production chain that turns ore into a saleable product, and a Service sub-tree, which holds the auxiliary energy and utility services that the production technologies draw on. Figure 16.1 shows the overall structure.
As described in the Sector Overview, each node carries a competition rule. Fixed-ratio nodes impose the unavoidable engineering sequence of process steps, while tech-compete nodes host competitions among alternative technologies on the basis of lifecycle cost (see Chapter 4). In the mining tree, the disaggregation of products and process stages is built from fixed-ratio nodes, and the technology choices — which extraction method, which crusher, which boiler, which class of motor — occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 16.1: Energy-service flow model of the mining sector (region-agnostic master tree). The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — metal (open-pit iron and non-iron, and underground) and potash — and a Service sub-tree of auxiliary energy services structured on the EIA MECS end uses.




16.3.1 Products: metal mining
Metal mining divides first into Open Pit and Underground, reflecting the substantial difference in their energy profiles (most importantly the ventilation load that underground operations carry). Open-pit mining is then split into an Iron path and a Non-Iron path, because iron ore and base/precious-metal ores follow different processing routes:

The Iron path runs ore through a Raw Product stage (Extraction and Transportation), Primary and Secondary Crushing, and an Agglomeration stage that binds fine iron concentrate into a form suitable for downstream ironmaking.
The Non-Iron path runs ore through Raw Product (Extraction, Transportation), Primary and Secondary Crushing, and Primary Milling (fine grinding), but no agglomeration.

Both open-pit paths feed a set of shared stages — Mineral Separation, Cleaning (concentrate drying), Tailing Disposal, and an Unassigned Energy node. Underground mining carries the same processing chain (grouped under a Processing node: Raw Product, Primary and Secondary Crushing, Primary Milling) together with its own Mineral Separation, Cleaning, Tailing Disposal, and Unassigned Energy nodes.
The Unassigned Energy node is a reconciliation device: it carries metered sector energy that has not yet been allocated to a specific process stage, so that the modelled total matches reported energy use while the more detailed allocation is still being developed.
TODO: Progressively reassign the Unassigned Energy at each mine type to specific process stages and technologies, and reduce it toward zero as the bottom-up representation improves.


16.3.2 Products: non-metal mining
Non-metal mining is represented in the same Product sub-tree as a sibling of Metal. The dominant non-metal commodity by energy use is potash, whose structure is shown in Figure 16.2. Potash production is met from two distinct mining methods that have markedly different energy profiles, and the model represents both:

Conventional mining — underground extraction (at depths around 1,000 m), with its own Extraction, Transportation, Crush-and-Screen, and Dissolution stages.
Solution mining — used for deeper deposits (beyond roughly 1,500 m), where the ore is dissolved in situ and pumped to surface, with a simpler Extraction and Transportation chain.

Both methods feed a shared surface-processing and finishing train — Crystallization and Flotation (under Processing), followed by Drying, Compaction, and Tailings Disposal — and, like the metal mines, both draw on the cross-cutting energy and utility services.






Figure 16.2: Potash flow model. Potash is a non-metal product sibling of Metal; conventional (underground) and solution mining feed a shared processing and finishing train.



Canada’s other non-metal mining is smaller in energy terms but is within the scope of this sector and is included here for completeness. The most significant omissions are uranium and diamonds, both of which are material parts of the Canadian mining industry even though their energy intensity is lower than that of metal milling.
TODO: Add uranium mining (Saskatchewan, Athabasca Basin — e.g. McArthur River and Cigar Lake). Saskatchewan supplies roughly a quarter of world uranium; it is currently absent from the sector.
TODO: Add diamond mining (Northwest Territories) and other northern non-metal mining, once the corresponding regional data are in place.
TODO: Confirm whether lower-energy non-metal extraction such as salt, gypsum, and aggregates should be represented explicitly or remain aggregated, given their small share of mining energy.


16.3.3 Auxiliary energy and utility services
Mining’s production technologies draw on the shared Service sub-tree rather than specifying their own utility equipment. These services are common to the industrial sectors and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part; their general structure — and the “existing versus more efficient equipment, with fuel-switching where relevant” convention they follow — is set out in the Sector Overview. This chapter does not repeat that detail. The services the mining sector draws on are:

Machine Drive — see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter. Mining’s largest electrical loads sit here: comminution under Materials Processing, mine ventilation under Fans, and haulage and conveyance under Materials Handling, alongside Pumps and Compressed Air.
Steam — see Low-Temperature Industrial Heat, which covers boiler-raised steam and its fuel options.
Cogeneration — see Cogeneration for combined heat-and-power.
Methane Blend — the gaseous-fuel supply node, where natural gas competes with biogas, biomass gasification, and hydrogen.
HVAC (space heating and cooling) and Lighting for mine facilities.

TODO: The current regional input files still implement an earlier, more detailed auxiliary structure (per-horsepower machine-drive classes; separate pumping, compression, ventilation, and conveyance sub-trees) and predate the Product/Service split. Migrate these files to the region-agnostic master tree and the shared General Services chapters referenced above.

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Mining’s emissions are dominated by diesel in mobile equipment and by the electricity and combustion that drive comminution, process heat, and ventilation. The main decarbonisation levers therefore sit at the Extraction and Transportation nodes (mobile equipment), the comminution stages (Crushing, Milling), Cleaning (concentrate drying), and underground ventilation, alongside the shared services documented in the General Services chapters. The technologies below are admitted to the relevant tech-compete nodes; representative performance and maturity are summarised in Table 16.1. The figures quoted are indicative ranges from industry and techno-economic reviews (Mungyeko Bisulandu et al. 2026), not the calibrated values used in the model.

16.4.1 Mobile equipment and haulage
Diesel haulage is the largest single diesel load at most surface mines. Trolley-assist systems feed the truck’s electric drive from an overhead catenary on the energy-intensive loaded uphill segments, cutting energy use on those segments by roughly 40–60% and lifecycle CO₂ by about 28–36% where the connected grid is low-carbon; the technology is commercial and deployed at several open-pit operations (Mungyeko Bisulandu et al. 2026). Battery-electric haul trucks, now offered by the major equipment makers, remove tailpipe diesel entirely but are constrained by range and charging time and remain early-commercial; hydrogen fuel-cell haul trucks are at the demonstration stage. Biodiesel and renewable diesel are drop-in fuels that cut lifecycle CO₂ without new equipment and are already represented in the tree (the “Extraction Biodiesel” and “Biodiesel truck” technologies). In CIMS these options compete at the Extraction and Transportation nodes.


16.4.2 Comminution efficiency
Comminution is the single largest electricity consumer at a metal mine, so efficiency gains here have an outsized effect. High-pressure grinding rolls (HPGR) pre-fracture ore between counter-rotating rolls and reduce downstream grinding energy by about 20–30%. Vertical roller and stirred mills can deliver on the order of 40% energy savings relative to conventional ball mills and combine grinding with drying in a single unit. Ore sorting and pre-concentration reject barren rock before milling, lowering the energy spent per unit of contained metal, though their applicability is deposit-specific (Mungyeko Bisulandu et al. 2026). These compete at the Crushing and Milling nodes, while ore sorting acts as a service-side reduction in the feed sent to milling.


16.4.3 Electrified and low-carbon process heat
Concentrate drying (Cleaning) and process steam are met largely by combustion today. The low- and zero-emission alternatives — electric and heat-pump drying, electrode and electric-resistance boilers, biomass and hydrogen boilers, and mechanical vapour recompression — are described in the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter and reached through the Steam service; the Methane Blend node additionally substitutes biogas, biomass gas, and hydrogen for natural gas in any remaining gas-fired duty.


16.4.4 Ventilation and auxiliary drive (underground)
Ventilation can account for roughly 40–50% of an underground mine’s energy use. Ventilation on demand (VOD) matches airflow to where vehicles and crews are actually working and can cut ventilation energy by up to about 50% (ABB 2024); high-efficiency fans and motors with variable-speed drives further reduce auxiliary drive energy. These are represented through the Fans and other machine-drive end uses described in the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter.


16.4.5 Potash-specific options
Conventional potash mining already relies on electric continuous miners and electric hoisting, so its decarbonisation depends mainly on grid emissions intensity and on electrifying surface haulage; VOD applies in the underground workings. Solution mining and the surface Drying and Compaction stages are heat-intensive and decarbonise through the same low-carbon heat options as above — in particular mechanical vapour recompression for crystallization and evaporation duties, and electric or biomass boilers for drying.


16.4.6 Indicative capital and operating costs and energy use
Table 16.2 gathers order-of-magnitude capital and operating costs and energy characteristics for the main comminution and mobile-equipment technologies. The estimates are drawn from public techno-economic literature (Coalition for Eco-Efficient Comminution 2021; Mungyeko Bisulandu et al. 2026; SRK Consulting 2024) and expressed in 2025 Canadian dollars: US-dollar sources were converted at the mid-2025 rate of roughly 1.37 CAD/USD and adjusted to 2025 where the source year differed. Because mining capital is dominated by site-specific concentrators and mobile fleets, the figures are given per piece of equipment or relative to a baseline rather than per tonne of capacity where that is more meaningful; energy intensity is per tonne of ore. Fixed O&M follows the heavy-industry convention of roughly 4–6% of capital cost per year. The values are for relative comparison only, not project budgeting, and are separate from the plant-specific values the model carries internally.

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, a service request for the energy or upstream service it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
A few sector-wide conventions are worth noting. Mining technologies are discounted at a high rate (35% in the current data). These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital: they sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions, and CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation (see the discount-rate discussion in the Theory chapter and Chapter 4). Heterogeneity (variance) parameters at the process nodes are set so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all. Fuel prices entering the service-cost calculation are scaled by a sector-level block of price multipliers, allowing the mining sector to face prices that differ from the generic delivered price of each fuel.
Greenhouse-gas costs enter through the fuels: combustion emissions follow from each technology’s fuel service requests and the prevailing carbon price, so fuel-switching — from diesel haulage to biodiesel or electric, or from natural gas to hydrogen or biogas in the methane blend — is the model’s main channel for emissions reduction.
TODO: Mining has no carbon-capture (CCS) service in the current tree (see the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage chapter), on the assumption that its emissions are predominantly combustion-related and dispersed. Confirm this is appropriate, and add process-emissions representation if any mined commodity warrants it.

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.6 Regional coverage and differences
Because the tree is region-agnostic, every province and territory is built from the same master structure, and a region simply carries no production on the branches that do not apply to it. Regional differences therefore show up in where production sits rather than in the shape of the tree:

Potash production is concentrated in Saskatchewan, which carries essentially all of the potash branch.
Iron ore is concentrated in the Atlantic region (the Labrador Trough, on the Québec–Newfoundland border) and Québec, which carry most of the open-pit iron path.
Base- and precious-metal mining is spread across British Columbia, Ontario, Manitoba, Québec, and the Atlantic region (for example nickel in Manitoba and Ontario, and copper and gold in British Columbia), populating the non-iron and underground branches.
Territorial mining — diamonds in the Northwest Territories and gold and iron ore in Nunavut — populates the metal and (future) non-metal branches in those regions.

TODO: Several regions are not yet populated in the current input files. Build out mining throughput and technology data for Alberta and the three territories (the territories are not yet represented anywhere in CIMS — see the Architecture chapter), so that the region-agnostic tree is exercised everywhere it should be.
TODO: The Atlantic, Manitoba, Ontario, and Québec metal mines are currently represented generically rather than by commodity. Consider whether the Iron / Non-Iron split, plus any commodity-specific energy intensities, adequately capture the real mix in each region, and refine where the averaging is too coarse.

title: 16  Mining
text:
16.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The mining sub-model is a deliberately simplified representation. The TODOs above record the main gaps between this design and both the current input files and the real Canadian mining sector: the auxiliary-service migration to the MECS structure; the reassignment of Unassigned Energy; the addition of uranium, diamonds, and the smaller non-metal commodities; full provincial and territorial coverage including Alberta and the territories; and the question of commodity-level detail within metal mining. Together these define the path from the current state of the model to the region-agnostic, fully populated design described in this chapter.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.1 Scope
The industrial minerals sector — the non-metallic mineral products industry — is represented in CIMS by an energy-service flow model. The emphasis is on the structure of that model: the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them, rather than the chemistry or economics of individual plants. The model tree is region-agnostic: a single master structure is instantiated for every province, and regional differences are expressed through which branches carry production and through the data attached to each node. The sector is defined by high-temperature thermal processing — calcining, clinkering, and glass melting — and, like chemicals, a large share of its emissions are process emissions released by the chemistry of calcination rather than by burning fuel. That single fact shapes both the sub-model and its decarbonisation options.
CIMS represents the four energy-intensive branches of the non-metallic mineral products industry: cement, lime, glass, and bricks. Cement and lime dominate the sector’s energy and emissions because both depend on calcining carbonate rock at high temperature. The driving variable is the physical output of product in tonnes; a forecast of demand — closely tied to construction activity — drives every upstream process and energy service and is set exogenously, as for the other industrial branches.
Several adjacent activities are deliberately handled elsewhere in CIMS to avoid double-counting energy and emissions:

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
Quarrying and extraction of the raw minerals (limestone, silica, clay, aggregates) are part of the Mining sector and the upstream supply; the industrial-minerals sub-model begins with raw-material preparation inside the plant gate.
Concrete batching and downstream fabrication (ready-mix concrete, precast products, finished glazing) are downstream manufacturing and are not part of this sub-model, which ends with cement, lime, glass, and brick as saleable products.
Fuel and electricity supply enter through the energy-supply sub-models and the shared fuel nodes.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.2 Real-world context
The industrial minerals sector is small in tonnage relative to its emissions, because calcination releases CO₂ as an unavoidable part of the chemistry. Canadian cement manufacturing alone emitted about 11.2 Mt CO₂ in 2019, roughly 1.5% of national emissions, and calcination accounts for some 60–65% of the CO₂ from clinker production — released when limestone (CaCO₃) is broken down into lime (CaO) and CO₂ — with the rest coming from the fuel burned to reach clinkering temperature (Cement Association of Canada and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada 2022; International Energy Agency 2024). Lime production is chemically the same calcination step without the clinkering, and carries an even higher process-CO₂ intensity per tonne of product. Glass is melted rather than calcined, so its emissions are dominated by furnace fuel and by the carbonate batch materials, and brick is fired clay.
Production is concentrated in the populous provinces and tracks construction demand, so unlike most heavy industry it is growing in the model. Ontario is the largest producer, followed by Québec and a fast-growing Alberta, with British Columbia and the Atlantic region smaller. Because so much of the sector’s CO₂ is intrinsic to the chemistry, deep decarbonisation depends on options that most other sectors do not need — carbon capture on the kiln, substitution of clinker with other materials, alternative raw meals that avoid carbonate, and CO₂ mineralisation (carbon curing) — alongside the fuel-switching and efficiency levers common to all industry. The CIMS structure reflects this: it carries explicit process-emission factors on the clinker and lime nodes, a shared CCS service, and a family of clinker-substitution, alternative-fuel, electrified-kiln, and carbon-curing options.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into a Product sub-tree, holding the cement, lime, glass, and brick production chains, and a Service sub-tree, holding the auxiliary energy and utility services including a sector-level Heat service and the shared CCS service. Figure 17.1 shows the overall structure.
As described in the Sector Overview, each node carries a competition rule. Fixed-ratio nodes impose the unavoidable engineering sequence of process steps, while tech-compete nodes host competitions among alternative technologies on the basis of lifecycle cost (see Chapter 4). In the industrial-minerals tree, the disaggregation into products and process stages is built from fixed-ratio nodes, while the technology choices — which kiln, which furnace, which fuel, which clinker route — occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 17.1: Energy-service flow model of the industrial minerals sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree holds cement, lime, glass, and brick chains; the Service sub-tree holds a sector-level Heat service, the MECS-aligned Machine Drive, and the shared CCS service that the calcination routes draw on.




17.3.1 Products: cement
Cement is the most important chain. At the top, a Cement competition selects the overall production strategy — conventional Std process, Increased clinker substitution (replacing clinker with supplementary cementitious materials), and Carbon curing (curing concrete by mineralising CO₂, which the model treats as a net-negative emission). Beneath this, Portland cement resolves into:

Clinker — the energy-and-emissions core, produced in a Dry process rotary kiln or a Fluidized bed. The rotary-kiln node competes a wide range of routes: conventional and efficiency-retrofitted kilns, new preheater and precalciner designs, waste-heat-recovery cogeneration, a new preheat Eff with CCS route, an electrochemical synthesis (electrified clinker) route, and a Std process with calcium minerals route that uses a non-carbonate raw meal to avoid process CO₂ altogether. The fluidized-bed node competes a range of fuels — natural gas, coal, petcoke, distillate oil, and waste-derived and hazardous-waste fuels.
Finish Grinding — ball mills and roller mills with high-efficiency separators that grind clinker into cement.
Dry Ground Cement — raw-meal preparation.

The clinker routes carry an explicit process-CO₂ factor (about 0.44 t per unit in the data) reflecting calcination; the calcium-mineral and carbon-curing options are the model’s way of breaking that link.


17.3.2 Products: lime, glass, and bricks

Lime is produced in Kilns (and a Dolomitic branch) competing rotary and vertical-shaft kilns on a range of fuels (NG, coal, petcoke, residual oil), with preheater and internals variants for efficiency, CCS-equipped rotary kilns (NG and coal), and an electrochemical synthesis route. Lime carries the sector’s highest process-CO₂ factor (about 0.75 t per unit).
Glass divides into Container, Flat, Fibreglass, and Blown/Pressed glass, each a chain of Preparation, Furnaces, and Form and Finish (flat glass adds Temper; blown/pressed adds Fire Polish). The furnace competitions are where the energy and emissions are decided, and they include regenerative and oxy-boosted melters, fluidized-bed cullet/batch preheaters, advanced glass melters, and all-electric melters (including fluidized-bed electric melters).
Bricks are fired in Hoffman or tunnel kilns on natural gas, coal, or residual oil.



17.3.3 Services, including process heat and CCS
The services follow the standard pattern and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part; their structure is set out in the Sector Overview. Two are worth noting here:

Heat — a sector-level process-heat service whose technology set is unusually broad, competing natural-gas (standard and efficient), oil, coal, coke, biomass, waste-fuel, hydrogen, and CCS-equipped (NG and coal) heat supply. This is a key fuel-switching lever for the non-calcination heat demand.
CCS — the shared carbon-capture service that the CCS-equipped clinker, lime, and heat routes request; its broader treatment is in the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage chapter.

The remaining services — Machine Drive (see Industrial Machine Drive Systems), Methane Blend, HVAC, and Lighting — are the cross-cutting utilities common to all sectors.

They also name the product branch Products rather than the master tree’s Product. Migrate these files to the region-agnostic master tree and the shared General Services chapters.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Because most of the sector’s CO₂ comes from calcining carbonate rock, its decarbonisation problem is unusual: efficiency and fuel-switching can only reach the combustion share, so deep cuts require capturing or avoiding the process CO₂ as well. Roughly the first 30–40% of cement emissions can be abated with clinker substitution, alternative fuels, and efficiency, while the remaining 60–70% — the calcination CO₂ — needs CCUS or alternative production chemistry (U.S. Department of Energy 2023; Cement Association of Canada and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada 2022). The model represents the full ladder. Table 17.1 summarises maturity and Table 17.2 gives indicative costs.

17.4.1 Reducing and substituting clinker
The cheapest cement reductions come from making less clinker per tonne of cement. Supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) — slag, fly ash, calcined clay, limestone, and natural pozzolans — replace a share of clinker; limestone calcined clay cement (LC3) can cut cement CO₂ by around 40% and is commercial (U.S. Department of Energy 2023). The model represents this as the Increased clinker substitution route at the Cement node. A complementary lever is the Std process with calcium minerals clinker route, which uses a non-carbonate raw meal so that calcination releases no CO₂ at all.


17.4.2 Alternative fuels, efficiency, and waste-heat recovery
The combustion share of kiln emissions is addressed by alternative and waste-derived fuels (biomass, refuse-derived and hazardous-waste fuels in the fluidized-bed routes and the Heat service), by preheater/precalciner designs and efficiency retrofits that cut fuel use, and by waste-heat-recovery cogeneration that turns kiln exhaust heat into on-site power. These are mature and often cost-saving, but they cannot touch the calcination CO₂.


17.4.3 Carbon capture, electrification, and mineralisation
Deep cuts require attacking the process CO₂. The model offers three routes: CCS on the kiln (cement and lime), which captures most of the CO₂ but adds 30–50% more plant equipment and a capture energy penalty; electrochemical/electrified clinker and lime, which both remove the combustion CO₂ and produce a purer CO₂ stream that is cheaper to capture; and carbon curing, which mineralises CO₂ into concrete and is the one route the model scores as net-negative. On the glass side, electric and oxy-fuel melters and cullet preheating electrify or concentrate furnace emissions. Low-carbon process heat — biomass, hydrogen, and CCS-equipped boilers in the Heat service — addresses the non-calcination thermal demand, drawing on the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, service requests for the energy and upstream services it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Industrial minerals technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes in the current data, with some auxiliary and capital-intensive nodes at 40–50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital. They sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions; CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters at the process nodes are mostly set around 10 so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all.
The sector’s emissions accounting is distinctive. Combustion emissions follow from each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price, as in the other sectors. In addition, the clinker and lime technologies carry explicit process-emission factors (about 0.44 and 0.75 t CO₂ per unit) representing calcination, applied independently of fuel use; the carbon-curing route carries a net-negative emission factor; and the CCS service applies an emissions-removal factor to the technologies that request it. Switching among conventional, substituted, alternative-fuel, captured, and electrified production is therefore the model’s main channel for emissions reduction, driven by the interaction of fuel and material costs with a carbon price that applies to both the combustion and the process CO₂.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.6 Regional coverage and differences
Because the tree is region-agnostic, each modelled province is built from the same master structure and carries no production on branches that do not apply. Five regions are represented — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Ontario, and Québec — and differences show up in scale and growth rather than in the shape of the tree:

Ontario is the largest producer and grows over the projection.
Québec and a fast-growing Alberta follow, reflecting construction-driven demand.
British Columbia and the Atlantic region are smaller.

Unlike most heavy industry, modelled output rises in every region, because cement, lime, and glass demand tracks population and construction rather than declining commodity markets.

title: 17  Industrial Minerals
text:
17.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The industrial minerals sub-model is detailed on the product side but carries the same structural debts as the other older sector files. The TODOs above record the main gaps: the migration of the auxiliary services to the MECS-aligned Machine Drive and the Product/Service split; the disaggregation of clinker substitution into specific SCM pathways; and broader provincial coverage. The sector’s growth trajectory and its large process-emission share make it one of the most important to keep current, since it is one of the few industrial branches whose absolute emissions are projected to rise without intervention.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.1 Scope
The chemical products sector is represented in CIMS by an energy-service flow model. The emphasis is on the structure of that model: the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them, rather than the chemistry or economics of individual plants. The model tree is region-agnostic: a single master structure is instantiated for every province, and regional differences are expressed through which branches carry production and through the data attached to each node. Unlike most other industrial branches, chemicals is not dominated by a single energy-intensive product; it is a collection of distinct production chains, and a large share of its emissions are process emissions — CO₂ released by the reforming and cracking of hydrocarbon feedstock, and N₂O from acid production — rather than combustion of fuel. This shapes both the structure of the sub-model and the decarbonisation options it admits.
CIMS represents the energy-intensive chemical products that dominate the sector’s energy and emissions, organised as separate production chains: ammonia and methanol; the chlor-alkali group (chlorine, caustic soda) together with sodium chlorate and hydrogen peroxide; adipic acid; and other petrochemicals — the olefins and aromatics made by steam cracking and reforming, and the polymers made from them. The driving variable is the physical output of chemical product in tonnes; a forecast of demand drives every upstream process and energy service and is set exogenously, as for the other industrial branches.
Several adjacent activities are deliberately handled elsewhere in CIMS to avoid double-counting energy and emissions:
The sub-model stops at saleable primary and intermediate chemicals and polymers; downstream compounding and plastics fabrication belong to the manufacturing branches.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
Petroleum refining — the production of fuels and refinery streams from crude oil — is covered in the Petroleum Refining chapter; the chemicals sub-model takes refinery and gas-plant streams (ethane, naphtha, natural gas) as feedstock rather than producing them.
Merchant hydrogen production is covered in the Hydrogen chapter; where the chemicals sub-model uses hydrogen as a reactant (for example in electrolytic ammonia) it draws on that representation rather than rebuilding it.
Fuel and feedstock supply (natural gas, oil, ethane) enters through the energy-supply sub-models and the shared fuel nodes; the chemicals sub-model consumes these as priced inputs.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.2 Real-world context
Canada’s chemical industry is large, export-oriented, and strongly regionalised, and it sits on the country’s cheap natural gas. Alberta hosts the largest concentration of chemical and petrochemical plants in Canada, centred on the Industrial Heartland northeast of Edmonton: its four ethane crackers have a combined capacity of about 4.1 Mt/yr of ethylene, roughly 80% of national capacity, and the province is also the centre of ammonia, urea, and methanol production, which locate near low-cost gas feedstock (Invest Alberta 2025; Canada Energy Regulator 2024). Ontario has the most diverse slate, including the country’s adipic-acid production, alongside petrochemicals and chlor-alkali; Québec and Saskatchewan add ammonia/fertilizer and petrochemical capacity; and British Columbia is dominated by the pulp-bleaching chemicals — chlor-alkali, sodium chlorate, and hydrogen peroxide — rather than petrochemicals.
What distinguishes chemicals from the other industrial sectors is the central role of feedstock and process chemistry in its emissions. In ammonia and methanol, natural gas is reformed to make synthesis gas, and the carbon in that gas is released as CO₂ as an unavoidable part of the chemistry; grey ammonia carries roughly 1.8–2.4 t CO₂ per tonne on this basis (RMI 2024b). In steam cracking, high-temperature furnaces break naphtha or ethane into olefins, releasing both combustion and process CO₂. In adipic and nitric acid production, nitrous oxide (N₂O) — a greenhouse gas with roughly 270–300 times the warming potential of CO₂ — is the dominant emission. The CIMS structure is built around exactly these distinctions: it carries explicit process-emission factors (CO₂ and N₂O) on the relevant technologies in addition to their fuel use, and it admits the abatement options — carbon capture, electrolytic hydrogen, N₂O destruction, and bio-feedstock — that target each.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into a Product sub-tree, which holds the distinct chemical production chains, and a Service sub-tree, which holds the auxiliary energy and utility services the production technologies draw on. Figure 18.1 shows the overall structure.
As described in the Sector Overview, each node carries a competition rule. Fixed-ratio nodes impose the unavoidable engineering sequence of process steps, while tech-compete nodes host competitions among alternative technologies on the basis of lifecycle cost (see Chapter 4). In the chemicals tree, the disaggregation into products and process stages is built from fixed-ratio nodes, while the technology choices — which synthesis route, which electrolysis cell, which cracker — occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 18.1: Energy-service flow model of the chemical products sector (region-agnostic master tree). The sector divides into a Product sub-tree of distinct chemical chains — ammonia and methanol, chlor-alkali, sodium chlorate, hydrogen peroxide, adipic acid, and other petrochemicals — and a Service sub-tree of auxiliary energy services structured on the EIA MECS end uses, plus the shared CCS service.




18.3.1 Products: ammonia and methanol
The Ammonia Methanol chain is the most emissions-significant in the sector, because reforming natural gas to synthesis gas releases process CO₂ before any fuel is burned. The model carries three production nodes — Ammonia Synthesis, Methanol Synthesis, and a Combined Ammonia Methanol Synthesis node for co-production plants — each a tech-compete node among:

Reform and synthesis — the conventional steam-methane-reforming route (grey ammonia/methanol), carrying a process-CO₂ factor of about 0.9 t per unit in the data.
New AMV process and Advanced reforming reactors — more efficient reforming routes.
Advanced reforming reactors CCS — the same route with carbon capture (blue ammonia/methanol).
Hydrogen ammonia synthesis — ammonia made from electrolytic (“green”) hydrogen, which displaces reforming entirely.

This is exactly the grey → blue → green progression along which the real industry is moving, and the model represents it as a cost-and-carbon-price-driven competition.


18.3.2 Products: chlor-alkali, sodium chlorate, and hydrogen peroxide
These electrochemical and bleaching chemicals are grouped together and are largely electricity-driven, so their emissions track the grid:

Chlor-Alkali splits into Chlorine Electrolysis — competing membrane, diaphragm, and the legacy mercury cells — and Caustic Sodium, with a Caustic Process (electrolytic or non-electrolytic) and an energy-intensive Chlor-Alkali Evaporation stage offering progressively more efficient evaporator trains.
Sodium Chlorate competes graphite-electrode and metal-anode electrolysis cells and a bipolar membrane route that yields caustic as a by-product.
Hydrogen Peroxide competes the dominant anthraquinone route against a methyl-benzyl-alcohol route.



18.3.3 Products: adipic acid and other petrochemicals
Adipic Acid (a nylon precursor) is a tech-compete node whose significance is its N₂O process emission; the competition is between conventional Production and Production with N₂O controls, the latter destroying most of the nitrous oxide.
Other Petrochemicals is the olefins-and-aromatics chain. A Pyrolysis (steam-cracking) node makes the primary product gas and competes:

Product gas — conventional steam cracking (process-CO₂ factor ~0.85);
Product gas new catalyst — a higher-efficiency variant (~0.68);
Product gas CCS — cracking with carbon capture (~0.24);
Ligno Fischer-Tropsch naphtha steam cracker — a bio-based feedstock route.

Downstream, Petrochemicals covers Intermediate Production, BTX Reforming (benzene-toluene-xylene aromatics), and All Polymerization (conversion of monomers to polymers).


18.3.4 Auxiliary energy and utility services
The remaining services are common to the industrial sectors and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part; their general structure — and the “existing versus more efficient equipment, with fuel-switching where relevant” convention they follow — is set out in the Sector Overview. This chapter does not repeat that detail. The chemicals sector draws on:

Machine Drive — see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter. The sector’s large motive loads sit here: compressors (a major load in synthesis and refrigeration), pumps, fans, and materials handling and processing.
Steam — see Low-Temperature Industrial Heat, covering boiler- and turbine-raised steam and its fuel options, including electric, hydrogen, and CCS-equipped variants. Steam is a large load in chemicals.
Methane Blend — the gaseous-fuel supply node, where natural gas competes with biogas, biomass gasification, and hydrogen.
HVAC (space heating and cooling) and Lighting for plant facilities.
CCS — the shared carbon-capture service that the reforming, cracking, and other equipped routes request.

TODO: The current regional input files still implement an earlier, more detailed auxiliary structure (six per-horsepower machine-drive size classes; separate Compression, Conveyance, Pumping, Ventilation, and Direct Drive sub-trees) and predate the Product/Service split and the MECS-aligned Machine Drive grouping. Migrate these files to the region-agnostic master tree and the shared General Services chapters.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Because so much of the sector’s emissions are tied to feedstock chemistry rather than to energy use, its decarbonisation levers are unusual: the decisive choices are the synthesis and cracking routes (and whether their process CO₂ is captured or avoided), and the destruction of N₂O in acid production, alongside the electrification of heat and the decarbonisation of the grid that already powers the electrochemical products. The technologies below are admitted to the relevant tech-compete nodes; representative performance and maturity are summarised in Table 18.1. The figures quoted are indicative ranges from techno-economic reviews (RMI 2024a, 2024b), not the calibrated values used in the model.

The cost estimates in Table 18.2 gather order-of-magnitude capital and operating costs and energy characteristics for the main chemical products and routes, drawn from public techno-economic literature (International Renewable Energy Agency and Ammonia Energy Association 2022; RMI 2024b, 2024a) and expressed in 2025 Canadian dollars: US-dollar sources were converted at the mid-2025 rate of roughly 1.37 CAD/USD and adjusted to 2025 where the source year differed. Overnight capital costs are normalised per tonne of annual product capacity (the specific product is noted where it is not the headline product), fixed O&M follows the heavy-industry convention of roughly 3–6% of capital cost per year, and energy intensity is per tonne of product and includes feedstock energy where the feedstock is also the energy source (as in reforming and cracking). The values are for relative comparison only, not project budgeting, and are separate from the plant-specific values the model carries internally.

The conventional reform-and-synthesis route carries a large process-CO₂ emission; the model competes it against efficiency improvements, a CCS variant (blue), and an electrolytic-hydrogen route (green), with CCS-equipped routes drawing on the shared CCS service.




18.4.1 Feedstock and synthesis routes: blue and green ammonia and methanol
Reforming natural gas is the single largest source of process CO₂ in the sector, and Figure 18.2 shows how the model represents the alternatives. Two routes cut it. Blue production keeps the reformer but captures its CO₂ — represented as Advanced reforming reactors CCS, drawing on the shared CCS service. Green production replaces the reformer with electrolytic hydrogen — represented as Hydrogen ammonia synthesis — cutting emissions by roughly 95–98% relative to grey ammonia when the electricity is low-carbon (RMI 2024b). Both compete against the conventional and efficiency-improved reforming routes as costs and the carbon price evolve.


18.4.2 Electrified and low-carbon cracking
Steam cracking is both energy- and emissions-intensive. The model represents three decarbonisation paths at the Pyrolysis node: carbon capture on the cracker (cutting the process-CO₂ factor from ~0.85 to ~0.24 in the data), a higher-efficiency catalyst (to ~0.68), and a bio-naphtha feedstock from lignocellulosic Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, which substitutes renewable carbon for fossil. Beyond what the current tree contains, the most prominent emerging option is electrified steam cracking, demonstrated at pilot scale by a BASF–SABIC–Linde plant, which can transfer about 95% of its heat to the process and cut cracking-furnace CO₂ by up to ~90% when run on low-carbon electricity (BASF 2024; RMI 2024a).
TODO: Add an electrified steam cracking technology to the Pyrolysis competition (electricity-driven furnace, near-zero direct combustion emissions), so the model can represent the electrification pathway now being demonstrated commercially.


18.4.3 N₂O abatement in acid production
Adipic and nitric acid production emit N₂O, which dominates their greenhouse-gas footprint because of its very high global warming potential. Catalytic N₂O destruction is a mature, high-impact abatement option, represented in the model as Production with N₂O controls at the Adipic Acid node. Because the abatement targets a non-CO₂ gas, its value in the model depends on the carbon price being applied to N₂O on a CO₂-equivalent basis.


18.4.4 Carbon capture
Carbon capture is represented as a shared CCS service that any equipped route requests. It is especially well suited to chemicals because several of the sector’s CO₂ streams — from reforming and from cracking — are relatively concentrated and therefore cheaper to capture than dilute flue gas. The CCS-equipped variants (Advanced reforming reactors CCS, Product gas CCS) route their CO₂ to this service; its broader treatment, including transport and storage and the associated costs, is in the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage chapter.


18.4.5 Electrified heat and efficient drives
Process steam and lower-temperature heat can shift from gas to electricity and hydrogen through the Steam and Methane Blend services described in the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter, and the large compressor and pump loads can move to high-efficiency motors and variable-speed drives in the Machine Drive service. The electrochemical products (chlor-alkali, sodium chlorate) are already electricity-driven, so their decarbonisation depends mainly on grid intensity and on choosing the more efficient cell and evaporator technologies the model already competes.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, service requests for the energy and upstream services it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
A few sector-wide conventions are worth noting. Chemicals technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes in the current data, with some auxiliary and capital-intensive nodes at 40–50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital. They sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions; CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters at the process nodes are set around 10 so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all.
Greenhouse-gas costs enter through three channels, which is what makes chemicals distinctive. Combustion emissions follow from each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price, as in the other sectors. In addition, many chemical technologies carry an explicit process-emission factor — CO₂ from reforming (~0.9 per unit) and cracking (~0.85, falling with efficient catalysts and capture), and N₂O from adipic acid and intermediate production — applied independently of fuel use. Finally, the CCS service applies an emissions-removal factor to the technologies that request it. Route-switching among grey, blue, green, and bio-based production is therefore the model’s main channel for emissions reduction, and it is driven by the interaction of feedstock prices, capital costs, and the carbon price applied to both CO₂ and N₂O.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.6 Regional coverage and differences
Because the tree is region-agnostic, each modelled province is built from the same master structure and simply carries no production on the branches that do not apply to it. Five regions are represented — Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — and regional differences show up in which products a region makes and at what scale:

Alberta is by far the largest, and is dominated by ammonia/methanol and petrochemicals, consistent with its gas-based Industrial Heartland; its modelled output grows over the projection.
Ontario carries the most diverse slate and is the only region with adipic acid, alongside ammonia/methanol, chlor-alkali, hydrogen peroxide, petrochemicals, and sodium chlorate.
Québec and Saskatchewan carry ammonia/methanol, the chlor-alkali group, and petrochemicals at smaller scale.
British Columbia carries the pulp-bleaching chemicals — chlor-alkali, sodium chlorate, and hydrogen peroxide — and ammonia/methanol, but no petrochemicals branch.

title: 18  Chemical Products
text:
18.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The chemicals sub-model is a deliberately simplified representation of an unusually heterogeneous sector. The TODOs above record the main gaps between this design and both the current input files and the real Canadian sector: the migration of the auxiliary services to the MECS-aligned Machine Drive and the Product/Service split; the addition of electrified steam cracking; an explicit link from green ammonia to the hydrogen sub-model; and the refresh of the exogenous demand trajectories. A further structural simplification is that Other Petrochemicals is represented as an aggregated olefins-aromatics-polymers chain rather than by individual product (ethylene, propylene, BTX, specific polymers); this keeps the tree tractable but limits product-level resolution.
