title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
19.1 Scope
As with the other industrial sub-models, the emphasis in the pulp and paper sector is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them — rather than on the chemistry or economics of individual mills. Pulp and paper is distinctive among the industrial branches in two ways. First, it is already largely powered by biomass — the spent pulping liquor and wood residues the mills produce themselves — so its on-site fossil emissions are concentrated in a few stages rather than spread across the whole process. Second, much of the traditional mill products have been declining for many years in Canada, as the long fall in newsprint demand works through the fleet. Both shape the sub-model and the decarbonisation options it admits.
CIMS represents the manufacture of pulp, paper and paperboard — the energy-intensive core of the sector — organised as a pulp-making chain feeding a set of paper-grade chains. The driving variable is the physical output of pulp and paper in tonnes; a forecast of demand drives every upstream process and energy service and is set exogenously, as for the other industrial branches.
Several adjacent activities are deliberately handled elsewhere in CIMS to avoid double-counting energy and emissions:
The sub-model stops at saleable pulp and paper grades.

title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
Forest harvesting and the supply of roundwood and residues are covered in the Forestry chapter; the pulp and paper sub-model takes logs, chips and recovered paper as inputs.
Converted paper products — boxes, bags, asphalt roofing, and other converting industries — are downstream manufacturing and are handled in the Light Industrial branch, not here.
Fuel and electricity supply enter through the energy-supply sub-models and the shared fuel nodes; the sub-model consumes these as priced inputs and, importantly, can also generate electricity and steam on site (see below).

title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
19.2 Real-world context
Canadian pulp and paper is large, export-oriented, regionally concentrated, and in long-run decline (unless significant changes occur within the sector). The industry is largest in Québec, Ontario and British Columbia, with significant capacity in the Atlantic region and a smaller presence in Alberta. Its economic output peaked around 2004 and fell by roughly 45% to 2018 as newsprint demand collapsed (Canada Energy Regulator 2019); the model’s exogenous demand trajectories reflect this, with output declining over the projection in every region except Alberta.
What most distinguishes the sector energetically is its reliance on self-produced biomass energy. Kraft (chemical) mills concentrate and burn the black liquor — the spent cooking chemicals and dissolved wood lignin left after pulping — in a recovery boiler that both regenerates the pulping chemicals and raises high-pressure steam; mills also burn hog fuel (bark and wood residues). Together these supply the majority of mill energy, and a growing number of mills run biomass cogeneration, meeting their own steam and power needs and selling surplus electricity to the grid: self-generation supplied on the order of a quarter of the sector’s electricity in recent years, across dozens of cogeneration units (Canada Energy Regulator 2019; Canadian Climate Institute 2023). Because this energy is biogenic, the sector’s fossil emissions are comparatively small and concentrated — most prominently in the lime kiln, which calcines lime for the kraft chemical cycle and has traditionally burned natural gas or oil, and in any remaining fossil-fired steam and drying (Pulp and Paper Canada 2024). The CIMS structure mirrors this: it carries an explicit Black Liquor service representing the recovery-and-energy cycle, it offers biomass and cogeneration options throughout the Steam service, and it concentrates the fossil-fuel choices at the lime kiln and the dryers.

title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
19.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into two sub-trees: a Product sub-tree, which holds the pulp-making and paper-making chains, and a Service sub-tree, which holds the auxiliary energy and utility services — including the sector-specific black-liquor recovery cycle. Figure 19.1 shows the overall structure.
In the pulp and paper tree, the disaggregation into products and process stages is built from fixed-ratio nodes, while the technology choices — which pulping process, which bleaching sequence, which dryer, which recovery furnace — occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 19.1: Energy-service flow model of the pulp and paper sector (region-agnostic master tree). The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — a pulp-making chain (log preparation, pulping, washing, bleaching, drying) and five paper-grade chains — and a Service sub-tree that holds the auxiliary energy services plus the sector-specific Black Liquor recovery-and-energy cycle.




19.3.1 Products: pulp
The Pulp chain turns wood (or recovered paper) into prepared pulp through a sequence of fixed-ratio stages, with technology competitions at the end of each:

Log Preparation — debark (ring, Rosser-head or biodegradable mechanical debarkers) and cut and chip.
Pulping — the key fork, where four distinct routes compete and, as in the real industry, generally serve different products rather than competing head-to-head:

Chemical (kraft) — batch and continuous digesters (including superbatch and blow-heat-recovery variants), the dominant route for strong, bleachable pulp; it is the route that produces black liquor.
Mechanical — stone groundwood, refiner, thermo-mechanical (TMP) and chemi-thermo-mechanical (CTMP) pulping, which use wood fibre efficiently but are very electricity-intensive.
Semi-chemical — neutral-sulphite digesters, used for specific grades.
Recycled — de-inking of recovered paper by washing, flotation or explosion; the lowest-energy route, limited by feedstock supply.

Washing — drum and diffusion washers that recover pulping chemicals.
Bleaching — competing fully and semi bleaching sequences built around elemental-chlorine-free (ECF) chemistry, oxygen delignification, ozone bleaching and chlorine-dioxide substitution.
Drying — pulp dryers (steam, and steam with electric vapour recompression) for market pulp.



19.3.2 Products: paper
The Paper chain branches into the five grades the sector reports, each a fixed-ratio sequence of Stock Preparation (disc or conical refining and screening), Forming, Pressing and Finishing, and Drying:

Newsprint — historically the largest grade, and the one whose decline drives the sector’s contraction.
Uncoated and Coated wood-free (fine) papers.
Linerboard — packaging board.
Tissue.

The Forming, Pressing and Finishing competitions include energy-saving extended-nip presses, which remove more water mechanically before the energy-intensive drying step. The Drying competitions are where much of the grade’s energy is decided, offering steam, electric, infrared, vapour-recompression, high-humidity-hood and high-intensity dryers.


19.3.3 Sector-specific service: the black-liquor recovery and energy cycle
The Black Liquor service is the energy and chemical heart of a kraft mill, and the feature that most sets this sector apart. It represents the closed loop, shown in Figure 19.2, that recovers pulping chemicals while generating most of the mill’s energy:

The Evaporator concentrates weak black liquor, competing multiple-effect evaporators (with computer control and integrated concentrators) and vapour-recompression evaporators.
The Recovery Furnace burns the concentrated liquor, regenerating cooking chemicals and raising steam. Technologies range from the conventional Tomlinson boiler through low-odour, high-solids-firing variants to cogeneration configurations (e.g. high-solids firing with 900–1200 psig cogeneration) and gasification, which raise the energy recovered from the liquor.
The Lime Kiln calcines lime to causticise the recovered chemicals. It is the sector’s main fossil-fuel choke point, and the model competes conventional natural-gas, oil and coal kilns against wood-waste gasification and lignin-precipitation retrofits that displace fossil fuel.







Figure 19.2: The kraft black-liquor recovery and energy cycle as represented in CIMS. Chemical pulping produces weak black liquor, which is concentrated in the Evaporator and burned in the Recovery Furnace; the furnace regenerates pulping chemicals (via the Lime Kiln) and raises steam and power for the mill, with surplus electricity exported. Biomass and black liquor are biogenic, so this energy carries no fossil CO₂; the kiln is the main fossil load.





19.3.4 Auxiliary energy and utility services
The remaining services are common to the industrial sectors and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part; their general structure — and the “existing versus more efficient equipment, with fuel-switching where relevant” convention they follow — is set out in the Sector Overview. This chapter does not repeat that detail. The Pulp and Paper sector draws on:

Machine Drive — see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter. Pulp and Paper’s very large motor loads sit here, especially the refiners of mechanical pulping (materials processing), along with pumps, fans, compressed air and materials handling.
Steam — see Low-Temperature Industrial Heat. This is the sector’s largest energy service, and its technology set is unusually rich: alongside natural-gas, oil, coal, electric and hydrogen boilers it includes solid-biomass boilers, biomass steam turbines and grate firing, and gas- and biomass-fired cogeneration, reflecting the mills’ reliance on hog fuel and on combined heat and power.
Methane Blend — the gaseous-fuel supply node, where natural gas competes with biogas, biomass gasification and hydrogen.
HVAC and Lighting for mill facilities.

title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
19.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Because the sector is already largely bioenergy-powered, its decarbonisation problem is unusual: it is less about replacing a single dominant fossil process than about (i) squeezing the remaining fossil fuel out of the lime kiln and any fossil-fired steam and drying, (ii) raising the efficiency of the energy-intensive drying, pressing and mechanical-pulping steps, and (iii) capturing the large, concentrated, biogenic CO₂ streams to deliver negative emissions. The technologies below are admitted to the relevant tech-compete nodes; representative performance and maturity are summarised in Table 19.1. The figures quoted are indicative ranges from techno-economic reviews (Canadian Climate Institute 2023; Pulp and Paper Canada 2024), not the calibrated values used in the model.

19.4.1 Efficient pulping, pressing and drying
The lowest-cost reductions come from using less energy per tonne. Recycled (de-inked) pulping is the least energy-intensive route and is admitted where recovered-paper feedstock is available; mechanical pulping with vapour recompression recovers the refiners’ large heat output as usable steam. On the paper machine, extended-nip presses remove more water mechanically so that less must be evaporated, and the Drying competitions admit electric, infrared, high-intensity and vapour-recompression dryers that either cut drying energy or shift it from fossil fuel to electricity. In the model’s bleaching competitions, the ECF, oxygen-delignification and ozone sequences reduce both energy and chemical use relative to legacy chlorine bleaching.


19.4.2 Black-liquor recovery, cogeneration and gasification
The recovery furnace is both a chemical reactor and the mill’s main power plant. The model competes increasingly capable configurations — high-solids firing, low-odour designs, and cogeneration at 900–1200 psig — that raise the steam and electricity recovered from each tonne of liquor. Black-liquor gasification goes further, lifting energy-recovery efficiency from roughly 65% for a conventional boiler to about 75–80% and producing a syngas that can drive a gas turbine or be converted to biofuels (IEA Bioenergy 2007). These options let a kraft mill meet more of its own demand and export more surplus power.


19.4.3 Decarbonising the lime kiln
The lime kiln is the single most stubborn fossil load in a kraft mill, because calcination needs high-temperature heat that has traditionally come from natural gas or oil (Pulp and Paper Canada 2024). The model competes wood-waste gasification and lignin-precipitation retrofits that substitute renewable fuel for fossil in the kiln. The emerging frontier option — electrified calcination (for example electric plasma kilns) — would remove the load entirely.
TODO: Add an electrified lime kiln (e.g. electric plasma calcination) and high-temperature heat-pump options to the relevant competitions, so the model can represent full electrification of the kraft mill’s remaining fossil heat.


19.4.4 Carbon capture and negative emissions (BECCS)
The pulp and paper sector is widely regarded as one of the most promising hosts for bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), because the recovery boiler and lime kiln emit large, relatively concentrated streams of biogenic CO₂; capturing them yields net-negative emissions at comparatively low cost.
TODO: Add a CCS / BECCS service for pulp and paper, attached to the Recovery Furnace and Lime Kiln, so the model can represent capture of biogenic CO₂ and the resulting negative emissions.

Table 19.2 gathers order-of-magnitude capital and operating costs and energy characteristics for the main pulping and papermaking steps and the black-liquor recovery cycle. The estimates are drawn from public techno-economic literature (Canadian Climate Institute 2023; Pulp and Paper Canada 2024; IEA Bioenergy 2007; Tran and Vakkilainen 2016) and expressed in 2025 Canadian dollars. Overnight capital costs are normalised per tonne of annual product capacity (except where another basis is noted), fixed O&M follows the heavy-industry convention of roughly 3–6% of capital cost per year, and energy intensity is per tonne of product. A defining feature of the sector is that much of the heat and power below is self-supplied from biomass (black liquor and hog fuel), so the relevant comparison is often net purchased energy rather than gross use.

title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
19.5 Economics
A few sector-wide conventions are worth noting. Pulp and paper technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes, with some auxiliary and capital-intensive nodes at 40–50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital. They sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions; CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters at the process nodes are set around 10 so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all. Fuel prices entering the service-cost calculation are scaled by a sector-level block of price multipliers.
The sector’s emissions accounting is distinctive. Unlike iron and steel or chemicals, the pulp and paper tree carries no explicit process-emission factors: essentially all of its emissions arise from fuel combustion, and they enter the model through each technology’s fuel service requests and the prevailing carbon price. Crucially, the large biomass flows — black liquor and hog fuel — are treated as biogenic and therefore carbon-neutral in the combustion accounting, so the carbon price bites mainly on the fossil fuels that remain, above all in the lime kiln and in any fossil-fired steam and drying. Fuel-switching from these fossil fuels to biomass, electricity, and hydrogen is therefore the model’s main channel for emissions reduction, reinforced by the mills’ ability to self-generate steam and power and export surplus electricity.

title: 19  Pulp and Paper
text:
19.6 Regional coverage and differences
Five regions are represented — Alberta, Atlantic, British Columbia, Ontario, and Québec — and regional differences show up in scale, grade mix, and trajectory:

Québec and Ontario are the largest, and both decline substantially over the projection as newsprint demand falls.
The Atlantic region carries significant capacity with a particularly steep modelled decline.
British Columbia is a major kraft- and mechanical-pulp region with biomass cogeneration, declining more gently.
Alberta is the smallest and the only region whose modelled output grows.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
20.1 Scope
The metal smelting and refining sector — the production of finished non-ferrous metals — is represented in CIMS by an energy-service flow model. The emphasis is on the structure of that model: the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them, rather than the metallurgy of individual smelters. The model tree is region-agnostic: a single master structure is instantiated for every province, and regional differences are expressed through which branches carry production and through the data attached to each node. The sector is unusual in two respects. It is dominated by a single metal, aluminium, whose production is overwhelmingly electricity-driven and located in Québec on cheap hydropower; and its hardest-to-cut emissions are process emissions — CO₂ from the consumable carbon anode in aluminium electrolysis, and SF₆ from magnesium melt protection — rather than ordinary combustion.
CIMS represents the smelting and refining of the major non-ferrous metals: aluminium, copper, nickel, zinc, and magnesium, with lead and titanium appearing in some regions. The driving variable is the physical output of refined metal in tonnes; a forecast of demand drives every upstream process and energy service and is set exogenously, as for the other industrial branches.
Several adjacent activities are deliberately handled elsewhere in CIMS to avoid double-counting energy and emissions:
Minor and precious metals (gold, silver, platinum-group, cadmium) are not represented explicitly because they are recovered in conjunction with the base metals or are produced in quantities too small to require their own representation.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
Iron and steel are explicitly excluded and covered in their own Iron and Steel chapter.
Mining and concentration of the ores are part of the Mining sector; the smelting sub-model takes concentrates (and, for aluminium, alumina) as inputs.
Downstream fabrication — rolling, extrusion, casting of finished goods — is downstream manufacturing and is not part of this sub-model, which ends with refined and cast metal.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
20.2 Real-world context
Canada is one of the world’s leading non-ferrous metal producers, and the sector’s structure is dominated by aluminium. Almost all Canadian primary aluminium is smelted in Québec, where abundant low-cost hydroelectricity makes the energy-intensive Hall-Héroult electrolysis economic; Canadian smelters are among the lowest-carbon in the world for this reason (International Energy Agency 2024). Nickel and copper smelting and refining are concentrated in Ontario (Sudbury) and Manitoba (Thompson), with zinc and other base metals across several provinces.
The sector’s emissions profile is distinctive. Hall-Héroult electrolysis consumes roughly 14 MWh of electricity per tonne of aluminium, but even on perfectly clean electricity it emits CO₂ because the carbon anode is consumed in the reaction — about 1.6–1.7 t CO₂ per tonne of aluminium — and intermittent anode effects release perfluorocarbons (PFCs), extremely potent greenhouse gases (International Energy Agency 2024). Magnesium production and casting use SF₆ as a melt-protection cover gas; SF₆ has roughly 22,000 times the warming potential of CO₂, so even small quantities matter. Pyrometallurgical copper, nickel, and zinc smelting burns fuel for roasting, smelting, and converting. The CIMS structure reflects all of this: it carries explicit process-emission factors for the aluminium carbon anode and for magnesium SF₆, and it admits the technologies — inert anodes, recycling, oxygen-enriched and flash smelting, and hydrometallurgy — that target each.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
20.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into a Product sub-tree, holding the per-metal production chains, and a Service sub-tree of auxiliary energy services. Figure 20.1 shows the overall structure.
As described in the Sector Overview, each node carries a competition rule. Fixed-ratio nodes impose the unavoidable engineering sequence of process steps, while tech-compete nodes host competitions among alternative technologies on the basis of lifecycle cost (see Chapter 4). In the metal-smelting tree, the disaggregation into metals and process stages is built from fixed-ratio nodes, while the technology choices — which anode, which smelting furnace, which metallurgical route — occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 20.1: Energy-service flow model of the metal smelting and refining sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree holds per-metal chains — aluminium (alumina, electrolysis, recycle) and the pyro-/hydro-metallurgical base metals — and the Service sub-tree holds the auxiliary energy services and oxygen supply.




20.3.1 Products: aluminium
Aluminium is the largest chain and has its own structure. Primary Aluminum runs through:

Alumina — refining bauxite to alumina by the Bayer process (natural-gas fired, with an efficiency retrofit). (Canada imports alumina, but the step is represented.)
Electrolysis — the Hall-Héroult cell, the energy and emissions core, competing Søderberg and several pre-bake anode designs (side- and centre-point feeders, with automation) against the inert anode with wetted cathode route that eliminates the carbon anode entirely.

A Recycle branch remelts scrap aluminium at a small fraction of primary energy, and dedicated Pre-bake Anode and Søderberg Anode nodes supply the consumable anodes for the conventional routes.
The conventional electrolysis routes carry a process-CO₂ factor of about 1.6–1.7 t per tonne, representing carbon-anode consumption; the inert-anode route is the model’s way of breaking that link.


20.3.2 Products: copper, nickel, zinc, and magnesium
The base metals share a common structure under Primary Metals, each resolving into a Metallurgy route and a Melt Cast finishing step:

Pyro Metallurgy — the conventional high-temperature route, broken into a Smelting Process (conventional roast–smelt–convert, or continuous smelting such as Mitsubishi) and a Refine step (electrolytic, anode-furnace, or fire refining). The smelting technologies compete fuels and furnace types — flash furnaces, reverberatory and electric-arc furnaces, fluidized-bed and hearth roasting, Pierce-Smith and top-blown rotary converters — with oxygen enrichment options.
Hydro Metallurgy — the aqueous route (pressure or percolation leaching, solvent extraction, electrolytic precipitation/electrowinning), which is more electricity-intensive but avoids high-temperature smelting.

Magnesium carries an explicit SF₆ process-emission factor on its melt-cast and refining steps, reflecting cover-gas use.


20.3.3 Services
The services follow the standard pattern and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part. The sector draws on Oxygen (cryogenic air separation, feeding oxygen-enriched smelting and converting), Machine Drive (see Industrial Machine Drive Systems), Steam (see Low-Temperature Industrial Heat), Methane Blend, HVAC, and Lighting. Notably, the sector has no CCS service in the current tree, which is a significant omission for the pyrometallurgical routes whose off-gases are relatively concentrated.

Migrate these files to the region-agnostic master tree (which places the sector under Metal.Smelting with the Product/Service split) and the shared General Services chapters.

20.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Because Canadian smelting already runs largely on clean electricity, its decarbonisation problem is less about the energy supply than about the process chemistry — the carbon anode, the SF₆ cover gas, and the fuel burned in pyrometallurgical smelting — and about using less primary metal through recycling. The model represents most of these levers; Table 20.1 summarises maturity and Table 20.2 gives indicative costs.

20.4.1 Inert anodes and clean-power aluminium
Because Québec’s aluminium already runs on hydroelectricity, its remaining direct emissions come almost entirely from the consumable carbon anode. The inert anode route — represented in the model as Hall-Héroult inert anode with wetted cathode — replaces the carbon anode with a non-consumable material that releases oxygen instead of CO₂, eliminating both the anode CO₂ and the PFCs from anode effects. This is the single largest lever for the sector. It is being commercialised by the ELYSIS joint venture in Québec, which produced primary aluminium at industrial scale with inert anodes in 2021 and targets broader commercial availability later this decade (ELYSIS 2024). Conversion cost is expected to fall below that of carbon anodes in new cells.


20.4.2 Recycling and base-metal process efficiency
Secondary (recycled) aluminium uses on the order of 5% of the energy of primary production and is represented as the Recycle branch; expanding it is a major lever as scrap availability grows. For the base metals, oxygen-enriched, flash, and continuous smelting cut fuel use per tonne, and hydrometallurgy avoids high-temperature smelting altogether for metals where it is applicable — both are in the model. Further electrification of smelting and process heat, and CCS on the concentrated off-gas streams of pyrometallurgical smelters, are the main options not yet fully represented.


20.4.3 Magnesium SF₆ replacement
Magnesium melt protection traditionally uses SF₆, one of the most potent greenhouse gases known. Replacing it with alternative cover gases (sulphur dioxide, or fluorinated ketones such as Novec 612) removes almost all of this emission at low cost and is mature; the model carries the SF₆ emission explicitly, so an SF₆-free option is a natural addition.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
20.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, service requests for the energy and upstream services it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Metal smelting technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes in the current data, with some auxiliary and capital-intensive nodes at 40–50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital. They sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions; CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters at the process nodes are set around 10 so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all.
The sector’s emissions accounting is distinctive. Combustion emissions follow from each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price, as in the other sectors. In addition, the aluminium electrolysis technologies carry an explicit process-CO₂ factor (about 1.6–1.7 t per tonne) for carbon-anode consumption, and the magnesium melt-cast and refining technologies carry an SF₆ factor — both applied independently of fuel use, with SF₆ entering on a CO₂-equivalent basis at its very high warming potential. Because there is no CCS service, the model’s main channels for emissions reduction are switching to the inert anode, expanding recycling, switching to lower-fuel smelting routes, and (indirectly) the carbon intensity of the electricity the sector draws.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
20.6 Regional coverage and differences
Because the tree is region-agnostic, each modelled region is built from the same master structure and carries no production on branches that do not apply. Five regions are represented — the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, and Québec — and the differences are stark:

Québec dominates the sector by a wide margin, carrying essentially all primary aluminium on its hydro power, and grows over the projection.
Ontario (Sudbury) carries nickel and copper smelting and refining.
Manitoba (Thompson) carries nickel; British Columbia and the Atlantic region carry smaller base-metal operations.

title: 20  Metal Smelting and Refining
text:
20.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The metal-smelting sub-model is detailed on the metallurgical side but carries the structural debts common to the older sector files, plus two sector-specific gaps: the absence of a CCS service and the incomplete representation of the non-CO₂ greenhouse gases (PFCs and the SF₆-abatement option). The TODOs above record these along with the auxiliary-service migration. Because the sector is already largely clean-powered, its remaining emissions are concentrated and high-leverage — the carbon anode, magnesium SF₆, and pyrometallurgical fuel — so closing these representational gaps matters more here than the sector’s modest energy total might suggest.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.1 Scope
The iron and steel sector is represented in CIMS by an energy-service flow model. The emphasis is on the structure of that model — the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them — rather than on the metallurgy or economics of individual mills. The model tree is region-agnostic: a single master structure is instantiated for every province, and regional differences are expressed through which branches carry production and through the data attached to each node, not through separate per-region structures. Iron and steel is one of the most energy- and emissions-intensive branches of Canadian industry, and almost all of its emissions are concentrated in a single step — the reduction of iron ore to metallic iron — which is also where the sector’s main decarbonisation choices sit.
CIMS represents the integrated process chain of primary and secondary steelmaking, from the preparation of iron-bearing feed through to finished steel products. The sub-model begins with the on-site agglomeration of iron ore and the production of oxygen and process gases, takes in scrap, runs the metallic charge through the ironmaking and steelmaking step that produces molten steel, and ends with casting and finishing into the three basic forms — slabs, blooms, and billets — and their many sub-forms. The driving variable is the physical output of steel in tonnes; a forecast of crude-steel demand drives every upstream process and energy service and is set exogenously, as for the other industrial branches.
Several adjacent activities are deliberately handled elsewhere in CIMS to avoid double-counting energy and emissions:
Coke-making and the on-site reducing gases are treated within the sector because they are integral to the ironmaking step and cannot be cleanly separated from it.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
Iron-ore mining and ore beneficiation are covered in the Mining chapter; the iron and steel sub-model takes ore (or pellets) as an input and stops short of the mine gate on the upstream side.
Smelting and refining of non-ferrous metals — aluminium, nickel, copper, zinc, and the rest — are covered in the Metal Smelting and Refining chapter, which explicitly excludes iron and steel.
Downstream fabrication of steel into final goods (structural fabrication, stamping, machining) belongs to the manufacturing branches and is not part of this sub-model, which ends with saleable cast-and-rolled steel forms.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.2 Real-world context
Canada produces on the order of 12 Mt of crude steel a year, placing it around sixteenth among steelmaking nations, against world output of roughly 1,900 Mt (World Steel Association 2024). Production is concentrated overwhelmingly in Ontario, which hosts the large integrated and converting plants at Hamilton (ArcelorMittal Dofasco and Stelco) and Sault Ste. Marie (Algoma Steel); Québec, with electric-arc operations at Contrecœur and Longueuil; and Saskatchewan, where the Regina works runs a scrap-based electric-arc mini-mill of about 1 Mt/yr (World Steel Association 2024). This geography maps directly onto the two production routes the model represents.
Two routes dominate world and Canadian steelmaking, and they differ enormously in energy and emissions:

The integrated, or primary, route reduces iron ore to pig iron in a blast furnace using coke (itself made on site from coal), then refines the liquid iron together with some scrap in a basic oxygen furnace (BOF) by injecting high-purity oxygen. The blast-furnace/BOF (BF-BOF) route is the most energy-intensive, at roughly 18–21 GJ and around 1.8–2.3 t CO₂ per tonne of crude steel, with most of the carbon entering as the coke that chemically reduces the ore (International Energy Agency 2020; Fan and Friedmann 2021).
The secondary, or recycled, route melts 100% scrap in an electric arc furnace (EAF). Because it skips ore reduction entirely, it uses on the order of 2–4 GJ of electricity per tonne and a small fraction of the emissions of the integrated route; its footprint is dominated by the carbon intensity of the grid that supplies it (Fan and Friedmann 2021).

The Canadian industry is in the middle of a historic shift from the first route to the second. Algoma Steel and ArcelorMittal Dofasco are both replacing blast furnaces with electric arc furnaces, conversions expected to cut each plant’s CO₂ by around 70% (CBC News 2025). Globally the EAF share of crude-steel output passed 29% in 2024 and is rising (World Steel Association 2024). The CIMS structure is built around exactly this distinction: it separates an Integrated ironmaking-and-steelmaking node from a Recycled (scrap-EAF) node, and it admits to the integrated node a family of emerging low-carbon primary routes — direct-reduced iron, hydrogen direct reduction, smelting reduction, and carbon capture — so that the model can represent the route shift endogenously as costs and carbon prices change.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.3 Model structure
Following the standard CIMS pattern, the sector divides into two sub-trees: a Product sub-tree, which is the physical chain that turns ore and scrap into saleable steel, and a Service sub-tree, which holds the auxiliary energy and utility services the production technologies draw on. Figure 21.1 shows the overall structure.
As described in the Sector Overview, each node carries a competition rule. Fixed-ratio nodes impose the unavoidable engineering sequence of process steps, while tech-compete nodes host competitions among alternative technologies on the basis of lifecycle cost (see Chapter 4). In the iron and steel tree, the disaggregation of products and process stages is built from fixed-ratio nodes, while the technology choices — which steelmaking route, which casting method, which reheat furnace, which class of motor — occur at the tech-compete leaves.






Figure 21.1: Energy-service flow model of the iron and steel sector (region-agnostic master tree). The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — molten-steel production (Integrated and Recycled routes), continuous casting and finishing, and foundry — and a Service sub-tree of auxiliary energy services structured on the EIA MECS end uses, plus the sector-specific Agglomeration, Oxygen, Iron Process Gas, and CCS services.




21.3.1 Products: molten steel
The heart of the sub-model is the Molten Steel node, where the metallic charge becomes liquid steel. The exogenous split between primary and secondary production is set here as a service request: a region directs part of its steel demand to the Integrated route and the remainder to the Recycled route. In the current data Ontario runs roughly two-thirds integrated and one-third recycled, drifting toward more EAF over the horizon; Québec starts similarly mixed and shifts to a majority-EAF split by 2050; and Saskatchewan is modelled as 100% recycled, reflecting its scrap-based mini-mill. The molten steel then passes through Ladle Refining and Ladle Preheat (electric or natural-gas) before casting. Figure 21.2 details the route competition.
The Integrated node is a tech-compete node whose incumbent is the conventional BF-BOF, but to which a full set of lower-carbon primary routes is admitted so they can win share as their costs and the carbon price evolve:

Direct-reduced iron with EAF (DRI + EAF) and its hydrogen variant (HDRI + EAF) reduce ore in the solid state with reformed natural gas or hydrogen and melt the DRI in an electric furnace, avoiding the blast furnace and coke entirely.
Smelting-reduction routes — Corex smelter, HIsarna, Smelter + EAF — reduce ore without coke ovens or sinter plants.
Top gas recycling strips CO₂ from blast-furnace gas and reinjects it to cut coke use.
Each of these (and BF-BOF itself, via the shared CCS service) has a + CCS variant that routes its flue CO₂ to the capture service.

The Recycled node is a tech-compete node among electric arc furnaces of increasing intensity — High power EAF, High power EAF + O₂, Ultra power EAF + O₂ — with an Ultra power EAF + O₂ + CCS option that captures the small process CO₂ from electrode and charge carbon. The EAF carries a small direct process-emission factor in addition to its electricity draw.
TODO: The Integrated/Recycled split is currently an exogenous service-request ratio per region. Consider making it (or the scrap-supply constraint behind it) responsive to scrap availability and price, so that the secondary route’s growth is limited by domestic and imported scrap rather than set by assumption.


21.3.2 Products: casting, finishing, and foundry
Cast and finished products are organised under a Continuous Cast node that branches into the three basic forms and their sub-forms, mirroring the way the industry reports product mix:

Slabs run through Casting (continuous, thin-slab, strip, or the older ingot route), Slab Roughing and Finishing mills, Pickling, Skin Pass, and a Cold Rolled chain (cold reduction, electrolytic cleaning, annealing and tempering, electric/tin-plate and galvanizing lines).
Blooms run through Bloom Casting to heavy structural shapes, tubes, and other heavy products.
Billets run through Billet Casting to bar, rod, and light structural shapes.

Casting and rolling technologies generally compete as natural-gas versus fuel-oil fired variants, and the casting node also carries the energy-saving near-net-shape options (thin-slab and strip casting) that reduce or eliminate downstream reheating.
The master tree also defines a Foundry product node alongside Continuous Cast, for cast-iron and cast-steel products that bypass the rolling chain. It is part of the intended design but is not yet populated in the regional input files.
TODO: Build out the Foundry product branch (technologies, energy intensities, and product split) in the regional input files; it currently exists in the master tree but carries no data.


21.3.3 Sector-specific services
Three services are specific to ironmaking and sit in the Service sub-tree alongside the cross-cutting utilities:

Agglomeration binds fine iron ore into sinter suitable for the blast furnace; it competes a conventional sinter technology against a sinter + CCS variant.
Oxygen is supplied by cryogenic air separation (compression and distillation) and feeds the BOF and oxygen-enriched EAF routes; oxygen is itself an energy-intensive input.
Iron Process Gas captures the energy value of blast-furnace, coke-oven, and BOF off-gases and uses them on site for Reheating and for Steam (process-gas boilers and cogenerators), displacing purchased fuel.



21.3.4 Auxiliary energy and utility services
The remaining services are common to the industrial sectors and are documented in their own chapters in the General Services part; their general structure — and the “existing versus more efficient equipment, with fuel-switching where relevant” convention they follow — is set out in the Sector Overview. This chapter does not repeat that detail. The iron and steel sector draws on:

Machine Drive — see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter. The sector’s large motive loads sit here: mill drives and materials processing, fans and blowers, materials handling, pumps, and compressed air.
Reheating — reheat furnaces (natural-gas or oil; unrecuperated, recuperated, induction, or direct-rolling) that bring semi-finished steel back to rolling temperature.
Steam — see Low-Temperature Industrial Heat, covering boiler- and turbine-raised steam and its fuel options, including electric, hydrogen, and CCS-equipped variants.
Methane Blend — the gaseous-fuel supply node, where natural gas competes with biogas, biomass gasification, and hydrogen.
HVAC (space heating and cooling) and Lighting for mill facilities.

TODO: The current regional input files still implement an earlier, more detailed auxiliary structure (six per-horsepower machine-drive size classes; separate Compression, Conveyance, Pumping, Ventilation, and Direct Drive sub-trees) and predate the Product/Service split and the MECS-aligned Machine Drive grouping. Migrate these files to the region-agnostic master tree and the shared General Services chapters.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.4 Decarbonisation technologies
The sector’s emissions are dominated by the chemical reduction of iron ore in the integrated route — the carbon in coke is the reductant, not merely a fuel — so the decisive decarbonisation lever is the choice of primary route at the Molten Steel Integrated node, backed by carbon capture and by the shift of melting and heating loads to low-carbon electricity and fuels. The technologies below are admitted to the relevant tech-compete nodes; representative performance and maturity are summarised in Table 21.1. The figures quoted are indicative ranges from technology roadmaps and techno-economic reviews (International Energy Agency 2020; Fan and Friedmann 2021), not the calibrated values used in the model.

The exogenous primary/secondary split feeds an Integrated node (BF-BOF and emerging low-carbon primary routes, each with a CCS variant) and a Recycled node (scrap EAFs of increasing power, with an oxygen-and-CCS option). Most routes draw on the shared Agglomeration, Oxygen, and CCS services.




21.4.1 Primary-route shift: DRI, hydrogen, and smelting reduction
The largest single emissions reduction available to the sector is to displace the coke-based blast furnace. Direct reduced iron (DRI) reduces ore in the solid state with a reducing gas and melts the product in an EAF; with reformed natural gas it already cuts CO₂ to roughly 1.4–1.7 t/t from the 1.8–2.3 t/t of BF-BOF, and when the reducing gas is green hydrogen the reduction step’s emissions essentially disappear, for an overall cut of up to about 95–98% relative to the blast furnace (Fan and Friedmann 2021). The model represents both as DRI + EAF and HDRI + EAF at the Integrated node. Smelting-reduction processes — HIsarna, Corex, and the generic Smelter + EAF — eliminate the coke ovens and sinter plant and cut energy and CO₂ by around a fifth on their own, rising toward 80% when paired with CCS (International Energy Agency 2020). These compete directly against BF-BOF as the carbon price rises.


21.4.2 Scrap-based electric steelmaking
Where scrap is available, the Recycled route is already the lowest-emission way to make steel, because it bypasses ore reduction altogether; its footprint then tracks the carbon intensity of the electricity grid, which is low in hydro-rich Québec and increasingly so in Ontario. The model represents progressively more capable furnaces — High power and Ultra power EAFs, with oxygen enrichment to speed melting — and an Ultra power EAF + O₂ + CCS option to capture the residual process CO₂. The practical limit on this route is scrap supply and quality, which is why the primary/secondary split is currently set exogenously rather than allowed to go fully to scrap.


21.4.3 Carbon capture
Carbon capture is represented as a shared CCS service that any equipped route requests; in the model it removes 90% of the CO₂ presented to it. It is the only way to deeply decarbonise the routes that still reduce ore with carbon — hence the BF-BOF + CCS, Corex + CCS, HIsarna CCS, Top gas recycling CCS, Smelter + EAF + CCS, and DRI + EAF + CCS variants. The broader treatment of capture, transport, and storage, and its costs, is in the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage chapter.


21.4.4 Electrified and low-carbon heat, and efficient casting
Beyond the reduction step, reheating and process steam are met largely by combustion today. The low- and zero-emission alternatives — electric and hydrogen reheat furnaces, electrode and electric-resistance boilers, and process-gas cogeneration — are reached through the Reheating, Steam, and Iron Process Gas services and are described in the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter; the Methane Blend node substitutes biogas, biomass gas, and hydrogen for natural gas in any remaining gas-fired duty. On the product side, near-net-shape casting (thin-slab and strip casting) reduces or removes the reheating step entirely, and oxygen-enriched, ultra-high-power EAFs cut melting energy. High-efficiency motors and variable-speed drives in the Machine Drive service reduce the large auxiliary load.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, service requests for the energy and upstream services it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
A few sector-wide conventions are worth noting. Iron and steel technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most process nodes in the current data, with some auxiliary and capital-intensive nodes at 40–50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital. They sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions; CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters at the process nodes are set around 10 so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all. Fuel prices entering the service-cost calculation are scaled by a sector-level block of price multipliers, allowing the sector to face prices that differ from the generic delivered price of each fuel.
Greenhouse-gas costs enter through two channels. Most emissions follow from each technology’s fuel service requests and the prevailing carbon price, so route-switching — from coke-based ironmaking to gas- or hydrogen-based DRI, or from natural gas to hydrogen and biogas in the methane blend — is the model’s main channel for emissions reduction. In addition, the EAF routes carry a small direct process-emission factor (electrode and charge carbon), and the CCS service applies an emissions-removal factor (90% of the CO₂ routed to it) to the technologies that request it.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.6 Regional coverage and differences
Because the tree is region-agnostic, each modelled province is built from the same master structure and simply carries no production on the branches that do not apply. Regional differences show up in where production sits and in the primary/secondary split rather than in the shape of the tree:

Ontario carries most of Canada’s steel and runs a mixed integrated and recycled fleet (about two-thirds integrated today), consistent with its large Hamilton and Sault Ste. Marie plants — and with the BF-to-EAF conversions now under way there.
Québec is modelled as mixed but shifting strongly to EAF, reaching a majority-recycled split by 2050.
Saskatchewan is modelled as 100% recycled, reflecting its single scrap-based mini-mill.

title: 21  Iron and Steel
text:
21.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The iron and steel sub-model is a deliberately simplified representation of a complex, fast-changing industry. The TODOs above record the main gaps between this design and both the current input files and the real Canadian sector: the migration of the auxiliary services to the MECS-aligned Machine Drive and the Product/Service split; the population of the Foundry branch; an explicit scrap-supply constraint behind the primary/secondary split; an explicit green-hydrogen reducing-gas supply for the HDRI route; broader provincial coverage; and the refresh of the exogenous route trajectories in light of the conversions now under construction. Together these define the path from the current state of the model to the region-agnostic, fully populated design described in this chapter.

title: 22  Light Industrial
text:
22.1 Scope
The light industrial sector — the “other manufacturing” industries — is represented in CIMS by an energy-service flow model. The emphasis is on the structure of that model: the hierarchy of nodes, the technologies that compete at each node, and the engineering ratios that link them. The model tree is region-agnostic: a single master structure is instantiated for every province, and regional differences are expressed through which branches carry activity and through the data attached to each node. Light industrial is the aggregate of the many manufacturing industries that are individually too small to merit their own sub-model but collectively consume a large share of regional industrial energy. Because it has no single physical product, it is the one industrial sector CIMS drives with a monetary output measure rather than a tonnage, and it is modelled as a set of generic energy services rather than specific chemical or metallurgical processes.
CIMS groups under light industrial the manufacturing industries not represented elsewhere: food, beverage, and tobacco; rubber and plastics; leather and textiles; wood products; furniture, printing, and machinery; transportation equipment; and electronics and other manufacturing. The driving variable is the real domestic product (RDP) of these industries — their economic output in constant dollars — rather than a physical tonnage, because there is no common physical unit across such a diverse group. A forecast of RDP drives the demand for each energy service and is set exogenously.
Several adjacent activities are deliberately handled elsewhere to avoid double-counting. The energy-intensive industries that do have their own sub-models — iron and steel, chemicals, pulp and paper, industrial minerals, metal smelting, mining, and the rest — are excluded here and covered in their own chapters; light industrial is, by construction, “everything else” in manufacturing. Fuel and electricity supply enter through the energy-supply sub-models and the shared fuel nodes.

title: 22  Light Industrial
text:
22.2 Real-world context
The “other manufacturing” group is heterogeneous but shares an energy signature: its demand is dominated by low- and medium-temperature heat, steam, motor-driven systems, and building services (space conditioning, water heating, lighting), rather than by high-temperature process chemistry. Food and beverage processing is typically the largest energy user in the group, and it is overwhelmingly low-temperature: on the order of 97% of its thermal demand is below about 130 °C — squarely in the range that modern industrial heat pumps can serve at a coefficient of performance of 3.5–4 (American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy 2024; Arpagaus et al. 2018). Wood products, plastics, textiles, and the rest add their own low- and medium-temperature loads.
This matters for decarbonisation. Because the sector’s energy is general-purpose rather than locked into a specific reaction, it is among the most readily electrified parts of industry: heat pumps, electric boilers, and resistance heating can replace fossil combustion for much of the heat, high-efficiency motors and drives cut the large motive-power load, and the remaining high-temperature or hard-to-electrify duty can switch to biomass or hydrogen. The CIMS structure reflects this by representing the sector almost entirely through the shared energy-service competitions — the same Heat, Steam, Machine Drive, and building-service structures used across industry — applied to an aggregate manufacturing output.

title: 22  Light Industrial
text:
22.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the manufacturing sub-groups whose aggregate output drives demand — and a Service sub-tree holding the energy services that supply them. Figure 22.1 shows the structure. Unlike the process-heavy sectors, almost all of the modelling detail is in the Service sub-tree.
As described in the Sector Overview, each node carries a competition rule. The manufacturing sub-groups are fixed-ratio output nodes that translate RDP into energy-service demand; the technology choices occur at the tech-compete leaves of the services (see Chapter 4).






Figure 22.1: Energy-service flow model of the light industrial sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree holds the seven manufacturing sub-groups whose aggregate output (RDP) drives demand; the Service sub-tree holds the generic energy services — process heat, steam, water heating, HVAC, lighting, and the MECS-aligned machine drive — through which essentially all of the sector’s energy is modelled.




22.3.1 Products: the manufacturing sub-groups
The Product sub-tree divides manufacturing into seven sub-groups: Food, Tobacco, and Beverage; Rubber and Plastics; Leather and Textiles; Wood Products; Furniture, Printing, and Machinery; Transportation Equipment; and Electronics and Other. Each is an output node whose RDP, multiplied by an energy-intensity ratio, generates requests on the shared energy services. The sub-groups differ in how much heat versus motive power versus building service they draw, but they share the same service technologies.


22.3.2 Services: where the energy is decided
Essentially all of the sector’s energy use — and all of its emissions — is decided in the Service sub-tree:

Heat — process heat, split into Direct (standard and efficient natural gas, electric, oil/HFO, and wood-waste) and Indirect (electric) firing. This is the central fuel-switching competition.
Steam — boiler- and turbine-raised steam competing natural gas, oil, coal, electric, hydrogen, solid-biomass, and cogeneration units.
Water Heating — standard, efficient, and high-efficiency natural-gas and electric units.
HVAC — space conditioning, competing building-shell efficiency levels with electric and gas systems.
Lighting — base, more-efficient, and most-efficient lighting.
Machine Drive — the motor-driven loads (pumps, fans, compressed air, materials handling, and processing), structured on the EIA MECS end uses; see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter. (The current files label this Motive Power with high- and low-efficiency options.)
Methane Blend — the gaseous-fuel supply node, where natural gas competes with biogas, biomass gas, and hydrogen.

The detailed structure and conventions of these shared services are set out in the Sector Overview and the General Services chapters and are not repeated here.

22.4.1 Electrified heat: heat pumps and electric boilers
The largest lever is electrifying the sector’s abundant low- and medium-temperature heat. Industrial heat pumps deliver heat up to about 120 °C at a coefficient of performance of 3.5–4, so each unit of electricity yields three to four units of heat — a strong economic and emissions case wherever the grid is clean, as in much of Canada (American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy 2024; Arpagaus et al. 2018). Where temperatures or duty cycles do not suit a heat pump, electric boilers and resistance heating electrify the remainder at high efficiency but higher running cost. These appear in the model as the electric options at the Heat, Steam, and Water Heating services, drawing on the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter.


22.4.2 Biomass, hydrogen, and cogeneration
For heat that is harder to electrify, biomass and wood-waste firing (already a Heat and Steam option, and a natural fit for wood-products manufacturers with on-site residues) and hydrogen and biogas through the Methane Blend node decarbonise the remaining combustion. Cogeneration raises the fuel utilisation of any remaining gas use and can export surplus power.


22.4.3 Efficiency in motors, lighting, and buildings
The motive-power load is reduced by high-efficiency motors and variable-speed drives in the Machine Drive service (see the Industrial Machine Drive Systems chapter), lighting by LED upgrades, and space-conditioning by building-shell and HVAC efficiency — all mature, low-cost, and already represented as the efficient options in their respective competitions.

title: 22  Light Industrial
text:
22.5 Economics
Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output (node-unit) basis, service requests for the energy it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Light industrial technologies are discounted at a high rate — 35% at most nodes in the current data, with some at 40–50%. These values are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates, not true financial costs of capital. They sit well above the single-digit rates a firm’s cost of capital would imply because they summarise the short payback horizons, risk aversion, and other non-financial barriers that govern real technology-adoption decisions; CIMS applies this behavioural rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 10 so that competitions respond to cost differences without collapsing to winner-take-all.
The sector’s emissions accounting is the simplest kind: there are no process emissions, so all CO₂ comes from fuel combustion in the Heat, Steam, and Water Heating services, entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price. Electrification (heat pumps), fuel-switching, and energy efficiency are therefore the only channels for emissions reduction, and their effect depends on the carbon intensity of the regional grid. Because output is measured in real dollars, energy intensities are expressed per unit of RDP, and the sector’s projected energy use is driven by the interaction of economic growth with these efficiency and fuel-switching choices.

title: 22  Light Industrial
text:
22.6 Regional coverage and differences
Light industrial has the most complete regional coverage of any industrial sector in the model: all seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the full structure, because every region has a substantial “other manufacturing” base. Differences are matters of scale and growth: Ontario and Québec are the largest, with Québec and Alberta growing strongly over the projection, while Ontario’s modelled output is roughly flat to declining. Because the sector is driven by economic output rather than a commodity, its energy use tends to rise with regional GDP unless offset by efficiency and electrification.
TODO: The relative energy intensities and sub-group mix are inherited from older calibrations. Revisit them against current CIEEDAC manufacturing energy-use data, since the composition of “other manufacturing” (and the share of food and beverage in particular) varies considerably by region.

title: 22  Light Industrial
text:
22.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The light industrial sub-model is deliberately a generic-services representation: it trades process detail for breadth, capturing a large and diverse slice of manufacturing through a compact set of energy-service competitions. Its main limitations follow from that design — it cannot represent process-specific options, and it depends entirely on the shared service technologies being kept current. The TODOs above record the priorities: migrating to the MECS-aligned Machine Drive, adding industrial heat pumps to the heat competitions, and refreshing the intensities and sub-group mix against current data.

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.1 Scope
The industry’s on-site greenhouse-gas footprint comes almost entirely from the diesel burned by off-road equipment — excavators, loaders, dozers, cranes, and the like working on building and civil-engineering sites — so the sector is represented as a single mobile-equipment energy service in which diesel competes against electric. The tree is region-agnostic, and the sector’s activity is measured directly in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent, signalling that emissions, not output, are its organising variable. The structure is deliberately coarse; the limitations below set out what a fuller representation would add.
CIMS represents the fuel use of construction’s mobile equipment — the off-road machinery that excavates, lifts, grades, and moves material on site — as one aggregate energy service. The driving variable is an exogenous forecast of the sector’s emissions in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. Importantly, this is the operational fuel of the construction process only. The far larger embodied-carbon question — the emissions of making the cement, steel, and other materials that go into a building — is accounted in the industries that produce those materials, such as Industrial Minerals (cement) and Iron and Steel, not here. The energy the finished building later consumes belongs to Residential and Commercial.

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.2 Real-world context
Construction’s direct emissions are an off-road diesel problem. Sites run a wide mix of heavy machines — excavators, wheel loaders, dozers, graders, cranes, dump trucks, and compactors — most of them diesel, often idling and working in stop-start cycles. The decarbonisation options are the familiar three for off-road fleets: drop-in renewable diesel or biodiesel that cuts lifecycle carbon with no equipment change, battery-electric machines, and hydrogen fuel-cell machines for the heaviest duty. Electrification has moved fastest here of any off-road sector, because many construction machines are compact, work fixed-hour shifts, and operate in cities where noise and local air quality matter: major manufacturers now ship battery-electric excavators and loaders, and electric machines increasingly match diesel on power and cycle time, at a purchase premium on the order of 50–100% that is partly offset by lower fuel and maintenance costs (IDTechEx 2024). The CIMS structure mirrors the core choice directly: a single competition between diesel and electric equipment.

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.3 Model structure
The sector is a single tech-compete node. Figure 23.1 shows the structure: the exogenous activity drives one Transport service, at which two technologies compete to provide the same mobile-equipment work.






Figure 23.1: Energy-service flow model of the construction sector (region-agnostic master tree). An exogenous activity forecast in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent drives a single Transport service node, a tech-compete between diesel equipment (which draws on the diesel fuel blend and emits CO₂) and electric equipment (which draws grid electricity). Lower-carbon drop-in fuels and hydrogen are noted as future options not yet in the model.



At the Transport node, diesel equipment (the entire base-year fleet) requests the diesel transportation fuel blend, while electric equipment requests grid electricity; both carry a twenty-year lifetime and the same energy requirement per unit of activity. Because the diesel option draws on the blended fuel, any renewable-diesel content in that blend lowers its lifecycle carbon automatically (see Biodiesel). Fuel prices at the node are currently borrowed from Agriculture as a proxy and flagged for review.

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.4 Decarbonisation technologies

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.5 Economics
Technology choice at the Transport node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. As elsewhere in CIMS, the intended discount rate is behavioural (revealed or empirical) rather than a true financial cost of capital, capturing the short payback horizons and adoption barriers typical of the trade (see the Theory chapter). In the current input files, however, the two technologies carry only a lifetime and their energy requests — capital cost, operating cost, the discount rate, and the heterogeneity (variance) parameter are not yet populated — so the diesel-versus-electric competition cannot yet resolve on cost and the fleet holds near its base-year shares. Emissions enter upstream through the fuels the technologies request: the diesel option carries the carbon of the diesel blend, while the electric option moves the load to the grid, where it is counted in Electricity.

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.6 Regional coverage
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the construction structure, scaled by an exogenous emissions forecast that tracks the scale of building activity: Ontario and Québec are the largest, with Alberta and British Columbia next, and the smaller provinces well below. The structure itself is identical across regions.

title: 23  Construction
text:
23.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The construction sub-model is a placeholder: it captures the sector’s dominant direct emission source — off-road diesel equipment — and the central diesel-to-electric choice, but little else. The off-road fleet is collapsed into a single aggregate Transport service rather than resolved by machine type or duty cycle; the competing technologies are not yet costed; the fuel prices are proxied from agriculture; and lower-carbon liquid fuels and hydrogen are not yet explicit options. The sub-model also covers only operational site fuel, not the embodied carbon of construction materials, which lives in the materials-producing sectors. The TODOs above record the priorities; populating the technology costs is the minimum needed for the diesel-to-electric transition to respond to policy at all.

title: 24  Residential
text:
24.1 Scope
The residential buildings sector is represented in CIMS as a demand-side sub-model, like the commercial sector: it consumes energy to deliver household energy services — space and water heating, cooling, lighting, appliances, and cooking — across the full range of dwellings. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the dwelling types and vintages that drive demand, the end-use services, and the technologies that compete to supply them. The tree is region-agnostic but climate-sensitive, so the housing stock is resolved by building type, construction vintage, and climate zone. The sector has no process emissions; all of its CO₂ comes from the fuels burned for space and water heating, so — as in commercial buildings — decarbonisation is fundamentally a story of electrification and efficiency.
CIMS represents the energy use of all residential dwellings — single-family detached houses, attached/row housing, low-rise walk-ups, and large apartment buildings (the last included here, rather than in commercial, because their consumption patterns fit the residential model). The driving variable is the number of households, projected exogenously from population growth; it sets the demand for every service except water heating and furnace-fan demand, which are determined by the heating and hot-water technologies themselves.
The residential sector accounts for roughly 17% of all energy consumed in Canada. Space heating is about 60% of that, water heating about 21%, and the remainder is lighting, appliances, and other uses (Natural Resources Canada 2024). The combustion of the delivered fuels is accounted here; the upstream supply of those fuels and of electricity is in the energy-supply sub-models.

title: 24  Residential
text:
24.2 Real-world context
Household energy is dominated by space and water heating, and that is where the direct emissions sit, because lighting and most appliances are already electric. Heating demand depends on the dwelling — its size, envelope, vintage, and climate — and on the heating system, which in Canada ranges from oil and natural-gas furnaces through electric baseboards and wood stoves to heat pumps.
The decarbonisation path mirrors the commercial sector: because household heat is low-temperature, the stock is highly electrifiable. Air- and ground-source heat pumps can deliver space and water heat at a coefficient of performance well above one, cold-climate and hybrid (heat-pump-with-fuel-backup) systems extend that into Canadian winters, and building-envelope improvements (tracked through construction-vintage cohorts and shell upgrades) cut the heat load at source. Efficient appliances, lighting (LED), and water fixtures reduce the rest. The CIMS structure captures all of this and, like the commercial model, links the building shell to the heating demand it creates.

title: 24  Residential
text:
24.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the dwelling stock, resolved by building type, vintage, and climate — and a Service sub-tree of the household end-uses. Figure 24.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4).






Figure 24.1: Energy-service flow model of the residential sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree is the dwelling stock — split by building type (High Density / Low-Med Density), construction vintage (building-code era), and climate zone (Cold / Marine), with cooling — and the Service sub-tree holds the household end-uses: water heating, lighting, and the major and minor appliances.




24.3.1 Products: the dwelling stock
The Building Type node resolves the housing stock along three dimensions:

Building type — High Density (apartments) and Low-Med Density (single-family detached, attached/row, low-rise), reflecting their very different heat loads per dwelling.
Vintage — construction-code cohorts (<1960, 1961–1980, 1981–2000, 2001–2020, 2021–2035, >2035), so that the model carries the thermal performance of each era of the stock and can represent both new construction to current codes and retrofits of older stock.
Climate zone — each vintage carries Heating (Cold) and Heating (Marine) competitions, since heating demand and heat-pump performance differ sharply between Canada’s cold interior and milder coastal regions.
Cooling — Central and Room air-conditioning, where applicable.

Within each dwelling/vintage/climate combination, the Heating node competes the systems: electric standard and baseboard, natural-gas and oil furnaces (existing, standard, and high-efficiency), wood, air-source heat pumps (with electric or gas backup), ground-source heat pumps, and gas-ASHP hybrids. The vintage-and-shell structure is how the model represents the interaction between envelope quality and heating demand: a better shell (newer vintage or a retrofit) lowers the load the heating system must meet.


24.3.2 Services: water heating, lighting, and appliances

Water Heating — storage and tankless units on electricity, gas, and oil; heat-pump water heaters (Electric- and NG-ASHP); and solar pre-heat with electric or gas backup. Water-heating demand is itself driven by the hot-water-using services (showers/faucets, dishwashing, clothes washing).
Lighting — efficiency levels from base stock to LED.
Major appliances — refrigerators, freezers, dryers (air-dry or machine), ranges, dishwashers (machine and non-machine), clothes washers, and air conditioners, each modelled by unit and market penetration with a range of efficiency levels.
Minor appliances — a diverse, growing category (electronics, block heaters, etc.) whose efficiency gains are often outweighed by rising ownership.

24.4.1 Heat pumps and the cold-climate question
As in commercial buildings, the central lever is the heat pump. The model competes air-source and ground-source heat pumps and, importantly for Canada, hybrid systems pairing a heat pump with an electric or gas backup for the coldest hours — which is why heating is split into Cold and Marine competitions. Cold-climate heat pumps that maintain output at low temperatures are the key enabling technology for electrifying heat across most of the country. Heat-pump water heaters and solar water heating electrify domestic hot water. These draw on the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat chapter’s broader heat-pump treatment.


24.4.2 Envelope, appliances, and behaviour
The vintage-and-shell structure makes envelope improvement a first-class lever: new dwellings built to tighter codes (the later vintage cohorts) and retrofits of older stock both reduce the heat load before any system runs. Efficient appliances, LED lighting, and low-flow hot-water fixtures cut the non-heating loads — the last also reducing water-heating demand.

title: 24  Residential
text:
24.5 Economics
Technology choice at every node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4, with extensive use of retrofit competitions: older-vintage dwellings can retrofit to better-insulated archetypes, and existing heating and water-heating stock can be upgraded, so the model represents improvements to the existing stock and not only new-build choices.
Residential technologies are discounted at high rates — around 25–30% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than financial costs of capital: households consistently behave as though they discount future energy savings far more steeply than a financial calculation would, and the behavioural rate encodes that wedge — risk aversion, up-front-cost sensitivity, information, and transaction costs. CIMS applies it throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters vary across the end-uses.
The emissions accounting carries no process emissions: all CO₂ comes from fuel combustion in space and water heating (and gas cooking), entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price. Electrification (heat pumps), fuel-switching, and efficiency are the only channels for reduction, and their emissions benefit depends on the carbon intensity of the regional grid — large where the grid is clean (Québec, BC, Manitoba), smaller where it is fossil-heavy (Alberta, Saskatchewan). Because the high behavioural discount rates make households reluctant to pay up-front for efficient equipment, the model reproduces the well-documented gap between cost-effective and actually-adopted efficiency — which is itself a target of policy.

title: 24  Residential
text:
24.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions carry the residential structure, and regional differences are pronounced because climate, fuel availability, and grid carbon intensity all vary:

The Cold / Marine climate split distinguishes most of Canada (Cold) from milder coastal British Columbia and parts of the Atlantic (Marine); coastal and interior British Columbia are modelled as distinct climates for single-family homes.
Fuel mix varies: natural gas dominates heating in the West and Ontario, electricity in Québec and parts of the Atlantic, and oil and wood remain significant in the Atlantic region and rural areas.
Air conditioning is a large load in hot-summer regions such as Ontario and much smaller elsewhere.

TODO: Confirm the regional dwelling-type, vintage, and fuel-mix shares against current housing-stock and Comprehensive Energy Use Database data, since heating demand and heat-pump economics depend heavily on all three.

title: 24  Residential
text:
24.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The residential sub-model is a detailed, vintage- and climate-resolved buildings representation with explicit retrofit competitions and a full set of heat-pump and efficiency options. Its limitations are the usual ones for a stock model: reliance on archetype generalisations, inherited calibration of dwelling and appliance intensities, and incomplete representation of behavioural and rebound effects (e.g. minor-appliance growth outpacing efficiency). The TODOs above record the priorities, of which cold-climate heat-pump performance and refreshed stock data matter most for current analysis.
