title: 25  Commercial and Institutional
text:
25.1 Scope
The commercial and institutional buildings sector is represented in CIMS as a demand-side sub-model: it does not make a physical product but consumes energy to deliver building energy services — heating, cooling, ventilation, lighting, refrigeration, cooking, hot water, and plug loads — across offices, stores, schools, hospitals, hotels, and the rest of the non-residential building stock. The emphasis, as elsewhere, is on the structure of the energy-service flow model: the building segments that drive demand, the end-use services, and the technologies that compete to supply them. The tree is region-agnostic, but building energy use is climate-sensitive, so the model splits the stock by climate zone. The sector has no process emissions; all of its CO₂ comes from the fuels burned for heating, so its decarbonisation is a story of electrification and efficiency.
CIMS represents the energy services of commercial and institutional buildings, driven by floor space. It deliberately excludes light industrial facilities (in Light Industrial) and high-rise residential apartments (in Residential). The commercial building sector accounts for roughly 20% of all energy consumed in Canada, of which lighting and HVAC together are about 60% (Natural Resources Canada 2024). The model includes the end-uses significant enough to matter — space heating and cooling, ventilation, lighting, refrigeration, cooking, hot water, and plug load — and drives each through engineering ratios that link it to floor space; floor space itself is projected exogenously from population and economic growth. Exterior lighting (street, parking, architectural) is not represented for lack of data.

title: 25  Commercial and Institutional
text:
25.2 Real-world context
Commercial buildings are diverse — a warehouse, a hospital, and a small office have very different energy profiles — but their energy use shares a common structure dominated by space conditioning and lighting. The most common fuels are, in order, electricity, natural gas, and light fuel oil; electricity is the sole source for lighting, refrigeration, plug load, cooling, fans, and pumps, while space and water heating use all three. Heating is where most of the sector’s direct emissions arise, since lighting and plug loads are already electric.
The decarbonisation path is correspondingly clear. Because the loads are general-purpose and mostly low-temperature, the sector is highly electrifiable: heat pumps (air- and ground-source) can serve space and water heating at a coefficient of performance well above one; LED lighting and efficient HVAC, controls, and refrigeration cut electricity use; and a tighter building envelope reduces the heating and cooling load at source. Larger facilities with coincident heat and power demand can use cogeneration. The CIMS structure captures all of these, and — distinctively for a buildings model — it represents the interaction between the building shell and the HVAC system, since a better envelope reduces the heat load the HVAC must meet.

title: 25  Commercial and Institutional
text:
25.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the building shell, disaggregated by building segment and climate zone — and a Service sub-tree of the energy end-uses. Figure 25.1 shows the structure. The building shell is the organising “product” because the choice of envelope determines the heating and cooling demand placed on the services. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4).






Figure 25.1: Energy-service flow model of the commercial sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree is the building shell, split by building segment (offices, retail, healthcare, education, accommodation, etc.) and by climate zone (Cold / Marine); the Service sub-tree holds the end-use services — HVAC, lighting, cooling, hot water, cooking, refrigeration, plug load, and machine drive — that the shell’s demand draws on.




25.3.1 Products: the building shell, by segment and climate
The Building Shell node disaggregates the stock into about a dozen building segments — Offices, Retail, Wholesale, Transportation and Warehousing, Educational, Healthcare and Social Assistance, Accommodation and Food Services, Arts/Entertainment/Recreation, Information and Cultural, and Other Services — each split by climate zone (Cold / Marine). Each segment competes shell options of differing thermal performance, which set the heat load passed to the HVAC service. This shell-to-HVAC link is the model’s way of capturing the main interactive effect in commercial buildings: investing in a better envelope reduces the energy the heating and cooling systems must deliver.


25.3.2 Services: the end-uses
The Service sub-tree holds the end-uses, each linked to floor space (or to the shell’s heat load) by historical engineering ratios:

HVAC (split Cold / Marine) — the dominant service, modelled as integrated single systems that compete electric and gas existing/improved units, air-source heat pumps (ASHP) and ground-source heat pumps (GSHP), hybrid heat-pump-with-gas-backup systems, oil and propane, and natural-gas cogeneration.
Lighting — three sub-categories (General Area, High Bay, Service), competing efficiency levels from base stock to advanced/LED.
Hot Water — efficient electric, gas, and oil units, heat-pump water heaters (Electric-ASHP), solar pre-heat, and service-load-reduction options.
Cooling, Refrigeration, Cooking, Plug Load — the remaining electric (and, for cooking, gas) end-uses, modelled at average intensities that evolve with equipment efficiency.
Machine Drive and Methane Blend — the shared motor and gaseous-fuel services.

25.4.1 Heat pumps: the central lever
The largest direct-emissions source in commercial buildings is fossil space and water heating, and the central decarbonisation lever is the heat pump. The model competes air-source and ground-source heat pumps, and hybrid systems that pair a heat pump with a gas backup for the coldest hours — a configuration well suited to Canada’s cold climate, which is why the model splits HVAC into Cold and Marine zones. Heat-pump water heaters electrify domestic hot water. These options draw on the broader treatment in the Low-Temperature Industrial Heat and Cogeneration chapters.


25.4.2 Efficiency: envelope, lighting, HVAC, and refrigeration
Reducing demand is as important as switching fuel. A tighter building envelope lowers the heating and cooling load before any equipment runs — the shell-to-HVAC link in the model captures exactly this interaction. LED lighting with controls sharply cuts the single largest electricity end-use, efficient HVAC with smart controls trims the next largest, and efficient, low-GWP refrigeration addresses both energy and refrigerant emissions.


25.4.3 Cogeneration in large facilities
Large institutions with steady, coincident heat and power demand — hospitals, universities, large offices, hotels — can use natural-gas cogeneration, which the model admits to those segments (limited exogenously to 30–50% of the relevant demand) and sizes to the facility’s heat load, selling any surplus electricity back to the grid.

title: 25  Commercial and Institutional
text:
25.5 Economics
Technology choice at every node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4, applied here to building equipment and shells. The sector also makes notable use of retrofit technologies: once existing stock retires, CIMS sets up a competition between leaving the “remembered” stock as-is (operating and maintenance cost only) and attaching a retrofit (adding annualised retrofit capital), so that efficiency upgrades to the existing stock are represented, not just new-build choices.
Commercial technologies are discounted at a high rate — generally 40% in the current data — reflecting the rapid-payback requirements, risk aversion, and capital constraints typical of commercial energy decisions. Two exceptions are encoded: cogeneration and the hospital and school shell/HVAC technologies are discounted at 30%, reflecting their longer, owner-operated planning horizons. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than financial costs of capital — the chapter’s own data notes they are “ex post measures … meant to encompass many more factors than simple rate-of-return criterion” — and CIMS applies them throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4.
The emissions accounting is the simplest kind: there are no process emissions, so all CO₂ comes from fuel combustion in the heating, hot-water, and cooking services, entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price. Electrification (heat pumps), fuel-switching, and efficiency are therefore the only channels for emissions reduction, and their effect depends on the carbon intensity of the regional grid. A known simplification is that energy prices are average per-unit charges, so the demand-charge savings of efficiency measures are not captured; the model also captures only the main shell–HVAC interactive effect, not the full set of inter-end-use interactions.

title: 25  Commercial and Institutional
text:
25.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions carry the commercial structure, and the Cold / Marine climate split is the key regional dimension: most of Canada is in the Cold zone, while coastal British Columbia and parts of the Atlantic are Marine, with milder heating demand and different heat-pump performance. Beyond climate, regional differences show up in the fuel mix — the model assumes essentially no new oil heating after 1990 except in the Atlantic region, where natural gas is less available and oil heating remains significant — and in grid carbon intensity, which determines how much electrification actually reduces emissions.
TODO: Confirm the regional building-segment floor-space mix and the Cold/Marine zone assignments against current commercial building-stock data, since both the heating demand and the heat-pump economics depend on them.

title: 25  Commercial and Institutional
text:
25.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The commercial sub-model is a mature, detailed buildings representation — segment- and climate-resolved shells, an explicit shell–HVAC interaction, retrofit competitions, and a full set of heat-pump and efficiency options. Its acknowledged limitations are the partial treatment of inter-end-use interactive effects (only the shell–HVAC link is quantified), the average-price treatment of energy (missing demand-charge savings), and reliance on inherited floor-space and intensity calibrations. The TODOs above record the priorities, of which cold-climate heat-pump performance and refreshed floor-space data are the most important for present-day analysis.

title: 26  Transportation (Passenger)
text:
26.1 Scope
Passenger transportation is the personal-mobility module of CIMS-Transportation (CIMS-T), a demand-side sub-model: it meets a demand for personal mobility (people moved, in passenger-kilometres) by competing transport modes and, within the dominant road mode, competing vehicle powertrains. The emphasis is on the structure of the service flow model: the mobility-demand nodes, the modes and vehicles that supply them, and the costs — financial and intangible — that drive the competition. The tree is region-agnostic. Passenger transport is distinctive in two ways: it is among Canada’s largest emitting sectors, and its technology choices are unusually shaped by consumer preferences (range, refuelling convenience, vehicle size, and power), which CIMS represents through explicit intangible costs alongside financial cost.
CIMS represents passenger mobility — urban and inter-city travel of people — driven by passenger-kilometre demand. It covers personal vehicles (cars and light trucks), urban transit (public bus and rapid transit), inter-city bus and rail, and inter-city air. The driving demand is projected exogenously and can itself respond to cost (the model can shift demand for mobility).
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: freight movement is in Transportation (Freight); off-road vehicles are handled separately; the fuels (gasoline, diesel, electricity, hydrogen, biofuels) are supplied by the energy-supply sub-models, including Ethanol, Biodiesel, Hydrogen, and Electricity; and vehicle manufacturing is in Light Industrial. This chapter covers the use of vehicles to move people.

title: 26  Transportation (Passenger)
text:
26.2 Real-world context
Transportation is responsible for roughly a quarter of Canada’s greenhouse-gas emissions, and light-duty passenger vehicles are the single largest part of it. The emissions come overwhelmingly from burning gasoline and diesel, with associated health costs estimated in the billions of dollars annually (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2023). Policy is now driving a rapid transition: Canada’s zero-emission-vehicle (ZEV) mandate requires 100% of new light-duty vehicle sales to be zero-emission by 2035, with interim targets of 20% by 2026 and 60% by 2030, where a ZEV is a battery-electric, plug-in-hybrid, or fuel-cell vehicle (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2023).
Two forces shape the transition in the model. First, vehicle electrification: battery-electric vehicles now cost roughly CAD 50,000–70,000 (entry models from ~$40,000) but have 66–77% lower fuel-and-maintenance costs than gasoline vehicles, and the gap is closing (Natural Resources Canada 2026). Second, mode shift and transit electrification: moving trips from single-occupant vehicles to higher-occupancy vehicles, transit, and active modes cuts energy per passenger-km, and electrifying transit buses cuts their emissions by around 93% ( 2025). But consumer choice is not driven by cost alone — range anxiety, refuelling availability, and preferences for larger, more powerful vehicles all matter, which is why CIMS-T carries intangible costs to reproduce observed behaviour. The structure captures all three levers: powertrain competition, mode competition, and the intangible-cost preferences that temper both.

title: 26  Transportation (Passenger)
text:
26.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the mobility demand by mode — and a Service sub-tree of the vehicles and transit systems that supply it. Figure 26.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); mode and powertrain shares are determined by lifecycle cost plus intangible cost.






Figure 26.1: Service flow model of passenger transportation (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree is mobility demand by mode — Urban (single- and high-occupancy vehicles, public transit, walk/cycle), Intercity Land (vehicle, bus, rail), and Intercity Air — and the Service sub-tree supplies it through passenger vehicles (size classes and competing powertrains), transit (public bus, rapid transit), and intercity bus and rail.




26.3.1 Products: mobility demand by mode
The Mode node splits personal mobility into:

Urban — single-occupant vehicle (SOV), high-occupant vehicle (HOV), public transit, and walk/cycle. The competition among these is the model’s representation of urban mode shift.
Intercity Land — passenger vehicle, bus, and rail.
Intercity Air — competing conventional, efficient, electric, and hydrogen aircraft.

Demand can shift between modes (SOV↔︎HOV↔︎transit↔︎active; vehicle↔︎bus↔︎rail) as relative costs change, one of the endogenous actions CIMS-T simulates.


26.3.2 Services: vehicles and transit

Passenger Vehicles — the size classes (small/large cars, small/large light trucks) — and Passenger Vehicle Motors, where the powertrains compete: gasoline (existing/standard/efficient), hybrid, plug-in hybrid, battery-electric (by range, e.g. 500 and 800 km), and hydrogen fuel-cell. Powertrain and efficiency are specified for new vehicles; older vintages are tracked and retired by a stock-turnover function.
Transit — Public Bus (diesel, hybrid, electric) and Rapid Transit.
Intercity Bus — diesel, gasoline, hybrid, biodiesel-hybrid, natural-gas, hydrogen.
Intercity Rail — diesel (and efficient diesel), electric, hydrogen, biodiesel-hybrid.

26.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Passenger-transport decarbonisation works through three channels: electrifying vehicles (and transit and rail), shifting modes toward higher-occupancy and active travel, and low-carbon fuels where electrification is hard (aviation, some intercity). 26.4.1 Electrifying the light-duty fleet
The dominant lever is electrifying personal vehicles. The model competes battery-electric (at different ranges), plug-in hybrid, hybrid, and fuel-cell powertrains against gasoline, with the ZEV transition emerging from their falling capital costs and much lower running costs — tempered by the intangible costs that capture range anxiety, charging/refuelling availability, and the consumer preference for larger vehicles. Because powertrain is set for new vehicles and the fleet turns over through retirement, the modelled transition is gradual even under a sales mandate.


26.4.2 Mode shift and transit/rail electrification
Beyond the vehicle, shifting trips from single-occupant cars to high-occupancy vehicles, public transit, and walking and cycling lowers energy per passenger-km — one of CIMS-T’s endogenous actions, governed by the intangible cost differences between modes. Electrifying transit buses (and, where lines justify it, rail) cuts those modes’ emissions by around 90% ( 2025), and the model competes electric and hydrogen buses and electric and hydrogen rail directly.


26.4.3 Decarbonising aviation
Inter-city air is the hardest to abate. The model already competes efficient, electric, and hydrogen aircraft (the last two viable mainly for short-haul), but the principal near-term route — sustainable aviation fuel and e-fuels — is not yet represented (see the TODO above).

title: 26  Transportation (Passenger)
text:
26.5 Economics
Technology and mode choice follow the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4, but passenger transport relies more than any other sector on intangible costs — the non-financial component of the choice. CIMS-T’s intangible costs encode consumers’ revealed willingness to pay for vehicle size and power, their preference for the range and refuelling convenience of gasoline over alternative fuels, and their preferences among urban modes. These are calibrated from market data and stated-preference surveys, and they are what allow the model to reproduce observed adoption rather than the cost-minimising choice a purely financial calculation would predict.
Financial costs are discounted at behavioural rates — around 8% for some capital-intensive, long-lived assets (rail, transit infrastructure) and around 25% for personal-vehicle decisions in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than pure financial costs of capital; together with the intangible costs they govern technology choice, as set out in the discount-rate and intangible-cost discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4.
Emissions arise from fuel combustion in the vehicles, buses, trains, and aircraft, entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price; battery-electric options have zero tailpipe emissions and inherit the carbon intensity of the grid. The emissions benefit of electrification therefore depends on regional grid intensity, and the benefit of biofuels on their life-cycle intensity from the Ethanol and Biodiesel sub-models. A note of caution carried from the original documentation: many of CIMS-T’s intangible-cost parameters are under active review against stated-preference survey data, so the modelled pace of the ZEV transition is sensitive to them.

title: 26  Transportation (Passenger)
text:
26.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions carry the passenger-transport structure. Regional differences show up in urban form — denser regions (the large metropolitan areas) support more transit and active-mode share, while dispersed regions are more car-dependent — and in grid carbon intensity, which determines how much electrification actually reduces emissions (large in hydro-rich Québec, British Columbia, and Manitoba; smaller in Alberta and Saskatchewan until their grids decarbonise). Fuel availability (charging and hydrogen networks) also varies and enters through the intangible costs.
TODO: Calibrate the regional mode-share baselines and the intangible costs of transit and active modes against current travel-survey data, since urban mode shift is sensitive to both and varies widely by region.

title: 26  Transportation (Passenger)
text:
26.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The passenger-transport sub-model captures the essential structure — mobility demand, mode competition, powertrain competition, and a rich intangible-cost representation of consumer preference. Its main limitations are the absence of sustainable aviation fuels and e-fuels, the reliance on intangible-cost parameters that are still being recalibrated, the exogenous treatment of some transit-technology choices, and stock-turnover dynamics that make the modelled transition gradual. The TODOs above record the priorities, of which adding SAF/e-fuels and refreshing the intangible costs are the most important.

title: 27  Freight Transportation
text:
27.1 Scope
Freight transportation is the goods-movement module of CIMS-Transportation (CIMS-T), a demand-side sub-model: it meets a demand for freight movement (goods moved, in tonne-kilometres) by competing transport modes — road, rail, marine, and air — and, within each, competing vehicle powertrains and fuels. The emphasis is on the structure of the service flow model: the freight-demand nodes, the modes and vehicles that supply them, and the refuelling and charging infrastructure they need. The tree is region-agnostic. The general CIMS-T framework — service flow model, intangible costs, and stock-turnover dynamics — is described in the Transportation (Passenger) chapter and is not repeated here.
CIMS represents the movement of goods by road (heavy trucks and light/medium commercial vehicles), rail, marine, and air, plus an off-road category (construction, agricultural, and other off-highway equipment). The driving variable is freight demand in tonne-kilometres, projected exogenously and able to shift between modes. The model also carries explicit infrastructure services — charging, overhead catenary, and hydrogen refuelling — recognising that zero-emission freight depends as much on infrastructure as on the vehicles.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: passenger mobility is in Transportation (Passenger); the fuels (diesel, electricity, hydrogen, biofuels, natural gas) are supplied by the energy-supply sub-models; and vehicle manufacturing is in Light Industrial. This chapter covers the use of vehicles to move goods.

title: 27  Freight Transportation
text:
27.2 Real-world context
Freight is a large and stubborn share of transport emissions, and it is dominated by on-road heavy trucks. In 2019, on-road freight produced about 64.8 Mt of Canada’s transport emissions, against 7.8 Mt from rail and 4.5 Mt from marine (International Council on Clean Transportation 2023). The disparity reflects efficiency as much as volume: rail freight is more than five times as emissions-efficient per tonne-kilometre as road, so shifting goods from truck to rail or intermodal can cut emissions by up to 30% (International Council on Clean Transportation 2023). Heavy trucks are also among the hardest road vehicles to decarbonise, because their weight, range, and duty cycles strain battery technology.
Three zero-emission pathways are competing for heavy freight, and the model represents all of them. Battery-electric trucks are favoured for lighter and shorter-range duty; hydrogen fuel-cell trucks are emerging for heavy long-haul, where range and refuelling time matter and where — as techno-economic studies including intangible costs find — hydrogen tends to win over batteries (International Council on Clean Transportation 2023; Pembina Institute 2023); and overhead catenary (eHighway) systems power trucks directly from the road on major corridors. By the 2030s, catenary and battery-electric trucks are projected to cost roughly 30–35% less to own and run than diesel, and hydrogen 15–25% less (International Council on Clean Transportation 2023). For rail, electrification, hydrogen, and biofuels apply; for marine, hydrogen, ammonia, and biofuels; and for aviation, sustainable aviation fuels and e-fuels. The CIMS structure captures these technology competitions and, distinctively, the infrastructure they require.

title: 27  Freight Transportation
text:
27.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — freight demand by mode — and a Service sub-tree of the refuelling and charging infrastructure. Figure 27.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); mode and powertrain shares are determined by lifecycle cost plus intangible cost.






Figure 27.1: Service flow model of freight transportation (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree is freight demand by mode — Land (heavy trucks and rail; light/medium vehicles), Marine, Air, and Off-Road — each competing diesel/biofuel against electric, hydrogen, and (for trucks) catenary powertrains; the Service sub-tree provides the EV charging, overhead-catenary, and hydrogen-refuelling infrastructure that zero-emission freight depends on.




27.3.1 Products: freight demand by mode

Land — Heavy — split into Trucks and Rail. Heavy Trucks compete diesel (existing/standard/efficient), biodiesel, natural gas, plug-in hybrid, battery-electric, hydrogen fuel-cell, and catenary (eHighway) powertrains. Heavy Rail competes diesel (and efficient diesel), biodiesel, electric, and hydrogen.
Land — Light/Medium — commercial vans and medium trucks, competing gasoline and diesel (existing/standard/efficient), propane, biodiesel, plug-in hybrid, battery-electric, and hydrogen.
Marine — competing fuel oil (existing/standard/efficient), biodiesel, and hydrogen.
Air — competing conventional, efficient, electric, and hydrogen aircraft.
Off Road — construction, agricultural, and other off-highway equipment, competing diesel (standard/medium/high-efficiency) and electric.

Freight demand can shift between modes — most importantly road to rail — as relative costs change.


27.3.2 Services: zero-emission infrastructure
A distinctive feature of the freight sub-model is that it carries the infrastructure zero-emission vehicles depend on as explicit services:

EV Infrastructure — Depot Stations (overnight/return-to-base charging) and Rapid Charging Stations (en-route fast charging).
Catenary Infrastructure — the overhead-wire (eHighway) system for catenary trucks.
FCEV Infrastructure — hydrogen refuelling.

Representing these explicitly means the model can capture the chicken-and-egg coupling between zero-emission trucks and the networks they need, rather than assuming the infrastructure is free.

text:
27.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Freight decarbonisation works through powertrain switching (electric, hydrogen, catenary, biofuels), modal shift (road to rail/marine), and low-carbon fuels for the hard-to-electrify modes (marine, aviation). Table 27.1 summarises maturity and Table 27.2 gives indicative costs.

27.4.1 Zero-emission trucks and their infrastructure
Heavy trucks are the centre of gravity for freight emissions, and the model competes the three contenders — battery-electric, hydrogen fuel-cell, and catenary — against diesel and biodiesel. Which wins depends on duty cycle and on the intangible costs of range, refuelling time, and infrastructure availability: studies that include these costs find battery-electric dominating lighter and regional duty while hydrogen emerges for heavy long-haul (International Council on Clean Transportation 2023). Crucially, all three depend on infrastructure — depot and rapid charging, overhead catenary, and hydrogen refuelling — which the model carries as explicit services, so the cost of building out that infrastructure is part of the competition.


27.4.2 Modal shift and the hard-to-electrify modes
Because rail is over five times as efficient per tonne-km as road, shifting freight from truck to rail and intermodal is a powerful lever, and the model allows freight demand to move between modes. Rail itself decarbonises through electrification, hydrogen, and biofuels. Marine and aviation are the hardest: marine switches to hydrogen, ammonia, and biofuels, and aviation to sustainable aviation fuels and e-fuels (the model currently competes efficient, electric, and hydrogen aircraft; SAF/e-fuels remain to be added, consistent with the passenger-aviation TODO).

title: 27  Freight Transportation
text:
27.5 Economics
Technology and mode choice follow the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4, combined — as throughout CIMS-T — with intangible costs that capture the non-financial barriers to alternative-fuel freight: vehicle range, refuelling time and availability, payload penalties, and operator familiarity. These are decisive for heavy trucks, where they tip the competition between battery-electric and hydrogen.
Financial costs are discounted at behavioural rates — around 12.5% for some capital-intensive, long-lived assets (rail) and around 25–30% for road-vehicle decisions in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than pure financial costs of capital; together with the intangible costs they govern technology choice, as set out in the discount-rate and intangible-cost discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4.
Emissions arise from fuel combustion in the trucks, trains, ships, and aircraft, entering through each technology’s fuel service requests and the carbon price; battery-electric and catenary options have zero tailpipe emissions and inherit the carbon intensity of the grid, while hydrogen inherits the intensity of the Hydrogen production mix and biofuels their life-cycle intensity from the Biodiesel sub-model. The emissions benefit of each option therefore depends on the upstream energy system, and the infrastructure services mean the model accounts for the capital needed to enable the switch, not just the vehicles.

title: 27  Freight Transportation
text:
27.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions carry the freight structure. Regional differences show up in mode mix — long inland corridors (the Prairies, Ontario–Québec) favour rail and long-haul trucking, coastal and Great Lakes regions add marine — in grid carbon intensity (which sets the benefit of electric and catenary trucks and electric rail), and in the hydrogen supply available regionally (Alberta’s blue hydrogen, hydro-based electrolytic hydrogen elsewhere). Infrastructure build-out — charging, catenary corridors, hydrogen refuelling — is inherently regional and enters through the infrastructure services and their intangible costs.

title: 27  Freight Transportation
text:
27.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The freight sub-model captures the essential structure — freight demand, mode competition, a full set of zero-emission truck powertrains, and explicit refuelling/charging infrastructure — which makes it well suited to analysing the heavy-duty transition. Its main limitations are the absence of sustainable aviation fuels, e-fuels, and marine ammonia; reliance on intangible-cost parameters still being recalibrated; the exogenous treatment of some freight-technology shares (noted in the CIMS-T overview); and stock-turnover dynamics that make the transition gradual. The TODOs above record the priorities.

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.1 Scope
The waste sector is unlike most others CIMS represents: its greenhouse-gas footprint is overwhelmingly a single non-CO₂ gas — methane generated as organic waste decomposes in landfills — rather than energy use. The sub-model is therefore built around the management of that landfill methane: whether it is vented, flared, or captured for energy. The emphasis, as elsewhere, is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — the nodes, the technologies that compete at each, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. Tellingly, the sector’s activity is measured directly in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent, signalling that emissions, not energy or output, are its organising variable.
CIMS represents the management of landfill gas at municipal solid waste disposal sites — the dominant source of greenhouse gases in the waste sector. Landfills are grouped by size (large, medium, and small), because the economics of gas collection and use depend strongly on how much gas a site produces. The driving variable is the methane-generation potential of the waste in place, expressed in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent; a forecast of that potential — which declines over the projection as waste diversion reduces the organic material sent to landfill — drives the sub-model.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere or fall outside the current model. Waste collection and haulage are part of the Transportation (Freight) sector; the energy services of waste-management facilities are small and not separately represented; and waste used as a fuel (waste-derived fuel in cement kilns, biomass boilers) is accounted in the consuming sectors. The current sub-model focuses on landfill gas; wastewater treatment methane and waste incineration are not yet represented (see the limitations below).

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.2 Real-world context
The waste sector is a small but stubborn share of Canada’s greenhouse-gas emissions, and it is dominated by landfill methane. As the organic fraction of municipal solid waste — food, paper, wood, yard trimmings — decomposes anaerobically in a landfill, it generates landfill gas that is roughly half methane and half CO₂. Because methane has a global-warming potential many times that of CO₂ (on the order of 28–30 over 100 years, and far higher over 20 years), uncontrolled landfill gas is the sector’s defining problem and its largest abatement opportunity.
The levers are well established. Capturing the gas with a collection system and flaring it converts the methane to CO₂, cutting the warming impact of that gas by roughly a factor of 25 at modest cost; capturing it and using it for energy — electricity generation, or upgrading to pipeline-quality renewable natural gas (RNG) — does the same while displacing fossil energy and earning revenue. Upstream, diverting organics from landfill through composting and anaerobic digestion prevents the methane from being generated in the first place. Canada has committed under the Global Methane Pledge to cut methane sharply by 2030, and federal regulations targeting methane from large municipal landfills (gas capture and control requirements) are a central part of the waste-sector effort (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2024). The CIMS structure mirrors the end-of-pipe choice directly: each landfill chooses among venting, flaring, and energy recovery, with the size split capturing the very different economics of large versus small sites.

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the landfill sites, grouped by size — with the gas-management technologies competing at each. Figure 28.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the landfill-gas options compete on lifecycle cost, with the carbon price (applied to methane on a CO₂-equivalent basis) as the main driver.






Figure 28.1: Energy-service flow model of the waste sector (region-agnostic master tree). Methane-generation potential (in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent) is allocated across landfill Sites by size (Large, Medium, Small); at each, three landfill-gas options compete — No Control (vents CH₄), Flaring (captures and burns the gas, converting CH₄ to CO₂), and Electricity Generation (landfill-gas-to-energy, which also produces electricity). Larger sites more readily justify capture and energy recovery.




28.3.1 Products: landfill sites and their gas-management options
The Sites node splits the landfill stock into Large Sites, Medium Sites, and Small Sites. At each, three technologies compete to manage the landfill gas:

No Control — the gas is vented uncontrolled, so the site emits its full methane potential as CH₄. This is the do-nothing baseline.
Flaring — a gas-collection system captures the landfill gas and flares it, combusting the methane. The emission becomes CO₂ rather than CH₄, cutting the warming impact of the captured gas roughly twenty-five-fold while producing no useful energy.
Electricity Generation — landfill-gas-to-energy: the captured gas (modelled as a biogas fuel) is burned in an engine to generate electricity, again emitting CO₂ rather than CH₄ and, in addition, displacing grid electricity (the technology returns power to the grid).

The site-size grouping is what lets the model represent the central real-world fact that large landfills generate enough gas to justify a collection system and an engine, while small sites often cannot and are more likely to vent or, at most, flare.
TODO: The model represents only the end-of-pipe management of landfill gas. Add upstream organics diversion (composting and anaerobic digestion) as a competing way to reduce the methane-generation potential itself, since diverting food and yard waste prevents the gas rather than treating it — and is the lever federal and municipal policy increasingly emphasises.

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.4 Decarbonisation technologies
Waste-sector decarbonisation means capturing and using landfill methane and, further upstream, preventing its generation. 28.4.1 Capturing and using landfill gas
The largest and cheapest lever is to stop venting. A gas-collection system with flaring converts captured methane to CO₂ at low cost and is the workhorse of landfill methane control; it is the Flaring technology in the model. Where a site generates enough gas, electricity generation does the same while earning power revenue — the model’s Electricity Generation technology, which returns electricity to the grid — and upgrading to renewable natural gas (not yet a distinct option in the model) displaces fossil gas instead. Larger sites favour energy recovery; smaller sites favour flaring or remain uncontrolled, which is exactly why the model resolves the stock by size.


28.4.2 Preventing methane: organics diversion
The deeper lever is to keep the organic material out of the landfill in the first place. Composting and anaerobic digestion of food and yard waste prevent the anaerobic decomposition that generates landfill methane, and anaerobic digestion additionally yields biogas. These upstream options reduce the methane-generation potential itself rather than managing the gas after the fact, and are the focus of much current policy — but the model does not yet represent them (see the TODO above).

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.5 Economics
Technology choice at each site follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each landfill-gas option carries a capital cost (collection system, flare or engine), an operating cost, the methane-generation potential it serves, any electricity it returns to the grid, and availability and lifetime years; these are combined into a lifecycle cost and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Waste technologies are discounted at rates of roughly 20–35% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real investment; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters govern how sharply the gas-management competitions respond to cost.
The emissions accounting is the heart of this sub-model and is almost entirely non-CO₂. The No Control technology emits the site’s full potential as CH₄, while Flaring and Electricity Generation emit the same quantity of carbon as CO₂ — so the difference between them, on a CO₂-equivalent basis, is the large methane-versus-CO₂ warming gap. Methane enters at its high global-warming potential, which is what makes capture so valuable per dollar. The Electricity Generation route additionally returns power to the grid, an avoided-emissions and revenue benefit that improves its lifecycle cost. Because the activity variable is itself in CO₂-equivalent and the abatement options are inexpensive relative to their methane benefit, even a modest carbon price (or a landfill methane regulation) drives a large shift from venting toward flaring and energy recovery.

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the waste structure, each with its large, medium, and small landfill sites. The methane-generation potential differs by region with population and waste arisings, and it declines over the projection as diversion programmes reduce the organic fraction sent to landfill. Regional differences also show up in the value of the recovered electricity, which depends on the local grid and power price, and in the share of large sites (which can justify energy recovery) versus small ones.
TODO: Calibrate the regional split of waste across large, medium, and small sites and the baseline control levels (vent / flare / energy) against Environment and Climate Change Canada’s National Inventory Report and provincial landfill data, since both the emissions and the abatement potential depend heavily on the site-size distribution.

title: 28  Waste
text:
28.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The waste sub-model captures the sector’s dominant emission — landfill methane — and the core end-of-pipe management choice between venting, flaring, and energy recovery, resolved by site size. But it is deliberately narrow, and several real-world levers and sources are missing. The TODOs above record the priorities: adding upstream organics diversion (composting and anaerobic digestion) that prevents methane generation, adding a renewable natural gas upgrading pathway alongside electricity generation, and representing gas-capture efficiency explicitly rather than as a binary control choice. Two further sources — wastewater treatment methane and waste incineration — are not represented at all and would round out the sector. Because waste emissions are largely non-CO₂ and cheap to abate, a faithful representation of these levers is valuable out of proportion to the sector’s small energy footprint.

title: 29  Agriculture
text:
29.1 Scope
Agriculture is unlike the other sectors CIMS represents: most of its greenhouse-gas emissions are not from burning fuel but from biological and chemical processes — methane (CH₄) from livestock digestion and manure, and nitrous oxide (N₂O) from soils — so the sub-model is built around those process emissions and the options that abate them, rather than around energy services. The emphasis, as elsewhere, is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — the process and service nodes, the technologies that compete at each, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. Tellingly, the sector’s activity is measured directly in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent, signalling that emissions, not energy or output, are its organising variable.
CIMS represents the greenhouse-gas-emitting activities of agriculture and the on-farm energy that supports them: livestock enteric fermentation and manure management (the CH₄ sources), agricultural soils (the N₂O source, together with the land-management practices that affect it), farm tractors (mobile diesel equipment), and farm process and building heat. The driving variable is the level of agricultural activity, expressed in CO₂-equivalent terms.
Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere to avoid double-counting: the manufacture of nitrogen fertiliser is in Chemical Products (ammonia synthesis); food and beverage processing is in Light Industrial; the biofuels that use agricultural feedstock are in Biodiesel and Ethanol (which carry their own Agricultural Input services); and the fuels burned on-farm are supplied by the energy-supply sub-models. This chapter covers the emissions and energy use of farming itself.

title: 29  Agriculture
text:
29.2 Real-world context
Agriculture is responsible for roughly 8% of Canada’s greenhouse-gas emissions, and the composition is distinctive: it is overwhelmingly non-CO₂. Enteric fermentation — the methane cattle and other ruminants produce as they digest forage — is the single largest source, around 46% of agricultural emissions; manure management (CH₄ and N₂O) adds about 27%; and agricultural soils emit N₂O, chiefly from nitrogen fertiliser and crop residues (National Farmers Union 2022). On-farm fuel use (tractors, grain drying, heating) is comparatively small and is mostly diesel and natural gas.
This composition shapes the decarbonisation problem. Because the emissions are biological, the levers are agronomic and dietary rather than purely technological: feed additives and rumen modification to cut enteric methane, manure management changes, nitrogen and tillage management to cut soil N₂O, and land-use practices (agroforestry, wetland restoration, reduced tillage) that store carbon in soils and biomass. The feed additive 3-nitrooxypropanol (3-NOP), for example, consistently cuts enteric methane by around 30% on average (Kebreab et al. 2021). The CIMS structure mirrors this: it carries explicit CH₄ and N₂O process-emission factors on the livestock and soils nodes and competes the abatement practices against conventional ones, while representing the on-farm energy through a small set of tractor and heat technologies.

title: 29  Agriculture
text:
29.3 Model structure
The sector divides into a Product sub-tree — the emitting agricultural processes — and a Service sub-tree of the on-farm energy services. Figure 29.1 shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see Chapter 4); the abatement options compete against conventional practice on a lifecycle-cost basis, with the carbon price (applied to CH₄ and N₂O on a CO₂-equivalent basis) as the main driver.






Figure 29.1: Energy-service flow model of the agriculture sector (region-agnostic master tree). The Product sub-tree holds the emitting processes — Enteric Fermentation and Manure Management (CH₄) and Soils (N₂O, with tillage and land-use options including net-sequestering practices) — and the Service sub-tree holds on-farm Tractors and Heat.




29.3.1 Products: the emitting processes

Enteric Fermentation and Manure Management — the livestock methane source. It competes conventional Livestock against Livestock + Vaccines + Rumen changes, a package of dietary and biological interventions (feed additives such as 3-NOP, methane vaccines, rumen modification) that cuts the enteric-CH₄ factor by roughly 60% in the data.
Soils — the cropland N₂O source, competing land-management practices that differ in their soil-N₂O intensity and carbon storage: Conventional Tillage, Minimal Tillage, and Zero Tillage (progressively lower N₂O), and Agroforestry and Wetland Restoration, which store carbon and can be net-sequestering.



29.3.2 Services: tractors and heat

Tractors — on-farm mobile equipment, competing standard and medium-efficiency diesel against a hydrogen option.
Heat — farm process and building heat (grain drying, livestock housing), competing standard and efficient natural-gas and electric units.

TODO: The model lumps manure management together with enteric fermentation in a single node. Separate manure management so that its distinct abatement options — anaerobic digestion (biogas capture), covered storage, and solid–liquid separation — can be represented, since manure is about a quarter of agricultural emissions and has different, often cost-effective, mitigation.

29.4.1 Cutting enteric and manure methane
The largest single source — enteric methane — is addressed by dietary and biological means: feed additives (notably 3-NOP), methane-suppressing vaccines, and rumen modification, represented in the model as the Livestock + Vaccines + Rumen changes package. Manure methane is best cut by anaerobic digestion, which captures the gas for energy, and by covered storage — high-value options the model does not yet separate from enteric emissions (see the TODO above).


29.4.2 Cutting soil N₂O and storing carbon
Soil N₂O falls with reduced and zero tillage and with better nitrogen management (right rate, source, timing, and placement — “4R” stewardship — and nitrification inhibitors). Agroforestry and wetland restoration go further by storing carbon in biomass and soils, and are among the few agricultural options that can be net-sequestering. The model competes the tillage and land-use practices directly at the Soils node.


29.4.3 On-farm energy
On-farm energy is a smaller lever: efficient and hydrogen tractors cut mobile-diesel CO₂, and electric and efficient farm heat cut heating emissions, drawing on the same low-carbon options as the other sectors.

title: 29  Agriculture
text:
29.5 Economics
Technology choice at every node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. Each practice carries a capital cost (often small), operating cost, an activity basis, any service requests, and availability and lifetime years; these are combined into a lifecycle cost and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.
Agricultural practices are discounted at about 30% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS this is a behavioural (revealed or empirical) discount rate rather than a true financial cost of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real farm decisions; CIMS applies it throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the Theory chapter and in Chapter 4. Heterogeneity (variance) parameters are set around 10–15.
The emissions accounting is the heart of this sub-model and is almost entirely non-CO₂: it carries explicit CH₄ factors on the enteric/manure node and N₂O factors on the soils node, applied per unit of activity and entering on a CO₂-equivalent basis at their high global-warming potentials. Some land-use practices (agroforestry, wetland restoration) can carry net-negative factors, representing carbon storage. Because the activity variable is itself in CO₂-equivalent, the carbon price acts very directly here: it makes the abatement packages — feed additives, reduced tillage, sequestering land use — cost-competitive against conventional practice, which is the model’s channel for agricultural mitigation.

title: 29  Agriculture
text:
29.6 Regional coverage and differences
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the agriculture structure. The mix of sources differs by region: the Prairie provinces (Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba) dominate both cattle (enteric and manure CH₄) and cropland (soil N₂O from extensive grain and oilseed production); Ontario and Québec have mixed livestock and cropping; and the Atlantic and British Columbia have smaller, more specialised agricultural sectors.
TODO: Calibrate the regional balance of livestock versus cropland emissions and the baseline tillage mix, since the effectiveness and cost of the abatement practices depend heavily on the regional activity mix.

title: 29  Agriculture
text:
29.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The agriculture sub-model captures the sector’s dominant emissions — enteric and manure methane, and soil N₂O — and the main practice-based abatement levers, but it is deliberately coarse. Its principal limitations are the lumping of manure with enteric fermentation (hiding the cost-effective digester and storage options), the absence of explicit nitrogen-management options, and the simplified treatment of soil-carbon sequestration, whose permanence and measurement are genuinely difficult. The TODOs above record these priorities. Because agricultural emissions are largely non-CO₂ and biological, they are among the hardest in the whole model to abate deeply, which makes a faithful representation of the available practices especially valuable.

title: 30  Forestry
text:
30.1 Scope
The logging industry’s on-site greenhouse-gas footprint comes almost entirely from the diesel burned by mobile harvesting and handling equipment — feller-bunchers, skidders, harvesters, forwarders, and loaders working in the bush — so the sector is represented as a single mobile-equipment energy service in which diesel competes against electric. The tree is region-agnostic, and the sector’s activity is measured directly in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent, signalling that emissions, not output, are its organising variable. The structure is deliberately coarse; the limitations below set out what a fuller representation would add.
CIMS represents the fuel use of forestry’s mobile equipment — the off-road machinery that fells, gathers, and moves timber at the harvest site — as one aggregate energy service. The driving variable is an exogenous forecast of the sector’s emissions in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. Everything downstream of the roadside is handled elsewhere: log haulage on public roads belongs to Transportation (Freight), and the milling of logs into lumber and pulp is in Pulp and Paper and the wood-products part of Light Industrial. The biological carbon of the forest itself — growth, harvest, and regrowth — is the domain of LULUCF, not this sector.

title: 30  Forestry
text:
30.2 Real-world context
Logging is energy-light compared with heavy industry, but what energy it uses is overwhelmingly diesel in rugged off-road machines that run long duty cycles far from grid power. That combination — high power demand, remote sites, and no charging infrastructure — is exactly what makes the harvest fleet hard to electrify, and it is why diesel still does essentially all the work today. The decarbonisation options are the same three that face any off-road diesel fleet: drop-in renewable diesel or biodiesel that cuts lifecycle carbon with no equipment change, battery-electric machines where duty cycles and charging allow, and hydrogen fuel-cell machines for the heaviest, longest-running equipment. Canadian work on zero- and low-emission options for the forest sector — much of it through FPInnovations — has so far concentrated on the haulage fleet, where battery-electric Class 8 trucks have demonstrated more than 60% lower energy use and at least 80% lower greenhouse-gas emissions than diesel, with the in-bush machines a harder and later problem (FPInnovations 2024). The CIMS structure mirrors the core choice directly: a single competition between diesel and electric equipment.

title: 30  Forestry
text:
30.3 Model structure
The sector is a single tech-compete node. Figure 30.1 shows the structure: the exogenous activity drives one Transport service, at which two technologies compete to provide the same mobile-equipment work.






Figure 30.1: Energy-service flow model of the forestry sector (region-agnostic master tree). An exogenous activity forecast in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent drives a single Transport service node, a tech-compete between diesel equipment (which draws on the diesel fuel blend and emits CO₂) and electric equipment (which draws grid electricity). Lower-carbon drop-in fuels and hydrogen are noted as future options not yet in the model.



At the Transport node, diesel equipment (the entire base-year fleet) requests the diesel transportation fuel blend, while electric equipment requests grid electricity; both carry a twenty-year lifetime and the same energy requirement per unit of activity. Because the diesel option draws on the blended fuel, any renewable-diesel content in that blend lowers its lifecycle carbon automatically (see Biodiesel). Fuel prices at the node are currently borrowed from Agriculture as a proxy and flagged for review.

title: 30  Forestry
text:
30.5 Economics
Technology choice at the Transport node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of Chapter 4. As elsewhere in CIMS, the intended discount rate is behavioural (revealed or empirical) rather than a true financial cost of capital, capturing the short payback horizons typical of resource industries (see the Theory chapter). In the current input files, however, the two technologies carry only a lifetime and their energy requests — capital cost, operating cost, the discount rate, and the heterogeneity (variance) parameter are not yet populated — so the diesel-versus-electric competition cannot yet resolve on cost and the fleet holds near its base-year shares. Emissions enter upstream through the fuels the technologies request: the diesel option carries the carbon of the diesel blend, while the electric option moves the load to the grid, where it is counted in Electricity.

title: 30  Forestry
text:
30.6 Regional coverage
All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry the forestry structure, scaled by an exogenous emissions forecast that differs sharply with the size of each region’s logging industry: British Columbia is by far the largest, with Québec and Ontario next, and the Prairie provinces much smaller. The structure itself is identical across regions.

title: 30  Forestry
text:
30.7 Limitations and planned extensions
The forestry sub-model is a placeholder: it captures the sector’s dominant emission source — off-road diesel equipment — and the central diesel-to-electric choice, but little else. The off-road fleet is collapsed into a single aggregate Transport service rather than resolved by machine type or duty cycle; the competing technologies are not yet costed; the fuel prices are proxied from agriculture; and lower-carbon liquid fuels and hydrogen are not yet explicit options. The TODOs above record the priorities. Because forestry’s footprint is small, this coarse treatment is a reasonable interim, but populating the technology costs is the minimum needed for the diesel-to-electric transition to respond to policy at all.

The auxiliary systems fall into four general categories: steam generation (boilers and cogenerators), lighting, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC), and electric motor systems including pumps, fans, compressors, and conveyors. Figure 9 shows the energy flow diagrams for auxiliary systems not included in Figure 8. In some cases, the energy service meets the direct need for steam, pumping, or compression, while in other cases, it serves only to provide suitable conditions for production to continue, as in the case of lighting and HVAC systems.
Figure 9. Auxiliary Flow Model Diagram
The sections that follow describe how key auxiliary systems and process specific components are captured by the CIMS industrial model. The section on auxiliary systems covers steam generation and electric auxiliary services. Lighting and HVAC are not described in detail because the energy demanded by these services is small. The section on process specific systems covers each of the CIMS industrial sub-models.

33.0.1 Auxilliary Systems

33.0.1.1 Steam Generation
A number of industry process technologies generate steam as a by-product. CIMS accounts for steam generated by these technologies in the overall steam demand in each industry. Any shortage of steam must be met by boilers and cogenerators.
Boiler efficiency can vary greatly depending on boiler design, age, and fuel used. For modern oil and gas boilers, thermal (first law) efficiencies may be 85% or higher. Boiler efficiencies can be increased by introducing non-condensing and condensing heat recovery systems and by installing regenerative burners with computerized fuel/air mixtures to maximize fuel efficiency.
Cogeneration is the sequential production of electricity and useful thermal energy, usually as steam or shaft drive power. In cogeneration a boiler is used in conjunction with a turbine system to generate electricity, with the “waste" steam going to meet process steam requirements. In comparison to conventional electricity generation, cogeneration facilities are capable of conversion efficiencies of up to 85% (including both the steam and electricity produced) as compared to utility condensing turbine systems which have an efficiency in the 30% to 40% range.


33.0.1.2 Electric Auxiliary Systems
The vast majority of electricity consumed by industry is used by motor systems. A motor is the core component of a much broader system of electrical and mechanical equipment that provides services, including hydraulic power, compressed air, motive power, and air flow. Opportunities for efficiency improvement exist in both the motor itself, and in the latter systems – pumping, air displacement, compression, conveyance as well as other types of machine drive that are unique to a given production process (direct drive).
Figure 3.3 above is a generic energy flow model representing motor and steam auxiliary systems as they appear in the various CIMS industrial sub-models. As the figure indicates, CIMS simulates six auxiliary groups related to process drive (in red). The first five demand shaft or mechanical drive provided by the sixth group, motors (machine drive). Each group simulates technology evolution of a specific system.
Increased disaggregation in some of the groups reflects differing end-uses and levels of efficiency. For example, compressor systems vary in electrical efficiency by size. Therefore, competition between different technologies must be separated by size. The energy flow model reflects this by displaying two sizes of compressors, which are available for use by the model.
Pumping, air displacement, compressing, and conveyance systems have been represented as packages within CIMS. The components of each of these systems are associated with the key end-use. For example, a pipe, throttle, and speed control device is attached to a pump, and the entire package is called a pump system. In the model, there are at least two types of systems:

The least efficient system comprised of the least efficient components
The most efficient system comprised of the most efficient components

The system efficiency is then a function of the efficiency of all the components within that system. In some cases intermediate efficiencies have also been listed. New technologies may be added to reflect the intermediate range.
Electronic variable speed drives (VSDs) provide speed control by varying the rotating speed of the induction motor to match variable speed requirements of driven equipment. Pumps and fans, for example, are often required to deliver varying qualities of fluid flow. When this control procedure is used the energy consumption of the fan or pump is dramatically reduced during part load operation, as compared to the conventional practice of using a valve or d

title: 34  Low-Temperature Industrial Heat
text:
34.1 Scope and Definition
Low-temperature industrial process heat in CIMS is modeled as the steam, hot-water, and direct-heating services supplied at end-use temperatures below approximately 200 °C. Process heat is partitioned into three temperature bands — low (below 200 °C), medium (200–400 °C), and high (above 400 °C). The bands are defined by end-use temperature rather than by energy or equipment type, because the technology set admitted to the relevant service nodes differs substantially across them. The 200 °C boundary follows the convention adopted by the U.S. Department of Energy, Natural Resources Canada, and applied in the recent peer-reviewed techno-economic literature (e.g., Schoeneberger et al. 2020). Industrial heat globally accounts for approximately two-thirds of final industrial energy use and roughly one-fifth of energy-related CO2 emissions; analyses across IEA member countries place 30–45 % of industrial heat demand within the low-temperature band (International Energy Agency 2022, 2024; Madeddu et al. 2020).
The allocation of base-year low-temperature heat demand across sub-models on a provincial basis is the result of a calibration exercise bringing together information from Statistics Canada and Natural Resources Canada’s Comprehensive Energy Use Database (CEUD), Environment and Climate Change Canada’s National Inventory Report (NIR), and U.S. Energy Information Administration Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey (MECS) data used for analogous subsector benchmarks. The CEUD does not publish process heat disaggregated by temperature band; end-use accounting nevertheless indicates that conventional steam systems, boilers, and process heating account for the majority of fossil-fuel consumption in Canadian manufacturing (Natural Resources Canada 2024).

title: 34  Low-Temperature Industrial Heat
text:
34.2 Industrial Subsectors and End-Uses
Low-temperature heat demand is concentrated in a defined set of CIMS industrial sub-models — Pulp and Paper, Chemicals, Mining, Industrial Minerals, Metal Smelting, Iron and Steel, and Light Industrial (which aggregates food and beverage, textiles, wood, and prefabricated building products, and general light manufacturing). Each sub-model is calibrated independently for base-year energy consumption, and service demand is assumed to scale with industrial sectoral output projections in future years. The relative share of low-, medium-, and high-temperature heat within each subsector is assumed to remain constant in projection years. Subsectors and representative end-use temperature ranges relevant to the Canadian industrial mix are summarized in Table 34.1; note that food and beverage processing, textiles and laundry services, wood products, and light manufacturing and assembly are not standalone CIMS sub-models but are represented within the Light Industrial sub-model.

section: 34.3 Technologies for Low- and Zero-Emission Heat Supply
text:
34.3 Technologies for Low- and Zero-Emission Heat Supply
This section describes the low- and zero-emission supply technologies admitted to the low-temperature service nodes in the CIMS industrial sub-models, together with their assumed performance parameters and data sources. Technology efficiencies and coefficients of performance (COPs) used to parameterize the technology competitions are summarized in Table 34.2. Combustion boiler efficiencies are estimated based on data from MECS; heat pump COPs are based on inputs from IEA Heat Pumping Technologies Programme Annex 58 (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2021; IEA Heat Pumping Technologies Programme 2023).

Combustion boilers and electric resistance boilers are assumed to have a lifetime of 25 years; industrial heat pumps and mechanical vapour recompression units a lifetime of 15 years; and solar thermal collectors a lifetime of 20 years.

34.3.1 Industrial Heat Pumps
Closed-cycle vapour-compression heat pumps upgrade ambient or recovered low-grade heat to a useful end-use temperature. Commercially available products reach temperatures of approximately 165 °C; units operating at 200 °C with novel working fluids are at the demonstration stage (Arpagaus et al. 2018; Zühlsdorf et al. 2019). Mechanical vapour recompression, an open-cycle heat pump configuration applied to evaporators in dairy, sugar, and pulp operations, is the most mature variant and is represented as a distinct technology in the food and beverage and pulp and paper sub-models.


34.3.2 Direct Electrification
Electric resistance and electrode boilers deliver low-pressure steam at near-100% end-use efficiency at lower capital cost than heat pumps, and are represented as the simplest like-for-like replacement for packaged gas-fired boilers. Application is favoured in retrofit configurations where capital constraints favour low first-cost equipment (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2024). Direct-contact electric processes (induction, infrared, microwave, and dielectric heating) are commercially deployed for specific drying, curing, and surface-heating duties in the corresponding service nodes (Madeddu et al. 2020).


34.3.3 Solar Thermal
Flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors economically supply heat up to approximately 100 °C; linear concentrating systems (parabolic-trough and linear-Fresnel) extend the addressable range to 200 °C and beyond. Schoeneberger et al. (2020) estimate that approximately half of global industrial heat demand falls within the temperature window addressable by current commercial solar thermal technologies. Within Canada, solar resources are most favourable in the Prairie region and the southern interior of British Columbia; representation in CIMS uses capacity factors calibrated to regional direct normal irradiance (International Energy Agency 2024).


34.3.4 Bioenergy
Biomass-fired boilers, anaerobic-digestion biogas, and renewable natural gas from landfill and agricultural sources are admitted as drop-in low-carbon supply technologies in facilities configured around combustion equipment. Biomass is the dominant on-site thermal energy source in the Canadian pulp and paper sector and is also relevant in food processing operations co-located with feedstock supply (Natural Resources Canada, CanmetENERGY 2026). Outside the pulp and paper sector, deployed bioheat in Canada is concentrated at the 50 kW–5 MW thermal capacity range tracked by CanmetENERGY’s Canadian Bioheat Database; the 2023 survey update reports that more than 90 % of catalogued commercial, institutional, and small-industrial systems use either wood chips (approximately 45 %, dominant in institutional, agricultural, and light industrial installations) or wood pellets (approximately 46 %, dominant in institutional and commercial applications), with hog fuel and agricultural residues uncommon at this scale and concentrated in pulp and paper and adjacent forest-products operations (Natural Resources Canada, CanmetENERGY 2023). Regional fuel-type preferences are pronounced: wood chips dominate in Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia, and Nova Scotia, while pellets account for nearly all use in New Brunswick and the Northwest Territories, with lesser amounts in Quebec and BC. These distributional facts inform the technologies admitted to the bioenergy supply node feeding the Light Industrial sub-model, and the regional weighting applied to wood-chip versus pellet capital and operating cost assumptions. Sustainable supply is the binding constraint at the system level and is represented in CIMS through energy supply curves rather than at the device level.


34.3.5 Geoexchange and Recovered Waste Heat
Shallow enhanced geoexchange coupled with a heat pump is deployable across all provinces for facility heat. Independent of geoexchange extraction, every industrial site is itself a source of low-grade waste heat — compressors, condensers, flue gases, and effluents — that is conventionally rejected to the environment. National-laboratory analyses estimate that 20–50 % of industrial process heat could in principle be supplied via recovered waste heat (Thekdi and Nimbalkar 2014). Process integration and heat-pump-assisted recovery are represented in CIMS as a service-side reduction in the demand directed to other supply technologies, parameterized by sub-model based on recoverable-heat fractions reported in MECS and CanmetENERGY studies, rather than as a competing supply technology at the service node.


34.3.6 Thermal Energy Storage
Pressurized hot water, molten salt, and solid-media storage shift electrified heat loads to off-peak hours and extend solar thermal coverage to continuous-process duty cycles. Storage is treated in CIMS as a distinct technology that competes at the same service node as the heat-supply technologies it enables, with round-trip efficiency, capacity, and discharge-duration parameters drawn from IEA reference values (International Energy Agency 2022).


34.3.7 Hydrogen
Direct combustion of hydrogen below 200 °C is not competitive with electrification under most modelled conditions: round-trip energy efficiency from electricity to hydrogen to heat is substantially lower than direct electrification or heat-pumps, and the system value of hydrogen is concentrated in genuinely high-temperature or feedstock applications. Hydrogen is therefore not included in the default low-temperature technology set; it remains available in the broader CIMS technology library for the medium- and high-temperature sub-models (Thiel and Stark 2021; Rissman et al. 2020).

title: 34  Low-Temperature Industrial Heat
section: 34.4 Implications for the CIMS Industrial Sub-Models
text:
34.4 Implications for the CIMS Industrial Sub-Models
The technology competitions in the food and beverage, pulp, and paper, chemicals, mining, and light manufacturing sub-models admit, at the relevant service nodes, conventional natuarl gas and (where regionally relevant) heavy fuel oil boilers, used for calibration to CEUD and NIR baseline data; electric resistance and electrode boilers, parameterized by provincial industrial electricity rates; industrial heat pumps disaggregated by sink-temperature class (≤ 100 °C, 100–150 °C, 150–200 °C) with explicit COP and source-temperature assumptions drawn from IEA HPT Annex 58; mechanical vapour recompression where evaporation duties exist; biomass and biogas boilers, with energy availability governed by the bioenergy supply sub-model; and solar thermal in provincial sub-models, parameterized to regional irradiance (Natural Resources Canada 2024; Environment and Climate Change Canada 2024; IEA Heat Pumping Technologies Programme 2023; Natural Resources Canada, CanmetENERGY 2026; Schoeneberger et al. 2020).
Existing boiler stock, distinguished by sub-model and temperature class, is estimated based on CEUD and NIR base-year data. All existing boiler stock is assumed to stay online for modeled lifetimes past the base year, after which replacement is required. Policy or other drivers may drive earlier retirement and replacement of some of these existing units. Capital costs, retrofit feasibility (as defined in the technology chapter), and electricity-price sensitivity vary substantially across these technologies.

title: 35  Cogeneration
text:
35.1 Scope and Definition
Cogeneartion (also referred to as combined heat and power) is the sequential or simultaneous generation of multiple forms of useful energy (usually mechanical and thermal) in a single, integrated system. Cogeneartion systems consist of a number of individual components—prime mover (heat engine), generator, heat recovery, and electrical interconnection— configured into an integrated whole. The type of equipment that drives the overall system (i.e., the prime mover) typically identifies the cogeneartion system. Prime movers for cogeneartion systems include steam turbines, gas turbines (also called combustion turbines), spark ignition engines, diesel engines, microturbines, and fuel cells. These prime movers are capable of burning a variety of fuels, including biomass/biogas, natural gas, or coal to produce shaft power or mechanical energy. Additional technologies are also used in configuring a complete cogeneartion system, including boilers, absorption chillers, desiccants, engine-driven chillers, and gasifiers. Boilers and gasifiers are discussed in Chapter 5 of this document. (U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and Partnership (2007))
Although mechanical energy from the prime mover is most often used to drive a generator to produce electricity, it can also be used to drive rotating equipment such as compressors, pumps, and fans. Thermal energy from the system can be used in direct process applications or indirectly to produce steam, hot water, hot air for drying, or chilled water for process cooling.
The industrial sector currently produces both thermal output and electricity from biomass in CHP facilities in the paper, chemical, wood products, and food processing industries. These industries are major users of biomass fuels—utilizing the heat and steam in their processes can improve energy efficiencies by more than 35 percent. In these applications, the typical CHP system configuration consists of a biomass-fired boiler whose steam is used to propel a steam turbine in addition to the extraction of steam or heat for process use.

title: 39  Data Processing
text:
39.1 Overview
The data processing step transforms data into model input files and calibration files for the CIMS energy-economy model. Raw data is never committed to this repository — only scripts, mappings, and this documentation are tracked. Raw data is stored on the External-CIMS sharepoint. Model input files are used to build the model with information like sectors, activity levels, services, technologies, model parameters, and fuel prices. Calibration files include the historical demand, emissions, and technology shares publicly available. During the calibration step, the user will attempt to match market shares, energy demand, and emissions in the model from 2000-last historical year to the calibration data. This step will help determine intangible costs and trends, and will be a vetted starting point from which the projection begins.
Step 1 - Assemble Raw Data (data/raw_data/): Raw data from various sources is gathered and placed in the External-CIMS sharepoint. Source data is documented in the source_detail.xlsx in data/raw_data/. The last historical year for the raw data is input into the control file data/mappings_conversions/control.py. This data is different by source and important to update as scripts will call on this year to begin projection assumptions in the following year. Any other important control information, such as which scenario to draw from the data, and currency country/years is also input into this control file.
Step 2 — Source processing (data/pipeline/source/): Each script takes in raw data, manipulates it, and writes a CSV to data/processed_data/ for user vetting. The data is often yearly, from 2000-2100, and covers all Canadian regions, depending on the data type. The processed_data csvs are not used elsewhere in the pipeline. The functions and data frames in the source processing scripts are called for the next step - sector assembly.
Step 3 — Sector assembly (data/pipeline/sector/): Each sector’s model_inputs script combines fixed structural parameters (data/raw_data/fixed_data/) with one or more processed data frames and writes final CIMS model input files to model_inputs/model/{sector}/. Each sector’s calibration script combines processed historical energy demand, emissions, and technology market shares and writes final CIMS calibration files to calibration/{sector}/.
